articles.title: Queen Sara? Prosec eyes Duterte as ‘pawns’ don’t know how CF was used
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Counsel for the prosecution Lorna Kapunan has likened Vice President Sara Duterte to a queen in a chess board. The lawyer thinks the reason why the prosecution will eventually…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Counsel for the prosecution Lorna Kapunan has likened Vice President Sara Duterte to a queen in a chess board.

The lawyer thinks the reason why the prosecution will eventually focus on the vice president is because pawns and the other pieces in the board game have not been able to explain how confidential funds (CF) have been used.
In her manifestation during Duterte’s impeachment trial on Tuesday, Kapunan compared the CF use of Duterte’s offices to a chess game where the queen appears to be the most important piece.
She explained that this is because the vice president can make different kinds of movements across the board.

Similarly, Kapunan said that they are going after Duterte since the personnel called from her offices as witnesses seemed to be like other chess pieces — pawns, bishops, knights and rooks — who always rely on the queen.
“In the game chess, we have what we call pawns. There are bishops. There’s a castle. There are horses,” the counsel enumerated.

“And the most important piece, more important than the king — and I speak this because not of my gender, but the queen is more important than the king, because the queen can move in many directions, and we have seen that,” she pointed out.

“We have seen that in the evidence presented, the pawns […] – the witnesses presented here – from the LandBank, we have been able to show that withdrawal – that there were confidential funds and these were withdrawn from two witnesses,” she noted.
“All of these pawns and castles and horses and bishops point to only one person, and that accountable person is the vice president,” Kapunan concluded.

Later on, the prosecution said that it will no longer be presenting other witnesses for Article I, or the allegation of CF misuse within Duterte’s offices, as the team will just ask Duterte later on to answer allegations raised against her.

However, when asked by Presiding Officer and Senator-judge Francis Escudero if the prosecution will seek a subpoena for Duterte, Kapunan said they will not yet ask for one, and will reserve the right to summon the vice president later on.

“We will be resting on this article, Your Honor, with the reservation of calling two possible witnesses, two possible witnesses at the end, Your Honor – the vice president herself and, perhaps, an amicus curiae to aid this honorable court on understanding the intent of the drafters of the Constitution on Articles of Impeachment on public officers, and public accountability,” she explained.

“The testimony of the vice president will be material to all four articles – the article on grave threats, Article IV; Article I on misuse and misappropriation of confidential funds; Article II on unexplained wealth; and Article III on bribery,” Kapunan identified.

“And that is why, at the end of all of these articles, we reserve the right to present the vice president herself,” Kapunan repeated. “But this will be done at the end of the presentation of the four articles.”

“And to summarize, there will be no more hearings, Your Honor. Trials on Article I, misuse and misappropriation of confidential funds. And lastly, I would like to thank all the subpoenaed witnesses for today who brave the rains and are here,” she added.
With this, Escudero advised the prosecution not to rest its case yet with regards to Article I, so that it can include Duterte’s possible testimonies as part of its evidence.
A total of twelve witnesses have been presented by the prosecution panel for Article I:

items: Land Bank of the Philippines (LandBank) department manager Violeta Constantino
LandBank department manager Nenita Camposano
State auditor Roderick Wamil
State auditor Xylene Mae del Campo
House Legislative Information Resources Management Director Marivic Pareja
Former Office of the Vice President (OVP) special disbursing officer (SDO) Gina Acosta
Army Col. Maranos Boransing II
Army Col. Magtanggol Panopio
OVP Assistant Secretary Lemuel Ortonio
Former Department of Education (DepEd) Undersecretary Michael Poa
Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) Assistant National Statistician Marizza Grande
Former DepEd SDO Edward Fajarda (stipulated)

blocks.text: Constantino and Camposano testified on the withdrawal of CF allocated to OVP from the fourth quarter of 2022 to the third quarter of 2023, and to DepEd for the first three quarters of 2023.
Wamil and del Campo, meanwhile, testified as the Commission on Audit – Intelligence and Confidential Funds Audit Office (ICFAO) auditors who checked on OVP and DepEd’s confidential expenditures.
Grande was called to ascertain the identity of the weird names who signed acknowledgement reports (ARs) for CF payments made by both OVP and DepEd, like the infamous Mary Grace Piattos.
The other witnesses, meanwhile, were asked about OVP and DepEd’s operations and procedures on confidential expenses.

For one, Acosta was asked to testify on where the CF for OVP went — to which she said that Duterte ordered her to hand the funds to Col. Raymund Dante Lachica, former head of the Vice Presidential Security and Protection Group (VPSPG).
Ortonio was asked the same thing.
Poa, on the other hand, was quizzed regarding the CF utilization by the DepEd, and the decision of Fajarda to hand over the funds to former VPSPG deputy chief Col. Dennis Nolasco.
Despite their different roles, all three admitted that it is Duterte, along with Lachica for OVP and Nolasco for DepEd, who knew how the secret funds were spent.

The prosecution has finished presenting evidence and witnesses for Article IV or the allegation that Duterte betrayed public trust when she threatened President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Marcos, and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez.
Previously, lead public prosecutor and Batangas Rep. Gerville Luistro said they intend to wrap up discussions for Article I by Wednesday, September 9.
But with the development, there will be no trial on Wednesday, with the day being devoted instead to the marking of additional evidence.
With the prosecution wrapping up, for now, Article I, the panel is expected to proceed to Article II or Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth by Monday, September 14. /apl

articles.title: Dole: NCR wage board awaiting NWPC’s decision on new increase order
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — A new wage increase order from the Regional Tripartite Wages and Productivity Board (RTWPB) in Metro Manila is just awaiting a decision from the National Wages and Productivity…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — A new wage increase order from the Regional Tripartite Wages and Productivity Board (RTWPB) in Metro Manila is just awaiting a decision from the National Wages and Productivity Commission (NWPC), the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) said on Tuesday.

At the hearing of the House of Representatives’ committee on appropriations regarding DOLE’s proposed budget for 2027, the department’s National Capital Region Regional Director Roy Buenaflor said that the RTWPB approved Wage Order No. 28 in Metro Manila on Monday night.
Under the rules, the NWPC is mandated to determine minimum wages at the regional, provincial, or industry levels while the RTWPB is under the NWPC.
“Ang Wage Order 28 na napagdesiyunan ng board last night ay sa kasalukuyan ay we already forwarded it to NWPC for another process in the commission,” Buenaflor said.
(The Wage Order 28 decided by the board last night is already forwarded to the NWPC for another process in the commission.)
“This is a one-time tranche of P60 and if ever the commission will affirm such wage order, perhaps we could publish this on Friday. The effectivity will be on September 26 or 27,” Buenaflor added.
When granted, he noted that this will bring the daily minimum wage of Metro Manila workers in the non-agriculture sector up from P695 to P755.

He also shared that the regional board arrived at a 4-3 voting during its deliberation on Monday, where three members from the government sector and one employer voted in the affirmative while two representatives of the labor sector and another employer dissented from it.

However, this announcement raised eyebrows among lawmakers present at the hearing, with Deputy Speaker and TUCP party-list Rep. Raymond Mendoza asking Buenaflor of the basis of the new wage board order, noting that the implementation of Wage Board No. 27 remains pending due to a Pasig City court’s order suspending its implementation.

Buenaflor said that the board came up with a decision to issue another wage increase order as “it is the best way that we can deliver immediately what has been waited by the workers which is the first tranche of the Wage Order 27.”
Mendoza then said that they are not satisfied with the answer, worrying that it might further complicate matters.

Last June 30, Labor Secretary Francis Tolentino announced the “historic” wage hike of P85 for minimum wage workers in Metro Manila under Wage Order No. 27, where the first tranche of P65 was supposed to be effective last July 25 while the second tranche of P20 was due on January 20 next year.

However, the Pasig City Regional Trial Court Branch 125 issued a temporary restraining order (TRO) on the implementation of the P85 wage increase in the region until August 13 following a petition filed by two construction companies. The wage increase implementation was further delayed as the court granted the writ of preliminary injunction sought by the two firms.
The Office of Solicitor General has asked the Pasig court to resolve its pending motion for reconsideration to lift the freeze order that halted the implementation of the P85 wage hike.
‘Wage decrease’

Kamanggagawa Party-list Rep. Elijah San Fernando also expressed his disappointment on the announcement of a new wage order, saying that the proposed P60 wage hike is a “wage decrease” to the Wage Order 27, which was supposed to grant a P85 daily wage hike.

“Dito sa Wage Order No. 28, P60 na lang ang dagdag sahod ng manggagawa. So in effect, wage decrease ito kasi ongoing pa yung usapin sa Wage Order No. 27,” San Fernando told reporters in an ambush interview.
(Here in Wage Order No. 28, the wage increase is just P60. So in effect, this is a wage decrease because the matters for Wage Order No. 27 is currently ongoing.)

San Fernando agreed that DOLE and the RTWPB further complicated themselves by issuing a new wage order while the Wage Order No. 27 is still pending, as it will raise a question on what would happen if another TRO is released.
“Malinaw ito na sa katotohanan lang, ayaw i-implement ng mismong DOLE yung dagdag sahod na P85 which is ang first tranche dapat ibinigay na noong July 25,” he added.
(This is clear that the DOLE does not want to implement the wage increase of P85 which the first tranche was supposed to be given last July 25.)

San Fernando maintained that DOLE can now implement the wage hike under the Wage Order No. 27 as the petitioner companies could not pay their bond worth P10 billion, which he said renders the writ of preliminary injunction ineffective.
During the budget hearing, Labor Secretary Francis Tolentino asserted that the court must decide the fate of the implementation of the wage increase, and not the agency. /mr

articles.title: Councils pay more than £125m a year placing vulnerable children in illegal care homes in England
articles.summary: Exclusive: Booming industry of businesses profit from shortage of beds for most at-risk children

blocks.text: Councils are paying more than £125m a year of taxpayers’ money to place vulnerable children in illegal care homes across England, an investigation has found.

The Guardian and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism (TBIJ) have uncovered a booming industry of businesses profiting from a shortage of beds for the most at-risk children in Ofsted-inspected homes.
Local authority payment records show that more than 480 private companies have been paid £250m for 1,800 unlawful placements of children over the past two years.
Even though it is a criminal offence to operate a children’s home that is not registered with Ofsted, almost every council in the country uses illegal care facilities.

Regulators have appeared reluctant to shut down illegal settings because councils say they have nowhere else to send traumatised, older children, whose behaviour often poses a risk to themselves or others. But growing concerns about criminal activity and safeguarding failings have led to a tougher stance, with Ofsted securing its first conviction last month.

The previously unseen dataset, obtained under freedom of information laws, identifies the companies dominating the illegal market. It shows more than £40m of public money has been paid to operators linked to care failures, including those involved in the care of a teenage girl harmed in a succession of illegal placements in hotels, Airbnbs and other properties.
Some of the children require around-the-clock supervision, with several carers, which can push up the price demanded by providers. At least nine councils paid more than £1m for a single placement.

Average earnings of more than £150,000 per placement have attracted entrepreneurs from outside the care sector. Analysis of the payment records shows property developers, builders and security company bosses, as well as musicians and ex-military personnel, are now running illegal homes.

Rachel de Souza, the children’s commissioner for England, said the findings revealed systemic failings. She said: “For too long, illegal children’s homes have been allowed to operate in the shadows, where children are treated as a business opportunity, and huge amounts of public money are spent on placements that are not properly registered or inspected.”
The market leader

The largest player in the illegal care market is Prospero Health and Social Care. The London-based nursing agency has been involved in staffing more unregistered provision than any other provider in England.

Over the past two years, the company was paid £7.6m by 14 councils for staffing 86 placements in unregistered children’s homes. It has openly advertised for child support workers for “unregistered settings” in England and Wales.

Prospero said it supplied staff but did not operate unregistered care homes. In a statement, it said: “Responsibility for placement decisions, assessment, care planning, care, supervision and control remains with the local authority responsible for the child.”

The company added that its job adverts referred to a “range of council-arranged environments in which staff might be asked to work” and were not intended to give the impression that Prospero was responsible for illegal accommodation.

However, Ofsted says agencies could be responsible for managing the home if their staff were on site day-to-day without council personnel present. Local authorities may also be liable if they book or rent unregistered accommodation where a child is living. The watchdog insists it has the power to prosecute anyone running an unregistered home, whether they come from an agency or not.

Prospero Health and Social Care has 11 offices in the UK as well as operations in Australia and New Zealand. Prospero Group’s accounts, which cover a range of recruitment sectors as well as social care, show owners Robert and Lesley Grays received more than £4m in dividends in the past two financial years.
Seven of the 14 English councils to have paid Prospero for staffing illegal placements told us they had received safeguarding complaints about its care workers.

In total, there were 44 allegations that staff had harmed or posed a risk to children between January 2024 and April 2026. Sixteen were upheld, four were deemed to be unfounded, and the outcomes of the others are either unknown or pending.

Prospero said it referred safeguarding concerns about its staff, who were subject to enhanced criminal record checks, to safeguarding authorities. It said an upheld concern was not, in and of itself, a finding that a young person had been harmed. It added that no local authority had suspended or ended its relationship with Prospero as a result of any safeguarding matter.

The company said the £7.6m represented revenue for staffing services, rather than placement fees or profits. It said most of the money paid to shareholders did not come from local authority staffing work.
A new crackdown

Unregistered care has expanded rapidly in recent years, with Ofsted identifying 710 illegal homes this year, up from 144 in 2020. One in 10 children in care are now thought to live in illegal premises at any given time.

Most unlawful operators have previously only received warning letters, but recent scandals have provoked a rethink. In July, Ofsted announced a crackdown after TBIJ exposed one of the worst safeguarding failures so far in unregulated care. A 15-year-old girl was abused by two ex-soldiers with criminal records in an illegal home in Durham. The then education secretary, Bridget Phillipson, described the case as “unspeakable evil” and pledged to end the use of illegal homes.

Last month, Ofsted secured its first-ever conviction, with Catalyst Care Ltd fined £92,000 for operating three unregistered homes in Kent. Catalyst received more than £1.7m from local authorities for operating illegal homes between 2022 and 2025, according to Ofsted.
The company’s directors – who include Davidson Lynch-Shyllon, a songwriter and music producer who has played at Glastonbury – are now banned from holding a financial interest in children’s homes.

Ofsted has also highlighted growing criminal activity in the sector. In August, TBIJ reported that Merseyside-based unregistered children’s homes operator SafeSpace4U had links to organised crime. The firm’s headquarters are owned by a convicted drug dealer, John McDonough, who has a child with the owner of SafeSpace4U, Sian O’Neill. She insists McDonough is not involved in the running of the company.

The dataset reveals that SafeSpace4U has been used by at least seven councils, which puts it in the top 2% of illegal operators in the country. It is being criminally investigated for operating homes without registration by Ofsted.
The holiday loophole

Some of the largest illegal providers use a loophole in care regulations, which allows looked-after children to spend 28 days on holiday in unregistered facilities. But Ofsted says firms are misusing the rule to operate illegally, to accommodate children on a long-term basis without a permanent legal placement elsewhere.
The Guardian has identified at least 11 companies offering 28-day breaks. Six are among the most prolific unregistered operators in the country.

The victim of the abuse in the Durham case was on a 28-day activity placement with Map Adventures, which has been used by three councils, according to the dataset. The girl stayed with the company, which has now gone into liquidation, longer than the 28 days allowed by law.

Another crisis break provider, Creative Outdoor Group (Cog), exceeded the legal limit with nearly half of its 29 placements. A former care worker claimed a boy lived in a tent on a farm for four months in 2022, a claim that is disputed by the company.

“They had a young boy from Cornwall … for well over 100 days … he lived in a tent,” said the carer. “The [only] facilities were a little gas cooker, and we had to walk up to the local shop every day.”

The company’s owner, Rob Hutchinson, said the boy chose to camp for several nights during the week, spending other nights in the house where he lived. “This person chose to receive his respite care in Cog so that he could camp for some of the time he was at Cog,” he said.

Hutchinson said Cog provided emergency 28-day respite care, with young people’s permanent addresses elsewhere. He added that young people placed with Cog lived in rented housing not on the farm where he lives. They occasionally stayed with Cog for longer periods of time if they were judged to be doing well, he said. Hutchinson said Ofsted would not register the company as it provided respite care and psychological therapy.
But Ofsted said many registered children’s homes provided these types of support.

Merseyside-based Servizi Care Services has published testimonials showing it has accommodated at least two children under “deprivation of liberty” orders – court orders restricting a person’s freedom. Ofsted believes any child subject to these orders should be in registered accommodation. A man answering Servizi’s phone said he “was not interested in speaking”. The company did not reply to emails.

The bills for some illegal placements can run into large sums. Thurrock council paid DMC Consulting Services £2.7m for two children in a two-year illegal placement. The council said it carried out rigorous quality checks of unregistered homes, which were visited regularly.

The owner of DMC, Tawanda Mudavanhu, has 28 other current and past company appointments, including for wholesale, property management, consultancy, renting cars, and electricity trade companies. Mudavanhu said: “I do not wish to comment on Thurrock council’s business.”

articles.title: FACT CHECK: No nationwide Facebook ban set to take effect on September 10
articles.summary: Malacañang has said there is no ban for now; the DICT earlier called the proposed move a ‘last resort’ amid concerns over possible harmful content online

blocks.text: Claim: A nationwide Facebook ban will begin on September 10, with violators set to face penalties.

Why we fact-checked this: Several videos containing the claim have been circulating on Facebook, Messenger, and TikTok as early as September 7. The most popular one has gained 9,600 reactions, 2,400 comments, and 14,700 shares as of writing.
The caption on one video reads: “Breaking news: September 10 start na Facebook ban na sa Pinas. Meron na penalty.”
(Breaking news: Facebook ban in the Philippines starts September 10. There is already a penalty.)

Text overlaid on the video reads, “Facebook ban na sa Pinas” (Facebook banned in the Philippines). The videos show a man delivering the alleged news, claiming that violators face fines and imprisonment of up to 10 years.
Some videos also include a link to a supposedly full version of the announcement.

The facts: There is no official government announcement confirming a nationwide ban starting September 10 or any penalty for Facebook use in the Philippines. No credible media outlet has reported about this supposed ban or penalty scheme either.

Officials from the Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (CICC) and the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) had previously raised the possibility of blocking the platform over child safety concerns following the Zamboanga school shooting.

Malacañang said the government is not banning Facebook, but is open to proposals to ban platforms found to be harmful to the youth. During an August 25 press briefing, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said officials needed to assess whether social media was fueling violence and fake news after the Ateneo de Zamboanga shooting.

On August 28, the Palace clarified that there is no move to block Facebook, saying that the platform has been cooperative in addressing the government’s concerns about disinformation and the rising cases of school violence. Meta has also pledged that it would share data over imminent threats with Philippine authorities.

AI-generated video, unrelated links: Several AI detection tools flagged the video as AI-generated. Hive Moderation results show it was 99.9% likely to contain AI-generated content, while Uncovai rated it 100% AI-generated and BitMind.ai rated it 89% AI-generated.

Meanwhile, link scanner urlscan.io found that the link included in the captions of some of the videos leads to an unrelated shopping site. Interacting with suspicious links can expose users to security risks, such as phishing scams. (READ: Phishing 101: How to spot and avoid phishing)

School violence linked to online extremism: The push to consider restricting Facebook followed the August 18 shooting at Ateneo de Zamboanga University. The incident resulted in the deaths of two people, including the shooter, who was a minor described by local officials as a “Roblox fanatic.” Roblox is a popular gaming platform where chat groups have been used to radicalize and groom minors, according to officials.

The shooting was livestreamed on Facebook, with the video staying up for around 14 minutes before being taken down. Senator Risa Hontiveros criticized Meta for this and warned of the broader threat of nihilistic violent extremism in a Senate hearing on August 20.
Debunked: Rappler has previously debunked similar false claims about a supposed Facebook ban, as well as other AI-generated videos falsely claiming a government ban or restriction:

items: FALSE: Grace Poe to file bill blocking Facebook in light of ABS-CBN shutdown
FACT CHECK: No ban on cellphone use starting April 15; video is AI-generated
FACT CHECK: No ban on consumption of processed meats; video is AI-generated
FACT CHECK: ‘News report’ about ‘angkas’ ban is false
FACT CHECK: Christmas parties in schools not banned – DepEd

blocks.text: – James Bones/Rappler.com
James Bones is a Research and Data volunteer at Rappler. He is a fourth-year Bachelor of Science in Industrial Engineering student at the Polytechnic University of the Philippines – Manila.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

articles.title: Physical bullying declines among PH learners; digital distractions, cyberbullying remain concerns -- study
articles.summary: Reports of physical bullying among Filipino learners declined substantially in the last seven years but cyberbullying and digital distractions as continuing challenges in schools, according to the…

blocks.text: Published September 8, 2026 4:53pm

Reports of physical bullying among Filipino learners declined substantially in the last seven years but cyberbullying and digital distractions as continuing challenges in schools, according to the 2025 Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA).
The Department of Education’s presentation of the PISA 2025 results showed a decrease in some forms of bullying between 2018 and 2025.
Reports of students being made fun of by schoolmates declined by 17 percentage points, while reports of students being hit or pushed is lower by 17 points.
Meanwhile, reports of students who feel threatened declined by 16 percentage points, while reports of students as subjects of nasty rumors fell by 13 points.
DepEd said the decline was encouraging, but bullying has not disappeared.
But the department said the reduction in traditional forms of bullying must be accompanied by attention to the digital environment, where cyberbullying remains a concern.

The PISA presentation noted that cyberbullying is a particular concern, with 14% of Filipino learners reporting that they had seen online false reports about them that are potentially harmful to their reputation.
DepEd said schools have to consider learner safety not only in the physical school environment but also online.
“The response is not simply to reject technology. The issue is ensuring that technology is used purposefully for learning.”
3 in 4 report digital distraction
Digital-device use also emerged as a classroom concern.
About 75% of Filipino learners said their peers are often distracted by digital devices during at least some Science classes.
More than 80% of Filipino learners attended schools with policies governing digital-device use, but DepEd said the challenge is making those policies effective inside actual classrooms.
The findings come as DepEd is also strengthening school-based learner support and child-protection mechanisms. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Thieves steal 3 paintings from Renoir Museum on French Riviera
articles.summary: Thieves stole three paintings from the Renoir Museum on the French Riviera early on Tuesday, the local mayor said.

image.caption: The collection on display in the Renoir museum includes 13 paintings from the master and some 40 sculptures, furniture and photographs. (Valery Hache/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New
Thieves stole three paintings from the Renoir Museum on the French Riviera early on Tuesday, the local mayor said.
One painting was dropped during police chase
The raiders broke into the museum a little before 6 a.m. local time and took four paintings, Cagnes-sur-Mer mayor Bryan Masson said on his Facebook page.
Police spotted the thieves and chased them, during which they dropped one painting but escaped with the other three, he said.
"Attacking the Renoir museum is attacking a part of the history and heritage of Cagnes-sur-Mer. These actions are particularly serious," Masson said in his message.

items: Thieves in balaclavas, on motorbikes steal crown jewels in Louvre heist

blocks.text: The museum was created in 1960 in the mansion of the impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir on a hill in Cagnes-sur-Mer, near Nice, where he died in 1919.
The collection on display in the museum includes 13 paintings from the master and some 40 sculptures, furniture and photographs.
Theft follows 2025 Louvre heist
Masson did not identify the paintings that were stolen. Renoir's most valuable works have fetched dozens of millions of dollars at auctions in the past.

Art thieves in Europe are committing more violent robberies and specialist gangs have been replaced by ad hoc ​opportunists recruited through social media, pan-European police body Europol said last month.

The heist at ‌the Louvre Museum in Paris in October last year was a prime example of this, Europol said, as the thieves threatened guards and visitors and stole €88 million ($141.5 million) worth of jewels, such ​as Empress Eugenie's tiara.

articles.title: Russian drone and missile strikes on Kyiv kill 2, ending pause in attacks
articles.summary: Russia pummelled Kyiv with drones and missiles early on Tuesday, resuming its air attacks after a brief halt for the visit of U.S. peace negotiators, killing two people and triggering fires across…

image.caption: A Russian drone and missile attack damaged at least 14 highrise buildings, a dorm, a school, a clinic, warehouses and other sites, officials said. (Alina Smutko/Reuterse)

blocks.text: World·New

Russia pummelled Kyiv with drones and missiles early on Tuesday, resuming its air attacks after a brief halt for the visit of U.S. peace negotiators, killing two people and triggering fires across the Ukrainian capital.
Russia resumes strikes after U.S. peace envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff leave Kyiv
Mayor Vitali Klitschko said 10 more had been injured in the city, while falling debris in one district caused fires at a five-storey apartment building and a three-storey residential block.
The attack damaged at least 14 highrise buildings, a dorm, a school, a clinic, warehouses and other sites, officials said.

Russia resumed its attacks after U.S. peace envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff left Kyiv following a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday, as the Trump administration renewed its push to end Russia's 4-1/2-year war in Ukraine.
They arrived from talks in Moscow, after which the Kremlin said it did not rule out the resumption of the three-way negotiations.
"The moment the U.S. president's peace envoys left, (Russian President Vladimir) Putin launched another massive, horrific attack against Kyiv," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on X.

"His ballistic missiles speak louder than his words on diplomacy," Sybiha said, urging allies to ramp up pressure on Moscow, as well as to provide interceptors to down ballistic missiles, since Kyiv's stocks of these run critically low.

Kyiv resident Iryna Barisenkova, 61, said she heard explosions while travelling on public transport and was told there was a large fire near the Darnytskyi Vehicle Repair Plant, or DVRZ, area on the capital's left bank.
"Everything was thundering on the left bank," Barisenkova said. "It was just brutal."

items: Russian air attacks kill 12 in Kyiv region on 6th day of strikes
U.S. officials optimistic after Kyiv trip

blocks.text: Prior to the talks, Russia stepped up air attacks on Kyiv and nearby areas to nearly round-the-clock for several days, rather than mainly at night, using faster jet-propelled drones that killed residents and disrupted activities.
The Russian defence ministry said Moscow hit military and logistic targets in Kyiv and the surrounding region, as well as in the Black Sea port of Chornomorsk, Russian newswires said.
U.S. officials optimistic after Kyiv trip
Poland activates aircraft
Amid explosions heard in Kyiv, neighbouring Poland, a NATO and European Union member, launched preventive operations against Russian missile attacks on Ukraine, the Polish army said.
Poland's Lublin airport has temporarily suspended flights because of the military operations.
In Russia, Ukrainian drones damaged civilian infrastructure and injured people in the Volga river city of Saratov, some 730 kilometres southeast of Moscow, the regional governor said.
The area is home to a large oil refinery run by state oil company Rosneft, as well as other industrial and military facilities.

Meanwhile, two people ‌were killed and ​one ​wounded ⁠in ⁠a ‌Ukrainian attack on ⁠the Crimean peninsula, which ‌was annexed by Russia ​in ⁠2014, ⁠Sergei ⁠Aksyonov, the ⁠Moscow-appointed ​regional governor, ​said.

articles.title: Australia to force social media platforms to allow users to opt out of algorithms
articles.summary:
Draft legislation enforces digital duty of care including limiting children’s exposure to misogynistic and eating disorder content

Australia will allow social media account holders to opt…

blocks.text: Australia will allow social media account holders to opt out of the powerful algorithms pushing dangerous and divisive content into users’ feeds, part of new laws designed to boost online safety.
Users over 16 years of age will be given new tools to turn off algorithm-driven content, with platforms facing fines of more than A$100m for non-compliance.
Under the plan – dubbed “my feed, my way” – users opting out of the algorithm will see content only from individuals and groups they have actively chosen to follow.
Users would be asked what they want their default feed to be through a pop-up message provided on their platform of choice.
New laws designed to provide a digital duty of care for social media users under 18 will also require services such as online games, apps and AI chatbots to protect children from specific harms.

They will include pornography; content that promotes, encourages or accelerates eating disorders; misogynistic content; content that glorifies crime or life-endangering stunts; and content that causes serious mental health distress, including abuse and bullying.
The regulator, the eSafety commissioner, will have the power to issue removal notices to social media companies, with platform operators required to document measures taken to address online harms.
The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, is expected to highlight the plans at the United Nations general assembly in New York later this month.
“This is not about giving government control, it is about giving people control,” he said.
Albanese dismissed concerns of possible retaliation by big tech platforms, and their owners, many of whom have close relationships with the US president, Donald Trump.

The Labor government will require the support of the Greens to advance the laws through parliament. The opposition Liberals and Nationals have flagged opposition, warning the government against efforts to censor the internet.
“Of course there will be opponents, because what this is about is changing the power relationship,” Albanese said.
“We’re taking power from big global tech companies and giving it to ordinary Australians. That is what we are doing. It’s the right thing to do.”
The communications minister, Anika Wells, said tech companies had for too long been allowed to run real-time, unregulated product testing on Australian users.
“There is a global reckoning coming for big tech,” she said. “And it started here in Australia, with the introduction of our world-leading social media minimum age laws.”
The legislation is expected to be introduced to parliament before Christmas, but will likely face a lengthy public inquiry and negotiations.

blocks.caption: Australia’s digital duty of care bill a ‘global reckoning for big tech’, minister says – video

blocks.text: The Greens communications spokesperson, Sarah Hanson-Young, warned the draft legislation should have a lower threshold for harm, and penalties for platforms should be a percentage of their global revenue.
“Opt out is not acceptable,” she said.

“Opt out is a recipe for big tech to manipulate and to get around it. They’ve got a lot of money, and we know that big tech will be looking for every crack, every possible workaround. So we need to tighten this up and make sure it is watertight.”
The Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, said Labor could not be trusted with “censorship powers”.
“Rather than trying to rig the algorithm, the government should focus on fixing the problems of too high prices, too much tax and too much migration.”
A spokesperson for DIGI, the lobby group representing tech companies including Meta, Snapchat and Google, defended algorithms as helpful to users seeking diverse content.
“We also recognise there is community concern about how these systems work and DIGI welcomes the discussion on the role of recommender systems in online safety,” they said.
“We support an approach that gives people meaningful choice and control over the content they see, while managing safety risks.”
Campaigner Chanel Contos, founder of Teach Us Consent, called the draft laws a good first step by the government.
“This reform sends the right message to Big Tech,” she said. “You cannot introduce harmful features into our digital lives without asking for our consent first.”

Tom Mooney, campaign director for Democracy Counts, an alliance of organisations concerned about the function of democratic institutions in Australia, said common facts and diversity of opinion was essential.

“Social media is where the majority of Australians get their news, where many people spend hours each day,” he said. “It is common sense to require platforms to give users choice over those experiences.”

Countries including France, Britain and New Zealand are following Australia in implementing social media bans for children, even as expert research showed the systems put in place in Australia in December is only partly effective.

articles.title: Nepal cracks down on online abuse against flood survivors
articles.summary: Authorities will "show no leniency" to people who "belittle" those who are suffering, the prime minister says.

blocks.text: Nepal is cracking down on online abuse directed at survivors of last month's deadly floods, with Prime Minister Balendra Shah warning that authorities will "show no leniency" to people who "belittle" those who are suffering.
Some have taken to social media to appeal for information about their loved ones and to urge officials to step up search efforts, only to be hit by hostile comments.
"People who make unnecessary remarks, belittle those in pain or seek to cause them further suffering at this sensitive time are criminals," Shah wrote in a Facebook post.
Nepali police say they are looking into where these comments have originated from to identify addresses and phone numbers.
A woman, whose brother has been missing since the floods hit two weeks ago, had earlier told the BBC that search and rescue operations were too slow.
"If the government had mobilised experts and equipment for rescue in time, would we have known the condition of our family members sooner?
"We still hope we can find him alive."
Days later, she wrote back saying she had "received many nasty comments" in response to her criticism of the search efforts.
"We are already suffering so much and this has only added to our pain," she said.
In a separate case, a young woman had expressed her anger at what she perceived as authorities' "lack of urgency" in searching for her husband.
"My husband is missing now, if the government cannot find him, can it at least show me his body?" she said in a video clip that has gone viral online – and attracted its fair share of insults.
One comment, for instance, urged her to "jump into the river" and help with the search, while another read, "not everything happens just by you putting the blame on the government".
But others have called out the insensitive remarks. "The victim should be consoled at this time, not cursed," one of them read.
Nepali police say they have convened a 10-member committee to look into these online comments.
Under the country's Electronic Transactions Act, those who use social media to defame or harass others could be jailed for up to five years and fined up to 100,000 rupees ($662; £490), or both.

Dovan Rai, the executive director of Body & Data, a Nepal-based non-profit organisation that advocates for a safe digital space, says some of the insensitive comments could have come from social media users who engage in "rage baiting" – that is, those who produce negative content as a "bait" to trigger outrage, or force people to click on or share their posts.
They could also have come from "staunch supporters of the government".
"There is also extremism that is very sympathetic to the government and condemns those who question it. That has further polarized the dialogue on social media," she told the BBC.

articles.title: Ex-BFP chief pleads not guilty to graft over alleged P10-M bribe
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Former Bureau of Fire Protection (BFP) chief Jesus Fernandez on Tuesday pleaded not guilty in one of the two graft cases against him pending before the Sandiganbayan. According…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Former Bureau of Fire Protection (BFP) chief Jesus Fernandez on Tuesday pleaded not guilty in one of the two graft cases against him pending before the Sandiganbayan.

According to prosecutors, the two counts each of graft and indirect bribery cases against Fernandez and Rosaverna Sangga stemmed from the P14.752-million bribe that the official allegedly received, in connection with the BFP’s procurement of 132 ambulances worth P485 million in 2025.
The money was allegedly delivered on two occasions, with Sangga handing over P10.752 million to Fernandez on Nov. 21, 2024, and another P4 million on Sept. 25, 2025.
The Sandiganbayan’s Second Division is handling the one count of graft involving the P10.752 million transaction, and the information containing this formal charge was read to Fernandez.
Sandiganbayan Presiding Justice Geraldine Faith Econg, the Second Division chair, asked: “What is your plea?”
“Not guilty, your honor.”
Econg also said the court is eyeing to give the prosecution and the defense “two weeks” each to present their evidence.
The court set the pretrial of Fernandez’s case on Sept. 29.
Reporters asked Fernandez for comment but he did not grant a media interview. /das

articles.title: Russia pounds Kyiv, ending three-day halt for US talks
articles.summary: KYIV, Ukraine – Russian missiles and drones pounded Kyiv overnight, killing two people and sending smoke billowing above the Ukrainian capital, ending Moscow’s temporary halt to strikes…

blocks.text: KYIV, Ukraine – Russian missiles and drones pounded Kyiv overnight, killing two people and sending smoke billowing above the Ukrainian capital, ending Moscow’s temporary halt to strikes on the city.
Russian President Vladimir Putin had ordered the pause in attacks as US President Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited the Russian and Ukrainian capitals at the weekend.
AFP reporters in the city heard fresh explosions ringing out in the early hours of Tuesday, triggering fires and sending locals down into basements and metro stations for shelter.

“The moment the US president’s peace envoys left, Putin launched another massive, horrific attack against Kyiv, damaging residential areas and killing at least two people,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga said on social media.
“His ballistic missiles speak louder than his words on diplomacy.”

Witkoff and Kushner’s trips provided no immediate breakthrough in ending the four-and-a-half-year war, but represented Washington’s reengagement with trying to broker a deal between the two sides, which had been on hold for months.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said people were trapped in a residential building after the strikes.
Russia’s army said it had a carried out a “massive strike” on military-industrial sites, logistics hubs and storage centres in Kyiv and its suburbs.
Civilian deaths in Ukraine are running at their highest rate since the first months of Russia’s invasion, according to statistics verified by the United Nations.
In the Moscow-annexed Crimean peninsula, Russian-installed officials said a Ukrainian attack killed two people.
US proposals

The strikes came hours after Witkoff touted “substantive progress” in the discussions with Ukraine and Russia, raising the prospect of reviving three-way peace talks to end Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II.
“President Trump is working hard to stop the killing and work towards a lasting and durable peace,” he said on X.
Witkoff and Kushner met Putin in Moscow on Saturday, before holding separate talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in their first official trip to Kyiv.

The Kremlin announced Monday that it did not rule out three-way talks, with spokesman Dmitry Peskov telling reporters “it is too early to say anything about the venue or the exact dates at this stage”.
Zelensky told US news outlet Axios that the United States was pushing to de-escalate the conflict ahead of the long winter.
Russia has struck Ukraine’s energy grid each winter since invading in February 2022, cutting power and heating to millions in temperatures as low as -20C.
Zelensky has said the weekend talks included US proposals around energy facilities, grain shipments and oil and gas exports, but declined to give further details.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov on Tuesday appeared to rule out a Turkish proposal for a truce on strikes in the Black Sea, saying it was “unrealistic” and “impossible to monitor”.
The two sides appear no close to agreeing on how the war should end.
Moscow is demanding Ukraine cede territory in its eastern Donetsk region that it still controls and renounce Western military support.
Kyiv has said such terms amount to capitulation and would only allow Russia to prepare a fresh attack in its bid to install a Moscow-friendly puppet government.

articles.title: PH posts highest PISA scores yet in reading, math, science -- DepEd
articles.summary: The Philippines posted its highest-ever mean scores in the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) in reading, mathematics and science in 2025, Education Secretary Sonny Angara…

blocks.text: Published September 8, 2026 4:30pm

The Philippines posted its highest-ever mean scores in the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) in reading, mathematics and science in 2025, Education Secretary Sonny Angara announced Tuesday.

According to the Department of Education (DepEd), the country recorded mean scores of 373 in science, 371 in mathematics and 367 in reading—up 17 points, 16 points and 20 points, respectively, from its 2022 results.
The results were presented by Angara during the national launch of the PISA 2025 results at Caloocan City Science High School.
The latest assessment also showed an increase in the share of Filipino learners who reached Level 2 or higher, the baseline proficiency level measured by PISA.
In science, the proportion rose from 23% to 32%; in mathematics, from 16% to 21%; and in reading, from 24% to 31%.
Based on mean scores, the Philippines ranked above 14 participating countries in science, 16 in mathematics and 18 in reading, DepEd said.

“This is a significant achievement for our learners and for the entire Philippine education system. But more than the numbers, we are seeing evidence that our learners are capable of making real and meaningful progress,” Angara said.
He said the results should encourage the country to build on the gains while continuing to focus on learners who remain behind.
“We should be proud of how far our learners and teachers have come, but we should be even more determined about how much farther we can go.”
PH 'fastest-improving' in reading
The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)’s 10-year trend analysis identified the Philippines as the fastest-improving country in reading performance, according to DepEd.
The OECD also identified the Philippines among the countries showing notable improvement in mathematics.
In science, the Philippines recorded a positive long-term trend even as science performance declined globally.
OECD Director for Education and Skills Andreas Schleicher congratulated Filipino teachers and school leaders on the results.

“My warmest congratulations to the teachers and school leaders of the Philippines because what you have achieved in this latest round of OECD’s PISA assessment is not just good news for the Philippines, it’s a story that deserves to be noticed far beyond your borders,” he said.
Angara: Gains must be sustained
Angara said the improvement reflected the collective work of teachers, school leaders, parents, local governments and other education partners.
The PISA presentation also highlighted the roles of school readiness, parents, local government units and the private sector in shaping learners’ performance.

Despite the improved results, DepEd said the findings also pointed to areas that still need work, particularly equity and sustained efforts to improve learning outcomes and support teachers and schools.
The department said it would also continue working with education partners on the responsible use of digital technology and addressing challenges such as cyberbullying and its effects on learning.
Angara said the latest PISA results should serve as a starting point for a more ambitious effort to improve learning outcomes for every Filipino learner.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Kenya moves to register frightened Burundians as tension over foreign traders rises
articles.summary: All foreigners without proper documents in Kenya are urged to register through their embassies.

blocks.text: Kenya says it will register undocumented Burundians and other East Africans living in the country, following days of anxiety over President William Ruto's directive targeting foreigners in small-scale businesses.
On Monday, hundreds of Burundians scrambled to process travel documents amid uncertainty over whether they could remain in Kenya.

Charles Owino, the Kenyan government spokesperson, has now said those without proper documents should register through their embassies or high commissions as the authorities work with diplomatic missions to regularise their status.
Those undergoing registration would be presumed legally in Kenya during the process, Owino said.

Ruto had set Monday as the deadline for foreigners operating small-scale businesses to cease work. The directive came after the trade ministry said some foreigners exploit visa rules to work without the required permits.
Long queues were seen outside Burundi's embassy in the capital, Nairobi, after it said it would offer free emergency travel documents to citizens who wanted to go back home.
Others were seen racing to buy bus tickets.
Some Burundians have reportedly faced hostility after President Ruto ordered action against foreign street vendors and those operating small shops, saying such jobs should be protected for Kenyans.
Kenyan officials have since sought to reassure neighbouring countries that there is no blanket ban on foreign traders.
Addressing a news conference on Monday, Owino said the government had opened registration and documentation of all foreign nationals residing in Kenya without valid documents.

He acknowledged that because of historical circumstances and regional dynamics, a number of East African nationals, including several Burundians, resided and operated in Kenya without full documentation.
"To address this constructively, the government of Kenya is establishing a formal documentation and registration window," Owino said.

"We call upon all undocumented East African community nationals, and specifically Burundian citizens currently residing in Kenya, to immediately present themselves to their respective high commissions or embassies for formal identity registration," he added.
As part of the process, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs is to work closely with the Embassy of Burundi and other regional partners to address and regularise these cases, according to Owino.
Meanwhile, senior Kenyan foreign affairs official Korir Sing'oei has apologised to Burundians over the harassment some have faced, saying the president's directive had been misunderstood.
"I want to say sorry to all the Burundi nationals here," Sing'oei said during a visit to the Burundian embassy in Nairobi on Monday.
He said the government would tighten security in areas where Burundians live.
Kenya hosts hundreds of thousands of migrants from across East Africa seeking work and business opportunities.
According to the United Nations refugee agency, there are around 16,000 Burundian refugees and asylum seekers in Kenya.
It is unclear how many are involved in small-scale trading.

On Monday, some of them were on Monday seen carrying all their belongings - from suitcases to mattresses - as they tried to leave Kenya. However, some of them said they could not afford the cost of travel and urged the Kenyan government to extend the deadline.
Ruto's directive follows a similar crackdown in Tanzania last year and rising anti‑migrant sentiment in South Africa.
Burundi's Foreign Affairs Minister Edouard Bizimana said in a post on X that "Kenyans in Burundi were living peacefully but if the hate speech against Burundi continues things will certainty change".
"Kenya government is responsible for the lives of Burundians living in Kenya," he added.
Ruto had said that while Kenya remained open to foreign investment, it could not be "that a person comes from China or elsewhere to be a hawker or open a small shop".
He argued that investors should create jobs and expand production rather than compete with Kenyans in small businesses.
His comments sparked mixed reactions, with some critics describing them as a populist move that risked stoking xenophobia. Government officials deny the allegation.
Some foreign nationals say they fear for their safety, while police have warned Kenyans against targeting them.

Bizimana organised an urgent meeting with representatives of the East African Community (EAC), an eight-member bloc which promotes economic integration in the region. Both Kenya and Burundi are part of the group.
He said he had asked the Kenyan ambassador to convey to his government Burundi's concerns and to ensure that no Burundian was subjected to abuse.
Alexis Ntinanirwa, the head of the Association of Burundians living in Kenya, told the BBC Great Lakes service that he was unhappy with Ruto's decision, but was urging Burundians to remain patient.
He warned that the issue could have wider regional consequences because Kenyans were also involved in small-scale businesses in other East African countries.

"This issue is not only going to cause problems for Burundians working in Kenya, but it is also going to cause problems in the region because there are also Kenyans doing these small jobs in our countries in Burundi, Tanzania and Uganda."
Ntinanirwa advised Burundians involved in hawking and other small businesses to avoid confrontation with police.
Additional reporting by Akisa Wandera and Prime Ndikumagenge

articles.title: Impeachment court asked to revisit voting threshold
articles.summary: Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo Tulfo says it should now be clarified as the trial of Vice President Sara Duterte moves closer to its end

blocks.text: IMPEACHMENT TRIAL. The Senate impeachment court in session for the trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.
Senate of the Philippines Facebook page
Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo Tulfo says it should now be clarified as the trial of Vice President Sara Duterte moves closer to its end

items: Senator Erwin Tulfo requested clarification on the voting threshold for Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial due to the absence of several senator-judges.
Four senator-judges were absent on Day 23, with reasons including medical leave and legal issues, raising concerns about potential acquittal by default.
The impeachment court will seek opinions from retired Supreme Court justices on the voting threshold, with a hearing scheduled for September 16 and a decision expected by September 23.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo on Tuesday, September 8 formally asked the Senate impeachment court to decide on the voting threshold for the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, citing the continued absence of some senators.
On Day 23 of the impeachment trial, Tulfo said it should now be clarified how many votes are required for Duterte’s acquittal or conviction as the trial moves closer to its end.

“If we insist that the voting basis fixed at 24, regardless of the evidence presented, regardless of the vote of the senators who are able to listen to the testimonies, the absence of those senators, whether we like it or not, will result in an acquittal by default,” Tulfo said.
Four senator-judges were absent on day 23 of the trial: Loren Legarda, Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa, Rodante Marcoleta and Jinggoy Estrada.
Legarda remains under extended medical leave abroad due to lung illness while Dela Rosa is in hiding in view of an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court (ICC).
Marcoleta and Estrada are detained for separate plunder charges.
The Senate impeachment court went on a 30-minute recess to discuss the matter. During the break, Escudero was seen talking with senator-judges as well as counsels from the defense and prosecution.
Senator-judges Pia Cayetano and Robin Padilla, for their part, opposed the lowering of the threshold and moved to retain Escudero’s July 16 ruling.

Escudero ruled that the impeachment court will seek the opinion of amici curiae or the”friends of the court” in resolving the issue. The hearing on this is slated on September 16, and the oral arguments plus the impeachment court’s decision on September 23.
Escudero refused to name who will be tapped to present various opinions but said they will include retired Supreme Court (SC) justices.
“We already talked about some retired SC justices but I’m not yet at liberty to state their names because we have not yet gotten in touch with them,” Escudero added.
Also on Tuesday, senator-judges weighed in on the possibility of allowing detained senators to participate in the trial.
Cayetano urged the Senate to consider allowing Marcoleta and Estrada to attend the impeachment trial, and vote without changing the rules.

Senator-judge Raffy Tulfo said, “Do we have the power to invite our two colleagues who are in custody, right now?… How about payagan sila mag-monitor if they want to vote?… Kung ‘di sila makapag-monitor sa proceedings, then they cannot vote intelligently?”

(Do we have the power to invite our two colleagues who are in custody, right now? How about we allow them to monitor if they want to vote? Because how can… then they cannot vote intelligently if they were unable to monitor.)
Escudero clarified it is not the impeachment court but the Senate, as a legislative body, which will decide on the issue. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Low turnout threatens Commons vote on assisted dying, say MPs
articles.summary:
Backers seek support for second attempt to get law through House of Lords after ‘undemocratic’ rejection last year

MPs on both sides of the assisted dying debate have voiced fears about…

blocks.text: MPs on both sides of the assisted dying debate have voiced fears about turnout affecting the vote on Friday, when the bill returns to the Commons for its second attempt to become law.

Those who back the change in the law in England and Wales have been emphasising the “undemocratic” nature of the bill’s rejection by the House of Lords after it was talked out by a handful of peers after passing the House of Commons. The bill fell despite multiple days of debate from peers because of the number of amendments tabled in the Lords.
Several former cabinet ministers and ministers say they intend to speak out on the bill now they are freer to express their views, especially on the conduct of the Lords.
The private member’s bill – originally sponsored by Kim Leadbeater – has been revived by the Labour MP Lauren Edwards. It had passed last year by a majority of 23 in the Commons.

In an article for the Guardian, Edwards said the bill was “the most pressing, progressive reform of this parliament. But it was blocked in the Lords earlier this year by a small minority of peers, led in part by former Tory ministers such as Thérèse Coffey and Mark Harper”. She said the Lords should not be “allowed to frustrate the will of the elected chamber a second time”.

Edwards said she rejected some accusations from Labour MPs that she was reopening divisions in the party at a moment when there was a chance to reunite it now that Andy Burnham had replaced Keir Starmer as prime minister.

“Exactly the reverse is true. MPs have already made their decision. In a democracy, we settle our differences by voting on them. Last time, opponents in the Lords prevented a vote taking place on the bill’s provisions,” Edwards said.
“Other major social changes such as a woman’s right to choose and gay rights were bitterly contested at the time. But once passed, the reforms were quickly accepted and ceased to be controversial.

“It is time to do the same and give terminally ill people the choice to exercise some control over the manner of their deaths. We owe it to them, and to the vast majority of voters who support them, not to sit back and allow a minority of unelected peers to stand in their way.”
Backers of the bill have stressed that MPs should see the vote as a moment to assert the Commons’ decision-making power, rather than rerun the arguments.

Jo Stevens, a former Welsh secretary, said: “I’ve always supported the principle of assisted dying. I have constituents and friends who desperately wanted one and a constituent who I helped after they were arrested for escorting someone who chose an assisted death at Dignitas.

“I and many other MPs, including MPs who didn’t support the bill, are furious at the outrageous behaviour of a small number of unelected peers who went against the will of the Commons. Many of these are former MPs who should know better, especially former ministers who were rejected by the electorate.”

However, several MPs said they believed it was the pro-side that was finding it hardest to convince MPs to stay and vote on Friday. “No one has changed sides, but the numbers are going to be tighter because people are absent,” one MP said.

Two MPs who voted in favour of the bill are no longer in parliament: Starmer, who quit as an MP last week and is yet to be replaced; and the former Makerfield MP Josh Simons, who was replaced by Burnham, who has said he will abstain.

Other high-profile supporters of the bill, including the cabinet minister Louise Haigh, minister Ian Murray and former chancellor Jeremy Hunt, have written to constituents previously saying they were uneasy about using the Parliament Act to pass the law. The act would come into force, within certain conditions, if the Lordswere to reject the bill a second time.

articles.title: DSWD seeks restoration of P800-M from capital outlay for upkeep of aging care facilities
articles.summary: The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) said Tuesday that it is seeking the restoration of its capital outlay under its proposed P200 billion budget for 2027 to maintain its care…

blocks.text: Published September 8, 2026 4:10pm

The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) said Tuesday that it is seeking the restoration of its capital outlay under its proposed P200 billion budget for 2027 to maintain its care facilities nationwide.
Among the department and its attached and serviced agencies, it is only the DSWD Office of the Secretary that was allocated with a capital outlay of P294.1 million for next year.
DSWD Secretary Rex Gatchalian said that the cuts on capital outlay may affect the maintenance of its care facilities, with some of them already more than 50 years old.

"We are very worried lalo na sa mga care facilities natin. Matatanda na ho ang ating mga facilities. While they are maintained to the best of their ability by our people on the ground, admittedly maraming issues ang umuusbong kapag luma na ang isang bahay," he said during the House budget deliberation.

(We are very worried, especially regarding our care facilities. Our facilities are already old. While they are maintained to the best of their ability by our people on the ground, admittedly, many issues emerge when a structure gets old.)

"So marami diyan 50 years old pataas, mas matanda pa sa akin. So sana ho maibalik ‘yung aming dinudulog na part of the listing we submitted to the committee, kahit yung capital expenditure for the upkeep, upgrade, and maintenance of our care facilities," he added.

(So many of those are 50 years old and above, older than I am. So we hope that what we are requesting—part of the list we submitted to the committee—will be restored, even just the capital expenditure for the upkeep, upgrade, and maintenance of our care facilities.)
Hence, the DSWD is hoping for P800 million for the upkeep of the said facilities which houses members of the vulnerable groups.
"We are actually asking for P800 million. Ayan din po ‘yung nawala. Maibalik man lang 'yun," said Gatchalian.
(We are actually asking for P800 million. That is also what was removed. If only that could be restored.)
The DSWD currently operates and manages 77 care facilities across the country.
For his part, Akbayan Party-list Perci Cendaña agreed the budget must be adjusted for the management of the care facilities.

"Itong budget cut when it comes to care facilities ay actually budget cut sa pagkalinga sa ating mga kababayan. So this is a very necessary amendment to the NEP...Kung wala pong budget para diyan, ibig sabihin hindi nagke-care ang gobyerno," he said.

(This budget cut when it comes to care facilities is actually a budget cut on caring for our fellow citizens. So this is a very necessary amendment to the National Expenditure Program... If there is no budget for that, it means the government does not care.)

The DSWD and three attached agencies had lower proposed budgets for 2027. One of the agencies with a budget cut is the National Council on Disability Affairs, whose funding was reduced from P187 million in 2026 to a proposed P91 million next year. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: Oil price approaches $100 a barrel after attacks on Saudi oil facilities – business live
articles.summary:
Saudi authorities said operations at some energy facilities have been attacked ‌by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis

Gas prices are rising this morning, putting pressure on European…

blocks.text: Introduction: Oil heads back towards $100 a barrel
Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy.
The global economy faces the prospect of $100 a barrel oil again, as the conflict in the Middle East continues.

Brent crude has risen back over the $98 a barrel mark already this week, its highest level since 24 July. Oil has been pushed up by reports that Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis attacked energy facilities in Saudi Arabia.
Saudi authorities said operations at some energy facilities had been halted today following attacks ‌by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis that wounded more than 70 people.
The attacks add to the pressure on oil and gas production in the region, which remains badly disrupted by the ongoing Iran war.
Yesterday, the Financial Times reported that Saudi Aramco’s oil facilities in the Saudi Arabian city of Jizan – where one of the country’s largest refineries is based – have been attacked
Earlier today, Iran threatened to create a new restricted zone in the Gulf if the US pressed on with its ‘economic warfare’ against Tehran.
Such a zone would, presumably, further undermine US efforts to reopen the strait of Hormuz.
Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said Iran had “ fundamentally recalibrated” its posture towards US forces.
Rezaei posted on X:

double quotation markIn recent days, Washington has received a clear warning from Iran’s new missiles. Economic warfare will be met by a maritime exclusion zone across the Persian Gulf to the blockade perimeter. The operational posture toward U.S. warships and bases has been fundamentally recalibrated.

Shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has already slowed this week – just seven commodity vessels sailing through the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, down from eight on Sunday. Before the war began, about 130 ships a day would cross the strait.

This is all a headache for central bankers, as high oil prices create inflationary pressures through the economy. Later today, MPs in London will question Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey, and colleagues, about their recent decision to hold the Bank Rate at 3.75%.
MPs are likely to question witnesses on the potential inflationary impact of the ongoing war in Iran and how the MPC considers recent developments in AI, the committee says.
The agenda

7.45am BST: French trade data for July
2.15pm BST: Bank of England policymakers appear before the Treasury select committee
