blocks.text: UK mortgage rates highest since June
UK mortgage rates have risen again today, as the recent bond market turbulence hits borrowers.
Data provider Moneyfacts reports that the average two-year fixed residential mortgage rate is at its highest since 7 June, while the average five-year is at its highest since 10 May.
This follows the rise in swap rates last week, which made it more expensive for lenders to borrow.
Here’s the details:

items: The average 2-year fixed residential mortgage rate today is 5.65%. This is up from 5.63% the previous working day.
The average 5-year fixed residential mortgage rate today is 5.70%. This is up from 5.68% the previous working day.

blocks.text: Lenders are also withdrawing some products from the market. There are currently 7,417 residential mortgage products available, down from 7,485 yesterday.
Philip Scott, partner, banking & finance at legal firm Walker Morris, has warned that businesses should be concerned too:

double quotation mark“The recent increase in bond yields and market expectations of higher interest rates is not just a concern for homeowners. Businesses across the UK should also be paying close attention because movements in the wider debt markets ultimately influence the cost and availability of corporate finance.” “For companies with existing facilities approaching maturity, refinancing may become more expensive than anticipated. Businesses considering acquisitions, capital investment or expansion plans may also find that the economics of those projects look different as borrowing costs rise.” “While lenders remain open for business, we are likely to see greater scrutiny around cashflow forecasts, leverage levels and covenant compliance. In that environment, preparation becomes increasingly important.”
Oil over $99 a barrel...
Oil is getting jolly close to the $100 a barrel mark, for the first time since July.
Brent crude, the international benchmark, is now up 2.2% and just touched $99.25 a barrel.
Novartis shares slide after drugs trial disappointment
Swiss pharmaceuticals group Novartis is heading for its worst day on the stock market ever, after releasing disappointing medical trial data.
Novartis reported this morning that its experimental drug for a muscle wasting disorder failed in a ⁠late-stage study.

The drug is called del-desiran. Novartis had been testing whether it helped patients with myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1), but found that it did not demonstrate statistically significant improvement versus a placebo.
Shreeram Aradhye, president, development and chief medical officer, Novartis, explains:

double quotation mark“Despite decades of research, there are still no approved treatment options for DM1, and patients and caregivers continue to face a significant daily burden. “Developing therapies for a complex disease like DM1 remains challenging, and setbacks are part of scientific progress. As we continue to evaluate the full HARBOR dataset, we remain committed to identifying the most appropriate development path for the del-desiran program and advancing innovative approaches for people living with DM1 and other serious neuromuscular diseases.”
Novartis’s shares are down 10%, which would be their biggest daily fall on record.

The company was created by the merger of Swiss chemical and pharmaceutical companies Ciba-Geigy and Sandoz in 1996. The Sandoz family remain its third-largest shareholder, through their Foundation, founded by sculptor and painter Édouard-Marcel Sandoz.
Gas prices rise amid growing nervousness over storage
Gas prices are rising this morning, putting pressure on European countries who need to stock up their storage levels before the winter.
The month-ahead UK gas price is up around 1% at 184p a therm, close to yesterday’s highs when gas hit its highest since January 2023.
Continental European gas prices are up 1.3%.
Rupert Thompson, IBOSS chief economist, reports that European gas prices are being pushed up by growing nervousness over “the relatively low storage levels ahead of winter.”
UK government borrowing costs are a little higher this morning.
The yield, or interest rate, on 10-year UK bonds has risen by 2 basis points (0.02 of a percentage point) to 5.19%. Thirty-year gilt yields are also up around 2bps at 5.83%.
These are small moves, and yields remain lower than last week – when 10-year yields hit their highest level since the 2008 financial crisis.
But they’re also a reminder of the pressures which higher oil prices, and resulting higher inflation, put on the public finances.
Copper hits record high amid US hoarding
Boom! The copper price has hit a new alltime high this morning.
The three-month copper contract on the London Metal Exchange hit a record high of $14,617 a ton this morning, surpassing the previous record set on Monday.

Copper is generally seen as a gauge of economic growth prospects. But the current rally is also being attributed to hoarding in the US, as importers try to stock up before Donald Trump imposes new tariffs on copper (as some people anticipate).
Saudi Arabia: energy sites near Yemen halted after attacks
Saudi Arabia has now said operations at several energy facilities in the kingdom’s south were halted after attacks ignited fires in the region bordering Yemen (where the Houthis are based).
Bloomberg has the details:

double quotation markThe strikes took place on Tuesday and wounded a number of people, the state-run Saudi Press Agency reported, citing officials at the energy ministry that it didn’t identify. It didn’t name any of the facilities. The Saudi energy ministry and Saudi Aramco didn’t have any further comments. A series of attacks have targeted Saudi Arabia’s southwestern region since Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi militants said they would blockade Saudi Arabia’s oil flows in response to Riyadh’s siege of the Yemeni capital, Sana’a. Oil facilities in Jazan, where a 400,000 barrel-a-day refinery has been shut since an earlier attack in July, were hit again on Monday.
The summer heatwave has dampened demand at British homeware retailer Dunelm, sending its shares sliding.

Dunelm reported this morning that trading had been significantly softer in the first six weeks of its new financial year (which began at the end of June). It blamed “the extended period of unusually hot weather”.
Dunelm, which sells home furnishings such as bedding, curtains, furniture, beds and mattresses, added that “we have seen better trading following cooler weather”.

Shares are down 8%, putting Dunelm at the bottom of the FTSE 250 index of medium-sized companies listed in London. The company also reported a 3.1% rise in sales in the last financial year, but profits were flat.
Tariff wars rear up as Canada retaliates against the US
Trade war tensions have also risen today, as Canada imposes retaliatory tariffs on US goods.
The tariffs kicked in this morning, targeting sectors including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics.
The move is in response to the US’s decision to impose a 50% tariff on $20bn of Canadian goods last month.
Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, says:

double quotation mark“Trade tensions and geopolitical stalemate are adding to inflationary concerns – pushing prices up across a large basket of commodities, which will feed through to household and business costs. The moves are adding to the note of caution reverberating on financial markets, as investors assess the likelihood that interest rates may have to stay higher for longer to keep a lid on consumer prices. Tariff wars have reared up again after Canada slapped billions of dollars of retaliatory tariffs on American goods, after talks with the US administration collapsed. The former trade allies have turned foes, with President Trump turning up the heat, and the latest measures are likely to add another layer of uncertainty for businesses and consumers. Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on around $20 billion of US goods came into effect today, with duties ranging from 15% to 50%.
Europe's stock markets dip at the open
European stock markets have opened in the red, as the rising oil price weighs on sentiment.
The FTSE 100 share index has dipped by 0.2%, or 20 points, to 10,801 points, with banks among the big fallers. Energy firms BP (+0.9%) and Shell (+0.35%) are higher, though.
Other markets are weaker, though – France’s CAC has dropped by 0.4%, and Spain’s IBEX is 0.2% lower.
Germany has been hit by a surprise drop in exports, knocking hopes that its economy was rebounding.
German exports fell by 0.8% in July compared with the previous month, data from the federal statistics office showed this morning.
This was due to a fall in shipments to European Union countries.
There is a renewed inflation risk coming from energy markets, warns Naeem Aslam, CIO of Zaye Capital Markets.

double quotation markOil has now risen for a third consecutive session, and the market is increasingly questioning whether higher energy costs could feed into transportation, manufacturing and consumer inflation. That matters for both U.S. and European equities because more expensive oil can squeeze corporate margins while simultaneously forcing central banks to keep monetary policy restrictive. Energy companies may benefit from higher crude prices, but airlines, industrial companies, retailers and other fuel-sensitive businesses face a less favourable cost environment.

articles.title: Abaca school bag production pushed in Leyte
articles.summary: TACLOBAN CITY — The Philippine Fiber Industry Development Authority (PhilFIDA) regional office here is pushing for abaca bag making as an alternative livelihood in Leyte provinces. This is part of an…

blocks.text: TACLOBAN CITY — The Philippine Fiber Industry Development Authority (PhilFIDA) regional office here is pushing for abaca bag making as an alternative livelihood in Leyte provinces.
This is part of an effort to revitalize fiber-based handicrafts.
PhilFIDA Eastern Visayas Regional Director Joseph Salas said in a phone interview on Monday that they have completed a training of trainers in Southern Leyte for school bag making on Sept. 1 to 4.
They are scheduled to roll out the training in Leyte on Sept. 8 to 11.

“The capacity-building activity aimed not only to develop participants’ skills in producing abaca-based products, but also to establish a pool of trainers capable of sharing these skills with communities across Leyte provinces and other parts of Eastern Visayas,” Salas said.
The agency tapped experts from Antique for the 25 trainers to learn more about various stages of abaca school bag production, including design, assembly, finishing and quality control.
They completed the required outputs and produced durable and functional school bags using locally produced abaca twine.
The newly trained participants now form an additional pool of abaca handicraft trainers who can help bring skills development closer to fiber-producing communities.
The agency will roll out that training with the support of local government units.
Southern Leyte is the top producer of abaca in Eastern Visayas.
In 2024, the province logged a 1,457 metric tons (MT) yield.
Leyte ranks third with 606.16 MT output.
Abaca, commonly known as Manila hemp, holds significant economic importance in the region. /apl

articles.title: PNP logs 41.77% drop in PH crime rates in August 2026
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police (PNP) has recorded a drop in focus crimes across the country, down from 3,584 incidents in 2025 to 2,087 in 2026 — or a 41.77 percent drop. In a…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police (PNP) has recorded a drop in focus crimes across the country, down from 3,584 incidents in 2025 to 2,087 in 2026 — or a 41.77 percent drop.
In a statement on Tuesday, the PNP said the data referred to focus crimes recorded from January to August 2026, compared with data for the same period in 2025.
Focus crimes refer to carnapping, rape, physical injuries, theft, robbery, and homicide.

“The figures reflect the value of sustained police presence and prevention efforts, while emphasizing that every remaining incident still calls for attention,” PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said in a statement.
“The PNP remains committed to sustaining the positive gains while addressing persistent concerns through responsive and responsible policing,” he added.

The PNP detailed that carnapping of motor vehicles declined by 67.74 percent in August 2026 compared to the same month in 2025, while rape cases declined by 58.65 percent and carnapping of motorcycles by 53.64 percent.
The national police force further noted that physical injury cases also decreased by 46.83 percent; theft by 41.67 percent; robbery by 33.16 percent; and homicide by 3.33 percent. /mcm

articles.title: 3 years on, Morocco earthquake victims still wait for help
articles.summary: On September 8, 2023, a devastating earthquake struck the Al Haouz region in Morocco, killing over 2,900 people, injuring more than 5,500 and causing widespread destruction. In the village of…

blocks.text: On September 8, 2023, a devastating earthquake struck the Al Haouz region in Morocco, killing over 2,900 people, injuring more than 5,500 and causing widespread destruction.

In the village of Ighermane in the High Atlas Mountains, about 50 kilometers (30 miles) southwest of Marrakech, Mohamed Ait Belaid, 72, feels like things are actually going pretty well for him three years later.
He had been living in a tent after the earthquake but now resides in a newly built house, even though it’s smaller than the one destroyed in the earthquake.

“I benefited from partial [state] support and received 80,000 dirhams [around €7,300] for rebuilding,” he told DW. “I added about 100,000 [€9,110] dirhams from my own pocket. And thanks to God, I like my new house and I’m comfortable in it. I’m at peace because my wife, my children and I are all healthy and I haven’t lost any of them.”
Around 40 kilometers away, in the town of Azgour, it’s a different story. Larbi Ait Jelloulat, also 72, is sitting in front of a pile of rubble that was once his house.

“I want to know where my rights have gone,” he said angrily. “Who took what’s rightfully mine? For three years, I’ve been going from one department to another, from one complaint to another, from one petition to another, just looking for an answer. Why have I been excluded? Am I not a Moroccan citizen?”

Ait Jelloulat was formerly a council employee and saved for years in order to build the large home that was destroyed in the 2023 earthquake. As far as he can tell, bureaucratic issues mean he must prove he was a resident in the area.
“My only dream was to spend the rest of my life in my own home, a rest after years of service,” he explained. “Now they say I’m not a resident … Where’s the logic in that?”

blocks.caption: Larbi Ait Jelloulat sits on the rubble of his home in Azgour; he’s been fighting to get state help but has been unsuccessful so far Image: Zhor Baki/DW

blocks.text: Why such different experiences?

Reconstruction seems to be happening faster in Ighermane, the village where Ait Belaid lives. About 90% of the village is rebuilt and most residents’ lives are back to normal, said Omar Saeed from the Ighermane Association for Development and Solidarity.
Of the village’s around 150 families, 114 received state support of some kind, although most also had to contribute some of their own money to rebuild.
Meanwhile, in Azgour, where Ait Jelloulat lives, there’s been more to do. Azgour was the village most impacted by the earthquake in the area.

There, about 76 families have had help with reconstruction, Ait Jelloulat said, while 56 others are still waiting for help. “What’s more, the 76 families who rebuilt their homes in a different location are also having problems connecting to water and electricity,” he added.

blocks.caption: Azgour village was among those hit hardest by the 2023 earthquake, and reconstruction is still ongoing Image: Zhor Baki/DW

blocks.text: Rebuilding difficult in remote mountain villages

According to a March statement from the High Atlas Development Agency, or ADHA, which was established in October 2023 to bring help to affected areas, 54,425 homes have been built or rehabilitated and more than 3,000 homes are still under construction. The government has given out more than 7.2 billion dirhams (€656 million/$770 million) to affected families. The sum includes funds to help rebuild as well as monthly emergency aid payments.

In terms of the pace of construction, Marrakech-based architect Mohamed Belmejjad believes the state is actually doing fairly well. “I believe the progress so far, relative to the timeframe, to be positive,” he told DW.
Given the circumstances, it would be hard for things to have gone much faster, he suggested.
Immediately after the earthquake, it was difficult to reach affected locations, especially remote mountain villages and towns. Then rubble had to be cleared before building could begin.

After that, other factors complicated reconstruction, including the distance of some villages from paved roads, the difficulty of transporting building materials in and debris out, problems with connecting water and power, and the need to relocate whole villages and construction sites to avoid dangers like landslides. There’s also a need to respect local building traditions, ensuring that construction materials are solid and will last.

“We also lack the necessary expertise here, whether that’s in terms of architects, design offices, contractors or even the labor required for construction,” Belmejjad pointed out. Given all that has happened reconstruction could actually be considered ahead of schedule, he suggested.
‘No one has remembered us’
Despite that, the National Coordination for Al Haouz Earthquake Victims reports receiving complaints from more than 3,000 families who haven’t had any state help.

Montasser Itri, a member of the organization, explains that some of these families were excluded because they had moved to other parts of the country to work and their national identity cards then show them as residents of places unaffected by the 2023 earthquake.

“The government is trying to make us, the victims of the Al Haouz earthquake, into mere statistics linked to the progress of construction and the removal of tents,” Itri told DW, “rather than treating us as human beings and with dignity.”

blocks.caption: In Amizmiz, local woman Fawzia Aliban is worried her house might collapse before she gets any help Image: Zhor Baki/DW

blocks.text: That’s why the coordinating committee is already demanding an independent and transparent investigation into how local authorities have handled the payouts. In the past they’ve organized demonstrations outside parliament buildings in the capital, Rabat, to demand compensation and rehousing solutions and to accuse local authorities of failing to honor commitments.
Other impacted locals are hoping the upcoming general election, slated for September 23, might make a difference.

“[Prime Minister Aziz] Akhannouch promised us a solution to the issue and God knows we are waiting,” said Fawzia Aliban, whose home in Amizmiz was damaged in the earthquake. “We hope the problems will be resolved because I was denied benefits even though my house is on the verge of collapse.”

“Three years have passed, and no one has remembered us […] but recently some political figures turned up and promised to solve the problem,” added Mohamed Belkaid, who is still living in a tent in the Amizmiz area with his four children.
He hasn’t received any aid to rebuild because he is listed as a tenant, not an owner, and is not optimistic things will change.

blocks.caption: Mohamed Belkaid has lived in this tent with his family since the 2023 earthquake Image: Zhor Baki/DW

blocks.text: “They promised to review our files, asking us to trust them and to vote for them,” he complained. “But this is exploitation. If they truly wanted to solve the problem, they would have done so before the elections. Where have they been all these years?” /dl

articles.title: Why thousands are paying to watch people play Dungeons & Dragons live
articles.summary: The growing world of "actual play" is taking tabletop role-playing games from living rooms and online streaming to sold-out theatres. Performers and scholars say its appeal lies in the…

image.caption: Brennan Lee Mulligan is set to bring his Endless Dungeon actual-play show to Vancouver's Queen Elizabeth Theatre for a sold-out performance on Sept. 10. (Leo Montero/@truffleimages)

blocks.text: There is no script, no fixed ending and no guarantee the heroes will make it out alive.
Onstage, performers build a fantasy world together while dice rolls and split-second choices can send the story to places nobody planned.

On Sept. 10, nearly 2,800 people will fill Vancouver's Queen Elizabeth Theatre for a sold-out performance of Endless Dungeon, led by comedian and game master Brennan Lee Mulligan. The Vancouver date follows a sold-out May performance at Toronto's Coca-Cola Coliseum.

Endless Dungeon is part of the growing world of "actual play" — tabletop role-playing games performed for an audience — a genre combining improvisational theatre, collaborative storytelling and game mechanics, with dice helping determine whether characters succeed or fail.
For performers and scholars, the appeal lies in uncertainty, intimacy and collaboration — and in knowing that no two performances will be exactly alike.
Mulligan told CBC News that part of the attraction is simply "the joy of live theatre."
"It's happening in front of your face," he said, adding that the audience reactions become part of the draw. "You are there, your gasps, your laughs, your groans at a bad D&D pun."
Why live D&D is drawing thousands — and changing who gets seen
A roller coaster with no track
The term "actual play" is recent, but the practice is a longstanding one according to Emily Friedman, a professor of English at Alabama's Auburn University who studies the format.

Online shows such as Critical Role, Mulligan's Dimension 20 and The Adventure Zone helped bring actual play into the mainstream. Live performances are often self-contained, with clearer character goals and story beats designed to reach an ending in a few hours. That makes the action "heightened and brightened and made sharper and quicker and faster," Friedman said.
She compared its appeal to being on a roller coaster where "the track is being laid in front of you at high speed."
Vancouver comedian Jess Lupini, who is joining Endless Dungeon for this stop, compared it to another form of unscripted entertainment.
"Watching actual plays is exciting in many of the same ways that watching hockey is exciting," she said. "You don't know what's going to happen."
'The feeling of being in the room'
But that unpredictable nature only partly explains why people pay to see a format they can watch online.
Abdul Aziz, a Vancouver comedian joining Mulligan for this Endless Dungeon performance, says the attraction is "probably the feeling of being in the room."
Aziz also performs on the actual-play podcast Spout Lore, which has tried to preserve the atmosphere of friends playing together even as those conversations became entertainment for strangers.
"We sort of are more focused on each other while playing than we are focused on the audience," Aziz said.

items: Level up your next Dungeons and Dragons adventure with these creative makers
Tabletop role-playing games can be intimidating. Here's one anyone can jump into

blocks.text: Friedman says audiences are watching two things at once: fictional characters and the real people creating them reacting genuinely when another player's choice surprises them.
Mulligan says performers have to make the audience feel included without sacrificing their connection to one another.

"The best part of live theatre is the preservation of authentic connection between performers and feeling totally invisible as an audience member, even as everything has been arranged to include you," he said.
"Whatever you do to delight your players will delight the audience."
A place to imagine differently
For Aziz, fantasy also offers room to question rules that can seem fixed in the real world.
Aziz, whose parents are from Egypt and who immigrated to Canada as a child, says growing up in a mainly white community gave him an outsider's perspective on cultural conventions.

items: How a Dungeons and Dragons club became a 'lifesaver' for a group of neurodivergent Ontario youth
From 'satanic panic' to church-approved, Dungeons & Dragons thriving after 50-plus years

blocks.text: That carried into Spout Lore. While building his barbarian character's homeland, Aziz drew heavily on Middle Eastern cultures.
"In a very literal sense, the outsider's perspective was immediately useful in our show," he said.
For Lupini, who is also a recurring cast member on BlackwaterDnD, an actual-play show streamed on YouTube and Twitch, taking on different characters became a way to explore herself.
Lupini, who is transgender, says tabletop role-playing games give people a chance to try on different identities, pronouns and personalities.
Before transitioning, she played characters who used she/her pronouns.
"That was really liberating and felt like a safe way of exploring a piece of myself that I had been conditioned to be really afraid of exploring," she said.

items: These girls are learning to master Dungeons and Dragons
The rise of Critical Role: How a crew of 'nerdy-ass voice actors' became Dungeons & Dragons rock stars

blocks.text: Friedman says women, gender-nonconforming people, 2SLGBTQ+ people and disabled people have always been part of tabletop gaming as players and creators, but were not always visible in traditional gaming spaces.
"It's just the shift of the spotlight in a lot of ways," she said.
Mulligan agrees, saying actual play didn't create those experiences, but made them easier to see.
"Actual play provided visibility for a reality that was always there," he said.
A safe place to play
That kind of exploration depends on trust, says Em Carlson, CEO and creative director of BlackwaterDnD and another performer joining Vancouver's Endless Dungeon.
Carlson, whose professional background is in mental-health therapy, says the group does extensive preparation around safety and collaboration and notes that "play can't happen if you're not safe."

Tabletop role-playing culture still hasn't fully achieved its ideals of inclusion, Carlson says, but the stories reaching audiences have broadened as people want stories that help them feel included in the narrative.
"They can be a part of that joy that the players experience at the table."
For Carlson, Endless Dungeon offers something increasingly uncommon in an era of endlessly replayable media: a story created once, for the people present.
"It's a one-night experience where a fantastic, amazing audience gets to come in and laugh with us and cry with us and feel big feelings and cheer."

articles.title: Parents are pushing back on classroom screen time in a 'techlash' over too much technology in schools
articles.summary: A pushback is emerging against screen time in school and tech tools woven into education today, with some parents linking it to a range of woes, from waning student attention spans to data breaches…

image.caption: Nursery students are seen using tablet computers in Stockholm in 2014. After years of a one-to-one device-to-student ratio symbolizing educational progress, a 'techlash' has emerged, led by some parents, educators and researchers now questioning ubitquitous tech use in schools. (Jonathan Nackstrand/

blocks.text: Canada·New

A pushback is emerging against screen time in school and tech tools woven into education today, with some parents linking it to a range of woes, from waning student attention spans to data breaches that put student privacy at risk.
'We do not need a Google account to learn,' says parent and educator
As an occasional substitute teacher for middle- and high-schoolers in Nova Scotia, Kim Herrick often gets a front-row seat seeing how teens use tech at school.

Whether students are tasked with assignments, work for another class or granted free time, Herrick regularly sees them checking Snapchat, TikTok or Instagram accounts, shopping online, gaming or even trading Bitcoin — easily bypassing school board security methods aimed at blocking such use.

The ubiquity of students engaging in non-educational online activities — and the futile attempts to clamp down on it — have contributed to her view that we need to reconsider the tech used by default in classes today.

But the alarm bells really started going off for Herrick when she discovered her elder daughter — who's starting Grade 2 this fall — has had a school Google account for three years, without Herrick knowing. Herrick said she couldn't log into the account and school officials said she couldn't opt-out or have it deleted, saying it was necessary for access to educational apps and "a requirement" for learning.
We have hundreds of years of going to school as humans, Herrick said. "We do not need a Google account to learn."

Many parents, educators, advocacy groups and experts are pushing back against the amount of screen time in schools and the prevalence of tech tools woven into the current education system, with some making links to a range of woes, from behavioural issues to distracted students to data breaches that put youngsters' privacy at risk.
Yet a rollback to classroom practices of the past isn't the answer to the current "techlash," say some education experts, who favour intentional and thoughtful use of technology as the way forward.
Changing approach to tech in education

For years, a one-to-one student-to-device ratio, web access and learning through game-like applications have been seen as symbols of educational progress. But amid a worldwide push to reduce teen smartphone and social media use, a vocal wave of parent groups — including Skills Before Screens in Canada, the U.K.-based Close Screen Open Minds, as well as Schools Beyond Screens and ScreenSense in the U.S. — is broadening this scrutiny to encompass educational tech usage more generally.

After having prioritized digital schooling for the past decade, for instance, Sweden has recently shifted back toward physical textbooks, pen-and-paper homework, reinvesting in libraries and screen-free classrooms (particularly for younger students), citing falling scores on international assessments.

items: Pen and paper, typewriters, probing Q&As: why these profs went old school in their classrooms

blocks.text: Poor reading scores have tech-friendly Norway making a similar return to physical books in its schools, as well as introducing a near-ban on Generative AI usage in elementary, with restrictions for high-schoolers.

In the U.S., parental demands have led to stricter tech policies at the country's two largest school boards. The Los Angeles Unified School District has already started the school year with limits on screen time in every grade, including a total device ban before Grade 2. On the opposite coast, New York is restricting one-to-one device time for Grade 2 and below and suggesting caps for older elementary students. It's also halting student-facing Generative AI use through Grade 8 and limiting use for high schoolers, for now.

Herrick says many parents, such as herself, are in the dark about the screens and apps their youngsters access in class, let alone what the responsible use or data privacy agreements are regarding those apps and school accounts.
Beyond privacy, the mother of two and former wilderness leadership educator in the U.S. is also concerned about what unfettered school tech use means for the long term.

She worries about susceptibility to distraction — she's had secondary students claim they're multitasking as they juggle a bevy of browser tabs, apps or screens — not to mention negative impacts on their mental and physical health down the road.
In the meantime, overreliance on tech also bogs down educators' precious time with policing student usage and dealing with tech support, rather than teaching, Herrick said.
Intention versus novelty

Classroom tech use varies across Canadian regions, schools and educators, but it's indeed integrated into teaching today, according to Johanathan Woodworth, an assistant professor at Mount Saint Vincent University in Halifax.

Whether teachers are getting students to research a project online, study the solar system via a virtual reality simulator or test out an AI chatbot, Woodworth emphasizes that tech use must be intentional, thoughtful and directly connected to the skills students are expected to learn.

items: Manitoba plans to ban AI chatbots for those under 16. This school uses them as an educational tool

blocks.text: "A lot of times teachers use technology in the classroom because of the novelty effect and engagement — but the novelty effect wears off," Woodworth said from Halifax, where he teaches educational technology to existing and prospective teachers.
"The first step is to think about 'Do I even need to use it? What is the purpose of me using it? Does it actually help me in my classroom?'"

It's important teachers are supported with guidelines and enough training on how to carefully and effectively use technology, he says, in order to understand it and, in turn, teach and model that knowledge to their students.
Striving for balance

Rolling back to no-tech classrooms isn't necessarily the answer either, Woodworth said, since a main reason schools employ tech today — text-to-speech and speech-to-text applications, for instance — is to accommodate students with disabilities.

Schools must balance "purposeful" tech use with the need to prep students for a tech-filled world, while also ensuring it's "not used as a distraction," according to education consultant Tom D'Amico, former director of education of the Ottawa Catholic School Board.

He says the concerns raised by parents — both the ones driving the current "techlash" and those pushing for their kids to build tech skills — are contributing to a "balanced and focused" approach by school boards.

In his current work advising school districts across Canada about artificial intelligence, D'Amico says he's noticing a shift: schools taking a more developmentally and age-informed approach to technology.

For instance, "that means regardless of the province, you're looking at the earliest grades not having a lot of device time, but still getting AI literacy. They still need to learn about digital citizenship, what it means to use a computer," he said, noting gradual introduction of more technology in middle and high school.

items: As more teens turn to AI for emotional support, experts say it's no substitute for human connection
What's the secret to perfect marks? Family, community, discipline and time management, top scholars say

blocks.text: "Critical thinking can be [taught] without the technology as well in the early ages," D'Amico added, emphasizing that this learning must be "embedded in the curriculum, so it happens every single year, in an age-appropriate manner."
Ultimately, he says, the top focus of schools should be student learning and strengthening students' connections with teachers and their classmates.
"What's the number one technology in a classroom? It's the student and their brain," he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Based in Toronto, Jessica Wong covers Canadian education stories for CBC News. In a past life, she covered national and international arts and entertainment news. You can reach her at jessica.wong@cbc.ca.
With files from Deana Sumanac-Johnson

articles.title: DSWD seeks P8M budget for special body on LGBTQIA concerns
articles.summary: The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) is seeking at least P8 million in its 2027 funding for a special committee that crafts policies for the LGBTQIA+ community.

blocks.text: Published September 8, 2026 3:57pm
The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) is seeking at least P8 million in its 2027 funding for a special committee that crafts policies for the LGBTQIA+ community.

During a House briefing on the DSWD's proposed P241.2-billion budget for 2027, Secretary Rex Gatchalian said the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) did not approve the department's proposed P8 million allocation for the committee.

"We made representations with the DBM to actually create a line item for the special body on LGBTQIA. Unfortunately, it was not granted. The allocation we were asking for was P8 million to run that office," Gatchalian said.

"Hopefully, the P8 million will be granted. That would give them more resources to come up with better policies and conduct better research on what the community needs and what new programs the department should run," he added.
Gatchalian was responding to a manifestation by Akbayan Party-list Representative Perci Cendaña, who questioned the committee's reported budget of less than P2 million this year.

"According to news reports, their budget this year is below P2 million. So imagine operating an office with a huge mandate with a budget of under P2 million. That is very small. Will the Secretary confirm this?" Cendaña said.
The special committee was created through an executive order issued by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. in 2023.
The committee was established “to ensure the country’s continuous compliance with its obligations under the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights.”
However, Cendaña said the lack of funding for the committee indicates that it is not a priority of the administration.

"If there is no budget, it means it is not a priority. So if it is not a priority, it means this is just pinkwashing. That is why we will measure the Marcos administration's commitment to the LGBTQIA community through the budget it allocates for programs for our community," Cendaña said.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: PISA 2025: Philippines breaks out of bottom 10, sees best lift in reading
articles.summary: The Philippines has secured its highest score in reading, mathematics and science, since the country first joined the PISA in 2018, though they remain below the OECD average.

blocks.text: September 8, 2026 | 3:52pm
Students look for their room assignment as classes open for the new school year at an elementary school in Manila on June 8, 2026.
AFP / Jam Sta Rosa

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippines posted its highest scores in science, mathematics and reading since the country joined the PISA in 2018, according to results released Tuesday, September 8 — but nearly two-thirds of Filipino students still fall below the test's baseline proficiency.
The Philippines scored 373 in science, up 17 points from 2022; 371 in mathematics, up 16; and 367 in reading, up 20.
The reading gain alone is worth roughly a year of schooling by the OECD's own rule of thumb, which treats 20 points as one year's worth of learning.

On the OECD's trend chart, which tracks all countries' mean performance in reading comprehension, the Philippines sits at the very top of the positive-trend column — ahead of Cambodia, Türkiye and Brunei — while Singapore, the United Kingdom and the United States all register declines.
The Philippines' 2025 showing has allowed it to escape a flatline trend since its last two participations in PISA.

In 2018, its first cycle, the Philippines ranked last of 79 countries in reading and second-lowest in mathematics and science. In 2022 it placed sixth-lowest in mathematics and reading and third-lowest in science among 81 countries.

The OECD average this cycle is 482 in science, 463 in mathematics and 461 in reading. That leaves Filipino students 109 points behind in science, 94 in reading and 92 in mathematics — between four and five years of schooling by the OECD's conversion.
Some 64.3% of Filipino students scored below Level 2 in science, reading and mathematics, the threshold the OECD treats as the minimum for participating in everyday economic and social life.
Only 0.3% of Filipino students reached Level 5 or 6, the top bands.

Part of the leaps made by the Philippines in this PISA round came after other countries' decline in all three subjects. Data shows OECD averages fell in all three subjects this cycle, by 15 points in reading, nine in mathematics and three in science.
According to the OECD, the organization that administers the PISA, the Philippines is the "fastest improving" nation in terms of reading comprehension.

articles.title: Ban on neo-Nazi White Australia party is ‘authoritarian’ and breaches constitution, high court hears
articles.summary: Lawyers also argue commonwealth does not have the power to ban a political party, as the high court ruled in 1951 over attempt to ban the Communist party

blocks.text: Lawyers for an outlawed neo-Nazi political party have argued anti-hate laws passed after the Bondi terror attack rely on the opinion of a politician and are “authoritarian in nature”.

The White Australia party, formerly known as the National Socialist Network (NSN), was designated as an illegal hate group in May after the Australian Security and Intelligence Organisation passed on its recommendation to the home affairs minister, Tony Burke.
The listing means that activities including supporting, funding, training, recruiting and joining the group constitute a criminal offence with a maximum penalty of 15 years in prison.

The far-right nationalist party is challenging the ban at the high court over two days this week, with its lawyers arguing the law breaches the implied freedom of political communication and that handing the decision to Burke breaches the separation of powers.

Lawyers also argued the commonwealth does not have the power to ban political parties, citing a major cold war-era high court ruling in 1951, which overturned a ban on the Communist party of Australia.
If successful, the ruling could wind back the laws that have also banned the Islamist group Hizb ut-Tahrir.
On Tuesday, the group’s barristers, Peter King and Shahed Sharify, argued a total ban on the party was akin to using a “sledgehammer on a nut”.

The arguments centre on proving part 5.3B of the criminal code – which allows the federal police minister to recommend to the attorney general that a group is listed as a prohibited hate group – is invalid.

Sharify argued the law’s breach of implied freedom of political communication was “authoritarian in nature” and suggested it could be used to ban any political party where its members had threatened or engaged in a hate crime with the assistance of the organisation.
The barrister said the banning of hate groups was determined by a politician, based on an opinion with no judicial fairness to appeal that decision.
Sharify said the law’s purposes would be better served by handing that decision to a judge rather than a “busy minister who flicks through a brief and decides in two hours”.
Acting for the government, Brendan Lim, denied the laws could be used for the “illegitimate purpose of quelling political competition”.
“It can’t happen,” he said.
Groups can be listed if it is considered “reasonably necessary to protect the Australian community or part of the Australian community against social, psychological, physical or economic harm”.
after newsletter promotion

Under the rules, Burke must receive advice from the head of Asio recommending that an organisation be considered for listing. The home affairs minister must then receive written agreement from the attorney general and brief the opposition leader.
Unlike the terrorist group listing, a listed hate group cannot make a de-listing application.
The government is also expected to defend the anti-hate laws by arguing the party is not a political party but an arm of White Australia, itself a rebranded version of NSN.
“Forming a political party was a calculated attempt to secure legal protection for members engaging in openly racist and anti-Semitic speech,” the commonwealth said in written submissions.
Members of the White Australia party sat in the front of the courtroom’s public benches, including its leader, Tom Sewell.
The 33-year-old was sentenced in June to a community corrections order – which includes 200 hours of community work – for behaving in an offensive manner in public.
A Melbourne magistrate had found the neo-Nazi leader emulated “Nazi thugs of 1930s Berlin” when he used “appalling racial slurs” during a stunt outside a Chinese consulate.

articles.title: Billionaire Chris Rokos, who paid £330m in tax last year, to quit UK
articles.summary: Hedge fund tycoon is latest financier to exit amid fears among super-rich over tax rises

blocks.text: The hedge fund billionaire Chris Rokos is poised to leave the UK, the latest in a string of high-profile exits among Britain’s super-rich.
The founder of Rokos Capital Management is preparing to move his residency to Greece, and will open an office in Athens as part of the move, according to Bloomberg.

He joins a number of billionaires who have left the UK, which many have blamed on the abolition of the non-dom regime, as well as higher tax on private equity investments, inheritance and capital gains.

Rokos, who founded his firm in 2015, was ranked third in the Sunday Times’s annual list of top taxpayers in the UK, paying an estimated bill of £330m in 2025. He has a net worth of about $4bn (£2.96bn), according to Bloomberg’s billionaires index.
This year he also made a record £190m donation to the University of Cambridge to fund the creation of the Rokos School of Government.
Rokos, who went to a state primary school before being offered a scholarship to Eton college and studying maths at Oxford, said at the time that he “would like to give something back to Britain”.

The publicity-shy tycoon and former Tory donor has spent much of the past decade presiding over one of England’s most expensive home renovations ever, of the 200-room Tottenham House mansion near Marlborough in Wiltshire, adding a tennis pavilion and private cinema in the £175m revamp.

Greece offers a 15-year high-net worth investor regime, which requires individuals to invest at least €500,000 ($430,000) in real estate, businesses or shares based in Greece within three years of applying for the tax status. In exchange, they can pay a flat tax of €100,000 a year on their income earned abroad.
His exit comes after the chancellor, John Healey, who will present his debut budget in October, said in his first big speech on Monday that he wanted to see Britain “as a country of wealth creation”.
Andy Burnham has previously expressed support for higher taxation on wealth, although in July signalled that he would not increase such taxes immediately after becoming prime minister.

There have been several high-profile exits from the UK after the Conservative chancellor Jeremy Hunt laid out plans to overhaul the non-dom system in 2024. They include Shravin Bharti Mittal, an heir of one of India’s richest families; Nassef Sawiris, an Egyptian investor; and Richard Gnodde, a veteran Goldman Sachs banker.
after newsletter promotion

Gnodde left for Milan, while Sawiris is reported to be resident in Italy and Abu Dhabi. Mittal listed the United Arab Emirates as his residency after previously naming the UK in an official registry filing.

The Labour government brought in a new regime last year, under which foreign income and gains are subject to UK tax after four years rather than the previous 15. A new residence-based system means also that their global assets are subject to inheritance tax after 10 years.

While there have been several high-profile moves, the extent to which higher tax has triggered an exodus of wealthy people is not yet clear in official data. The latest provisional figures show a modest 0.5% decline in the number of non-domiciled residents in the tax year ended in April last year, at 73,400.

Other European countries have created tax regimes designed to draw in rich foreigners, including Italy, which has proved a popular destination owing to its flat tax of €300,000 on foreign-sourced income.
A representative for Rokos was approached for comment.

articles.title: Ukraine’s prosecutor general resigns after corruption allegations as Russia resumes strikes on Kyiv – Europe live
articles.summary:
Ruslan Kravchenko leaves post after his offices were searched at the weekend, as Moscow renews attacks after pause for peace talks

Separately, European Commission president Ursula…

blocks.text: Morning opening: Ukraine's prosecutor general resigns as Russia resumes attacks

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa

Ukraine’s prosecutor general, Ruslan Kravchenko, resigned from his post over corruption accusations that saw anti-graft officers search his offices at the weekend as part of investigations into illegal call centres, AFP reported.

In a statement, Ruslav Kravchenko has denied he was involved in the alleged scheme, and said his resignation was a “political decision” as he wanted to avoid his position being used “as an instrument of political confrontation.”

His decision to step down poses another challenge for Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy after tricky summer which involved a government reshuffle and a political crisis linked to his controversial decision to sack popular defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov.
The latest political crisis comes as Russia has resumed its attacks on Kyiv after a brief pause over the weekend intended to facilitate peace talks with senior US representatives.

“It was a complex attack that the Russians tried to plan to cause as much harm to life as possible – ballistic missiles, cruise and anti-ship missiles, and jet-powered shaheds. There is significant damage to residential buildings and other civilian infrastructure in the capital,” Zelenskyy said this morning.
At least two people died in the attack, and 10 were injured. Further attacks were also reported in Dnipro, Kharkiv, Sumy and Zaporizhzhia.

Elsewhere, I will keep an eye on the latest from Germany as the fallout from the Saxony-Anhalt election continues, and on reports from France about thieves stealing four works of French impressionist painter Auguste Renoir during a night heist at a museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer.
It’s Tuesday, 8 September 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.

blocks.text: Four artworks stolen from Renoir museum in southern France
Two thieves have broken into a museum dedicated to the French impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir in southern France, stealing four artworks and dropping one as they fled, the mayor has said.

blocks.caption: A police officer patrols in front of the entrance of the Musee Renoir after four paintings were stolen from the museum with two suspects still at large, in Cagnes-sur-Mer France. Photograph: Valéry Hache/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: “This morning, two individuals broke into the Renoir Museum and stole four works of art,” said Bryan Masson, the far-right mayor of the town of Cagnes-sur-Mer.

“Spotted thanks to the town’s video surveillance cameras, the two individuals fled, abandoning one of the stolen paintings as they ran,” he said, adding that his office estimated the value of the stolen works at €9m (£7.7m).

The museum was opened in 1960 in the painter’s last home before his death in 1919. Its collection includes objects and furniture that belonged to Renoir, including his easel and wheelchair, as well as portraits, landscapes and nudes painted by the artist.
The mayor said it took five minutes for the authorities to respond. “The museum alarm went off at 5.48 am. At 5.53 am, just five minutes later, our municipal police were on the scene,” he said.

The theft comes less than a year after eight items valued at around €88m were stolen during a daylight robbery from the Louvre in Paris. The four suspected Louvre robbers have been arrested, but the stolen items have not been found despite extensive searches by French investigators in the Paris region, and exchanges with police in Belgium, Italy and beyond.
Art thieves in ‌Europe are committing more violent robberies and specialist gangs have ​been replaced by ad-hoc opportunists recruited through social media, Europol said last month.
EU's von der Leyen condemns 'shocking' funeral of Mladić in Serbia

Separately, European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen has condemned the presence of senior Serbian officials at yesterday’s funeral of Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladić, saying it showed “a failure to confront a dark chapter in Europe’s recent history” and questioned Serbia’s alignment with the EU.

blocks.caption: People gathered for the funeral procession wave a flag showing the former Bosnian Serb army commander Ratko Mladić on the day of his funeral. Photograph: Srđan Stevanović/Getty Images

blocks.text: Mladić, who died last week, was buried with military honours in after a memorial service attended by tens of thousands of people and led by Porfirije, the patriarch of the Serbian Orthodox church.
In a statement this morning, von der Leyen said:

“The images from Ratko Mladić’s funeral yesterday in Belgrade were shocking. Ratko Mladić was a convicted war criminal. He was responsible for genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity. He died while serving a life sentence for the Srebrenica genocide and other crimes. The elements of official support and the presence of some senior Serbian officials at the funeral are deeply regrettable. They demonstrate a failure to confront a dark chapter in Europe’s recent history and contradict the values underpinning Serbia’s path towards the European Union. Our thoughts are with all the victims of the crimes committed in the countries of former Yugoslavia.”

articles.title: Renoir Museum robbery: Three paintings missing
articles.summary: Police are on the hunt for thieves who stole three paintings from the Renoir Museum on the French Riviera in an overnight heist. A fourth stolen work was abandoned as they fled.

image.caption: The Renoir Museum occupies the former home of Impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste RenoirImage: Johanna Hoelzl/picture alliance

blocks.text: Two thieves have stolen three paintings from the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer on the French Riviera after breaking into the building early on Tuesday, the town's mayor said.
The heist follows a series of high-profile art and cultural-property thefts in Europe.
What happened at the Renoir Museum?
The thieves initially took four artworks, valued together at around €9 million ($10.5 million), but abandoned one as they fled.
The thieves broke into the museum shortly before 6 a.m., Mayor Bryan Masson said.
They were detected with the help of the town's video surveillance system. Police gave chase, but the pair escaped.
"During their flight, they abandoned one of the stolen paintings," Masson said.
Authorities did not immediately identify the three works that remained missing.

The museum occupies the former home and studio of French Impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir, who spent the final years of his life in Cagnes-sur-Mer. The property is surrounded by gardens and olive trees.
This is a developing story that will be updated...

articles.title: UK-US trade could suffer as a result of sanctions for illegal Israeli settlements, American ambassador warns – UK politics live
articles.summary:
UK foreign secretary to reassert support for Palestinian rights and a two-state solution in move drawing criticism from US and Israel

Good morning. It is hard to understand Labour/leftwing…

blocks.text: UK-US trade could suffer as a result of sanctions for illegal Israeli settlements, American ambassador warns

Good morning. It is hard to understand Labour/leftwing politics in the UK at the moment without reference to Israel and Gaza. Keir Starmer’s popularity with some progressive voters slumped in part because he was seen as unwilling to do enough to channel the anger they feel about how Israel is treating Palestinians – even though last year he took the historic step of formally recognising the state of Palestine. Quite a lot of what Andy Burnham has done in his early days as PM has had a “continuity Starmer” flavour, but today the new government will take a bold step that will recast the UK/Israel relationship, acting where the Starmer administration just dragged its feet.
In a statement to MPs, Ed Miliband, the new foreign secretary, will announce that Britain is banning trade with illegal Israeli settlements on the West Bank. Patrick Wintour has the story here.

For years, successive governments – Labour and Conservative – have condemned the decades-long expansion of Israeli settlements on Palestinian land on the West Bank – while doing precious little about it. But with Benjamin Netanyahu’s government escalating the process, Miliband will tell MPs that action is necessary now to stop the prospect of a two-state solution (Israel living alongside a viable Palestinian state) being killed off for good.

As Patrick reports in his story, Miliband is not giving pro-Palestinian supporters everything they are asking for. Quite what impact the measures will have on Israel remains to be seen. But it is still a big shift in policy. And, conveniently for Labour, it is coming just a day after the party moved the writ for the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, where what was a safe Labour seat is under threat from the pro-Palestinian Green party.

But the move isn’t without risks. The Conservatives argue that anything that jeopardises Israeli security cooperation with the UK could increase the terrorism risk to Britons. There are concerns that any government policy that stigmatises Israel is likely to heighten antisemitism. And there have been warnings that Israel and its allies – particularly the US – could retaliate.
This morning Mike Huckabee, the US ambassador to Israel, has said exactly that. In an interview, he told the Today programme:

double quotation markI don’t know if [the British government is] really aware of the implications and how it’s going to affect Brits. For example, 25% of pharmaceuticals that are used in the UK are made in Israel. Are they willing to give those up? It looks like they are. Are they willing also to do great damage to any Brits who are doing business in a number of states in the US? I don’t know what all of the national sanctions or repercussions or retaliations will be from the US. [That] hasn’t been announced yet. But I do know that there are a number of states – let me mention one, one of the largest US states, Florida – it has a law that if this action is taken, then Brits will not be able to do business with any company or business in Florida.

Huckabee – a very rightwing Republican and former governor, who like most US ambassadors was appointed because he was close to the president – went even further at the weekend, accusing the UK government of “Jew hate”.
I will post more from his interview soon.
Here is the agenda.
Morning: Andy Burnham chairs cabinet.
11.30am: John Healey, the chancellor, takes questions in the Commons.
Noon: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.
After 12.30pm: Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, makes a statement to MPs about his plan to impose a ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlements.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.
Key events

20m agoUK-US trade could suffer as a result of sanctions for illegal Israeli settlements, American ambassador warns

blocks.text: Tories dismiss ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlements as 'performative posturing'

The Conservatives have described the proposed ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlements as “performative posturing”. Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, used the phrase on the Today programme when he was asked about the announcement coming today.
Philp said:

double quotation markWe think it’s performative posturing. It’s very difficult to distinguish goods that come from the West Bank area versus the rest of Israel. So practically, it’s very difficult to implement. It also risks damaging an important security relationship because we do rely, the UK relies, on Israel for vital information and intelligence about terrorist threats. But I would also like to say, that said, we do oppose the building of settlements on land which is Palestinian, whether that’s sponsored by the Israeli state or simply allowed to happen, because we do think a two-state solution is the right solution, and building settlements on Palestinian land is obviously wrong.
The full details of the ban have not been announced. But the Foreign Office has not challenged the accounts of what Ed Miliband is expected to say later today.

articles.title: Romualdez ordered to appear in Sandiganbayan on Sept. 10
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Sandiganbayan Third Division has ordered former House Speaker Martin Romualdez to appear before the anti-graft court on Thursday, Sept. 10, for the hearing of his motion for…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Sandiganbayan Third Division has ordered former House Speaker Martin Romualdez to appear before the anti-graft court on Thursday, Sept. 10, for the hearing of his motion for continued hospital confinement.
Romualdez, who faces a non-bailable plunder case, has yet to appear before the anti-graft court as he remains hospitalized at the Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City.
“Accused Romualdez is directed to appear before the court should his condition permit,” the court order stated.
The court emphasized that custody of Romualdez already belongs to the court.

“If there are concerns regarding the accused’s medical condition, it is only this court that can determine whether such condition affects the implementation of the warrant, the confinement of the accused at a hospital, or his commitment to a jail facility,” the order further stated.
The Third Division also issued subpoenas ad testificandum to Romualdez’s doctors Rody Sy, Rogelio Libarres, Kurt Allen Sibayan and Rosalio Torres.

The Philippine National Police on Tuesday returned Romualdez’s warrant of arrest for plunder, after he did not appear in court as he filed an Urgent Motion ad Cautelam for Continued Hospital Confinement with the Third Division in a bid to extend his hospital confinement.
Police served Romualdez’s arrest warrant, and the lawmaker also underwent booking procedures while in confinement.
In his motion, Romualdez said he is suffering from Type 2 diabetes, hypertension, primary hypothyroidism and other illnesses.

The Sandiganbayan Third Division issued an arrest warrant against Romualdez, former Ako Bicol Rep. Zaldy Co and two others hours after the Office of the Ombudsman filed the information containing the formal charges against the accused.

According to the information containing the formal charges filed by prosecutors before the anti-graft court, Romualdez and Co were charged with “repeatedly receiving, directly or indirectly, on at least 15 occasions, commissions, shares, percentages, kickbacks, ‘commitments’ and/or other pecuniary benefits” worth at least P7.44 billion.

The amount allegedly came from contractors, persons and entities with interests in flood control, infrastructure and/or other government projects funded under the General Appropriations Acts for fiscal years 2022 to 2025, according to the information.
Romualdez, in response, said he respects the legal process and will face the allegations against him in accordance with the law, according to his counsel Ade Fajardo. /mcm

articles.title: 2,320 Bukidnon scholars to get ‘finisher fund’ worth P46.4M
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Some 2,320 graduating college students in Bukidnon are set to receive P46.4 million in financial assistance from the Office of the President (OP), Executive Secretary…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Some 2,320 graduating college students in Bukidnon are set to receive P46.4 million in financial assistance from the Office of the President (OP), Executive Secretary Ralph Recto said in a statement on Tuesday.
Malacañang referred to the assistance as a “finisher fund,” with each student receiving P20,000 under the OP’s Socio-Civic Projects Fund.
The money may be used for tuition balances, transportation, learning materials and other school-related expenses.

According to Malacañang, Recto discussed the program during a meeting with the 155 Presidential Scholars from Quezon town last Sept. 4, after inspecting the ongoing construction of the Bukidnon Airport.
The 155 scholars come from the municipality’s 31 barangays, with five students selected from each barangay. They are among the 2,320 beneficiaries identified across Bukidnon.
Recto said the assistance would help students who face financial difficulties during the final stage of their college education.
“Hindi dapat mapurnada ang ilang taong pagsisikap dahil lamang kapos ang pamilya sa panghuling gastos,” Recto explained in a statement.
(Years’ worth of hard work should not be foiled just because a family runs short of the last expenses they need.)
The Bukidnon beneficiaries are part of a nationwide program expected to assist more than 200,000 graduating college students from over 42,000 barangays.
Under the Presidential Scholars Program, each barangay receives P100,000 to provide P20,000 each to five college students.
The assistance is part of the government’s broader efforts to provide financial support and access to higher education. With reports from Rendell Ivan Manuel, INQUIRER.net trainee /mr

articles.title: PNP seeks P1.5B for infrastructure under proposed 2027 budget
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police (PNP) is seeking nearly P1.5 billion for infrastructure projects under its proposed P242.53-billion budget for 2027, as it continues assessing…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police (PNP) is seeking nearly P1.5 billion for infrastructure projects under its proposed P242.53-billion budget for 2027, as it continues assessing police stations and other facilities for repairs and improvements, the agency said Tuesday.
In a statement, the PNP said the proposed budget is about P16 billion higher than the P226.55 billion appropriated for the agency in 2026.

Of the proposed 2027 budget, P1.499 billion is earmarked for infrastructure projects, while P2 billion is allocated for the Capability Enhancement Program, covering mobility, communications, firepower and anti-terrorism equipment.
Another P3.12 billion is proposed for information and communications technology.
PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said the assessment of police stations and other facilities is ongoing, particularly those affected by tropical cyclones and heavy rains in recent weeks.
The assessment will help determine which facilities need to be constructed, repaired or improved, according to the PNP.
Nartatez said the PNP would ensure that funds allocated for infrastructure projects are used properly to improve police services.
“Police stations serve as the frontline of PNP services to the Filipino people, and we are committed to ensuring that all our facilities are accessible and presentable at all times,” Nartatez said.
The infrastructure allocation, Nartatez added, would also help provide police personnel with facilities that better support their duties.
The proposed budget remains subject to congressional deliberations and approval. — Rendell Ivan Manuel, INQUIRER.net trainee /das

articles.title: Pakistan: Can creating new provinces fix governance?
articles.summary: A politically sensitive debate has reignited in Pakistan over whether its four-province system can effectively govern a country of around 260 million people. Ahsan Iqbal, minister for planning and…

blocks.text: A politically sensitive debate has reignited in Pakistan over whether its four-province system can effectively govern a country of around 260 million people.

Ahsan Iqbal, minister for planning and development, recently called for a national political debate on administrative reform. He proposed creating 12 to 15 new provinces or setting up 160 empowered district governments to improve governance and the delivery of public services.
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, who first raised the idea of an administrative “reset” in July, said on Saturday that any new administrative units should be created with public support.
Defense Minister Khawaja Asif, meanwhile, has called for greater decentralization and devolution of power to the grassroots.
Despite the growing calls to create new provinces, no formal decision has been taken.
Even within the ruling coalition, there is disagreement over how and when such reforms should be pursued.
There are also questions about whether creating smaller provinces improves governance, or whether devolving power directly to local governments would be more effective.
More provinces, better governance?
Pakistanis broadly agree that the country needs more responsive and effective government, but many question whether creating more provinces is the solution.

“Smaller provinces are not a substitute for empowered local governments. Even with smaller provinces, you will still need empowered local governments to make the system effective and improve service delivery to the people,” Miftah Ismail, a former finance minister and economist, told DW.
Supporters of creating more provinces argue that Pakistan’s four existing provinces — Punjab, Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and Balochistan — have become too large and overly centralized.
Iqbal, the planning minister, has argued that the existing system has not delivered adequate improvements in health, education, and other social services.
Interior Minister Naqvi, on the other hand, has called for an administrative structure that is better suited to Pakistan’s growing population.
But there is disagreement over the solution.

“Without effective local governments, whether there is one province or 25, decision-making will remain centralized at the provincial level,” Abid Qaiyum Suleri, executive director of the Sustainable Development Policy Institute, an Islamabad-based think tank, told DW.

He said any proposal for new provinces or administrative units should be assessed against potential improvements in local tax collection and the costs of creating new provincial institutions, including secretariats, assemblies, and bureaucracies.
Suleri stressed that it should also be examined whether such changes would deliver justice and public services more effectively.
Altering the political balance

“Pakistan’s history suggests that empowering local governments is a better choice in terms of governance and provision of services,” Muhammad Shoaib, a political scientist and assistant professor at Quaid-i-Azam University in Islamabad, told DW.
The debate, therefore, is not simply about how many provinces Pakistan should have, but whether creating smaller units would actually make the government more responsive to citizens.
Creating new provinces could also affect the political balance in the country.
New provinces would mean new governments and assemblies, while potentially changing political representation and the distribution of federal resources.
Any attempt to redraw boundaries could also reopen disputes over water, taxation, and natural resources.

The political resistance has already begun, with Sindh’s provincial assembly has opposed creating new provinces or administrative units in the province, while political groups have warned against dividing existing territories.
A risky strategy?
Shoaib said dividing resources would present a major challenge, even if all provinces were reorganized at the same time.
“Even if all provinces are divided simultaneously, the division of resources like finances, water, and jobs, and special privileges for territories within provinces will be a challenge,” he said.
“Challenges like these require lengthy negotiations and compromises for political consensus,” he added.
The issue is therefore not only about administrative efficiency, as redrawing provincial boundaries could also redistribute political and economic power.
Ismail believes redrawing provincial boundaries would be risky, particularly in Sindh.
He said empowering existing local governments within current provincial boundaries would be a safer option.

“We can learn from the US and the southern states of India, where empowered small administrative units, while competing with each other, are more responsive to citizens and deliver better services,” Ismail said.

Shoaib said Pakistan could also learn from other countries, particularly democratic systems that have empowered local governments and taken time to work through the division of large states into smaller units.
“In Pakistan’s case, the risk of resistance and perpetual resentment is real. A partially finished division will aggravate existing ethnic tensions,” he said.
For Pakistan, the debate is therefore about more than whether the country should have four provinces or 12 or 15.

It is about whether changing the administrative map can actually bring power, resources, and accountability closer to its people, and whether such a transformation can be achieved without creating new political and ethnic tensions. /dl

articles.title: Centuries in the making: Singsons’ unrivaled power in Ilocos Sur
articles.summary: The clan has built an empire in Ilocos Sur and has 16 members currently holding seats in government

items: The Singson clan has maintained a strong political presence in Ilocos Sur for centuries, evolving from a merchant family during the Spanish colonial period to a dominant political dynasty.

Despite facing allegations of corruption and political challenges, the Singsons have successfully retained control over various government positions, with multiple family members holding significant roles in local governance.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
The Singson clan’s rise to power was built over centuries of carefully planned moves that entrenched the family in politics.
From the Spanish colonial period, where the family marks its origins, until today, the Singsons have controlled the province of Ilocos Sur.

They trace their beginnings to the marriage of a Chinese merchant, Joaquin Ayco, and a local from Vigan named Rosa Songnio. It was during the 19th century that the family began its ascent to power through wealth. They held gobernadorcillo positions for five terms and their influence continued over the American and Japanese occupations.

In 1945, the region turned to tobacco as a means of economic recovery, which boomed and led to the conflict between the Singsons and the Crisologo family, then closely intertwined — family patriarch, former Ilocos Sur governor Luis “Chavit” Singson is the nephew of then-congressman Floro Crisologo. Both families became fierce competitors over the tobacco trade.

Floro was assassinated inside a church on October 18, 1970, and the case remains unsolved. The political leadership of the Crisologos ended a year later when the Singson brothers were elected — Chavit became governor and his elder brother Evaristo “Titong” II became Vigan mayor. The family won through Chavit’s promise of streamlining tobacco production.
The clan’s power in the province remains unmatched despite alleged involvement in plunder and graft charges. Only a few have tried to defeat the Singsons and they ultimately failed.

In May 2026, Chavit claimed that 5,500 flood control projects in the country were non-existent. This challenged President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s announcement at his 2024 State of the Nation Address that 5,500 projects were completed nationwide.

He was charged with a private cyber libel complaint in June but was granted bail. Afterwards, Chavit proclaimed during a press conference that he would not be stopped and doubled down on his exposé of the anomalous flood control corruption scandal.

blocks.caption: PATRIARCH. Former Ilocos Sur governor Luis ‘Chavit’ Singson holds a press conference on the flood control controversy on September 19, 2025. Photo by Errol Almario/Rappler

blocks.text: No arrest, case, or political pressure will stop him from revealing the truth, he asserted.
This is not uncharted territory for him. With his family’s decades-long grip on power, he knows exactly how to play the long game.
The Singsons are one of the biggest and oldest political families. They hold numerous seats in the Ilocos Region.
Research by the Philippine Center for Investigative Journalism revealed that in the 2025 elections, Chavit had 23 relatives running for office.
Rappler’s research shows that 16 current officials are members of the Singson clan:

items: Ronald Singson – 1st District Representative (Ilocos Sur)
Richelle Singson Michael – Partylist Representative
Jeremias “Jerry” Crisologo Singson – Governor (Ilocos Sur)
Ryan Luis Singson – Vice Governor (Ilocos Sur)
Ericson Singson – 2nd District Board Member (Ilocos Sur)
Janina Medina-Fariñas – 1st District Board Member (Ilocos Sur)
Fayinna Zaragoza – 2nd District Board Member (Ilocos Sur)
Eric Singson – Mayor (City of Candon)
Randolf “Randy” Singson – Mayor (City of Vigan)
Goulart Germelina Singson – Mayor (Caoayan)
Kristelle Gocho Singson – Vice Mayor (City of Candon)
Juan Paolo Singson Ancheta – Vice Mayor (Caoayan)
Evaristo “Bobit” Singson III – Councilor (City of Vigan)
Jaime “Jimboy” Singson – Councilor (City of Candon) & Philippine Councilors League President – Ilocos Sur Chapter
Luis Charles Singson – Councilor (Narvacan)
