articles.title: Why India’s economic data has sparked a furore
articles.summary:
India’s statistical system once commanded respect, and its data on economic and social indicators was considered rigorous – that appears to have eroded

There isn’t much that we Indians agree…

blocks.text: There isn’t much that we Indians agree on these days. GDP numbers are no exception. Last week, India released glowing GDP numbers for the latest quarter – 7.8% growth – higher than the forecast 7%. It sparked a furore.

Subhash Garg, a former finance secretary under Narendra Modi’s government and now a critic, reframed what Modi called a “herculean feat” as mere smoke and mirrors. According to Garg, the government revised last year’s current-price GDP downwards to inflate this year’s number – he believes the real growth is only 2.6%.

The assertion, made on a television channel, immediately went viral. A flurry of op-eds and hot takes have been published since. Supporters of the government, predictably, rejected the claims. Those who have questions agree on a more fundamental problem: a lack of transparency and statistical credibility in India’s economic data. So why is there no consensus?

Over the past decade, critics say, the government has systematically hollowed out the integrity of its own data infrastructure, weaponising economic data for political gain and creating a trust deficit. Methodologies have been changed, crucial surveys have faced long delays and there have been attempts to suppress inconvenient findings.

In November, the International Monetary Fund rated India’s national accounts data a ‘C’ on a four-point scale, the second-lowest grade. In its report, the IMF said some of the methodologies are outdated, including relying on an old base year, unexplained discrepancies between GDP calculated from the production and expenditure side, as well as a lack of seasonal data.

blocks.caption: Critics say the government has hollowed out the integrity of its own data infrastructure. Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty Images

blocks.text: India’s statistical system once commanded respect, and its data on economic and social indicators was considered rigorous. There might have been disagreements on the quality of estimates but their independence was widely accepted. That trust appears to have eroded in recent years.

“There seems to be a systematic effort by the government to hide the truth,” said R Nagaraj, an economist who taught at the Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, adding that some of the other contested datasets include employment numbers, poverty numbers, health data and consumption data. “Over the last 10 years, the government has changed the methodology for many of these, raising questions. They have apparently also removed critical officials who headed some surveys. All of this adds to the scepticism.”

In one of the most prominent examples, from 2019, a Business Standard journalist revealed that the government had not published an official report showing unemployment at a 45-year high of 6.1%. Two expert members of the National Statistical Commission resigned in protest. The government initially denied it, calling it a draft. The figures were only released months later.

Then there is the census, which for the first time since independence, was delayed in 2021. Economists say relying on outdated demographic data means, among other things, inequitable allocation of welfare entitlements. (The first phase of the latest census finally began in April 2026.)

Nagaraj has witnessed some of this first-hand. He served on a subcommittee in 2014 whose report forms a part of the GDP. “The [numbers] we had discussed in the committee and what came out in the final report were different. So, I had to raise a red flag,” he said. The difference was notable: one figure in the published report had been inflated by 108%.

But government economists reject the ongoing criticism of the GDP numbers. Shamika Ravi, a member of the Economic Advisory Council to the prime minister, described it as a “noisy and very ill-informed debate” arguing that political leanings, not data, are behind the criticism.

The IMF rating was expected, she said. “The IMF rating of ‘C’ is the same rating that China has for its statistics. Several large developing or just developed economies have data issues.” Revisions to its calculations that the government was accused of having manipulated, she added, were precisely the sorts of changes the IMF had recommended.
The sticking point, as some including India’s former chief statistician Pronab Sen have pointed out, is the trustworthiness of the underlying data used.

Complicating this debate is the reality for many Indians. This year, young people have taken to the streets in frustration. Protests, which first began over leaked examination papers, have crystallised into a broader reckoning over systemic failures in education, jobs and the promise of a better future.

blocks.caption: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke at a protest against leaked exam papers, as young people in India face soaring rates of unemployment. Photograph: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Almost 40% of graduates under 25 are unemployed, a recent report by Azim Premji University concluded. An estimated 87 million (8.7 crore) Indians between 15 and 29 are neither working, studying, nor doing skill training, a government thinktank reported last month.

That is why we should care about data quality, economists say. Incorrect data means bad policy. As economist Reetika Khera wrote in her recent book, Freebies or Rights: “Data shines the light to guide policymaking and is important for informed public debates.” As evidence, she points to gaps in basic statistics such as urbanisation and literacy numbers due to the delayed census. The consequences, she argues, are not abstract. Because the government still relies on outdated population numbers to decide who gets food subsidies, she estimates approximately 100 million (10 crore) people who should be covered are being deprived.

The controversy is making waves further ashore. In Sri Lanka, where second-quarter GDP figures are expected, the Daily FT newspaper wrote: “One hopes Sri Lankan policymakers and experts are not watching the theatrics in India with watering mouths and dreaming up smart arguments. Spare us such theatre!”
What else we’re reading about

blocks.caption: Mumbai bound … British singer Olivia Dean is headed to Lollapalooza. Photograph: Isabel Infantes/Reuters

blocks.text: Lollapalooza | British pop star Olivia Dean is to perform in India for the first time in January when she headlines Lollapalooza 2027 in Mumbai. Limp Bizkit is another headline act at the two-day event. Indian artists on the lineup include Ricky Kej (performing with Stewart Copeland) and Aditya Gadhvi.

The price of gold | Prime Minister Narendra Modi asked Indians once again to refrain from buying gold and travelling abroad. He had first made an appeal to self-reliance in May, in part to conserve India’s declining foreign exchange reserves amid a rise in import prices and global energy shocks.

Census 2027 | The new and expanded questionnaire for the 2027 census is raising concerns, reports Scroll’s Anant Gupta. The questionnaire asks respondents for details about their identity documents, as well as their parents’ religion and place of birth. Several of these questions were part of the controversial National Population Register that has remained in abeyance since 2020 and was controversial due to fears that the data might be used to target minorities through a citizenship registry.

blocks.text: Singer Prateek Kuhad (@prateekkuhad), whose latest album, Full Moon Chamber, was released in July, shares an indulgent treat: “I’m a big fan of artisanal Indian chocolate makers. I really like Manam, Carra and Naviluna, and there are many others. Although India has been growing cacao [commercially] since the 1960s, its craft bean-to-bar movement is more recent. Even a plain chocolate bar from one of these makers can be remarkably complex and delicious. More people outside India should know about it and try it.”

Vibe check

blocks.caption: First of many mashups … Ismail Langa Group pose with a larger-than-life image of Shakira. Photograph: Ismail Langa

blocks.text: Earlier this year, Shakira’s concerts in India was postponed. But Rajasthani folk musicians the Ismail Langa Group (@ismaillanga_official) decided the music had to go on, in their own way. Their mashup of the Colombian star’s Hips Don’t Lie with the traditional folk song called Moruda has got everyone grooving (42m views and counting).

It took two months to pull off, says creative director Jagirdar RV. Most artists in the group, aged between 23 and 60, don’t speak or read English and learned the lyrics by rote. The song choice was simple, he said, because it “has a very nice vibe which matched our vibe”.

It’s been a breakout year for the group, which had a semi-final run on India’s Got Talent and are becoming known for taking folk songs to gen Z audiences on Instagram. They are working on their next English mashup – just not spilling which song, yet.

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Post offering cash, livelihood aid under Bong Go’s name is fake
articles.summary: The post claims to offer P29,000 in livelihood aid from Senator Bong Go, but its registration link redirects users to an unrelated website listing job vacancies

blocks.text: Claim: People in need of livelihood assistance can receive P29,000 from Senator Bong Go by registering online.
Why we fact checked this: An anonymous Facebook account posted the graphic in the “DSWD Cash Assistance Update PayOut” group on August 31. The group has 602,100 members as of writing.

The graphic claims that people who have no source of livelihood can receive P29,000 from Senator Bong Go by registering online. The post uses Go’s name and photo alongside the logos of government agencies, including the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD).
It also includes supposed registration links for the alleged livelihood assistance program.
The facts: The post is fake. There is no indication that the supposed P29,000 cash assistance advertised in the graphic is offered through an official government program.
In a Facebook post on September 5, Go warned the public against social media posts offering livelihood or investment assistance in his name.
“Huwag maniwala sa mga social media post na nangangako na magbibigay ng puhunan o pangkabuhayan na tulong sa pangalan ni Senator Bong Go. Walang Palista Program si Senator Bong Go,” the post read.
(Do not believe social media posts that promise Senator Bong Go will give business capital or livelihood assistance. Senator Bong Go does not have such a program.)
The senator also reminded the public not to provide their personal information through dubious links or social media posts.

Fake link: The supposed registration link included in the post redirects users to a website containing local and international job listings. Clicking “Apply Now” on the website redirects users to a job search website.
The job listings have no apparent connection to the P29,000 cash assistance promised in the Facebook post.

This is not the first time Go’s name has been used in a false cash assistance offer. In May 2025, Go debunked a Facebook post bearing his photo and the Senate logo that falsely claimed he was offering P5,000 in cash assistance to people who messaged a Facebook page. He warned the public against clicking suspicious links that ask for personal information, saying these could expose users to potential scams. (READ: Phishing 101: How to spot and avoid phishing)

Not offered by DSWD: The DSWD does not have a program that provides the P29,000 cash assistance advertised in the post, particularly one distributed through or associated with a specific politician. The department instead provides assistance through established programs such as the Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situations (AICS), which offers financial and other forms of aid to qualified individuals based on their circumstances and after assessment by DSWD social workers.

To apply for aid under AICS, applicants are required to submit a valid identification card and supporting documents appropriate to the type of assistance being requested to the nearest DSWD field office, Social Welfare and Development Office, or satellite office.

The DSWD has also repeatedly warned the public about fraudulent social media posts and messages promising cash assistance. In February 2026, the agency warned against scammers offering supposed DSWD cash aid in exchange for personal information. The DSWD said these offers were not authorized by any of its offices.

In April 2026, the agency again clarified that it does not ask for personal information through text messages or private social media messages in exchange for financial assistance. It also warned against posts asking people to pay a fee to receive cash aid, emphasizing that DSWD does not charge any amount to receive financial assistance.

The agency has likewise clarified that applications for its programs are not processed through private social media accounts, personal messages, or unauthorized intermediaries, and that there is no “backer system” for obtaining or expediting assistance. – Mark David Silencio/Rappler.com

Mark David Silencio is an Information Technology student at Bulacan State University in Plaridel, Bulacan. An Aries Rufo Journalism Fellow for 2026, he is also the managing editor for Administration of Pacesetter.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

items: Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. criticized China for disrespecting international law during the Seoul Defense Dialogue, particularly regarding the 2016 Arbitral Award affirming the Philippines' maritime rights.
Teodoro received a note from a Chinese representative during the dialogue, which he interpreted as a sign of China's coercive behavior and lack of decency in international forums.
The Philippines has taken a firmer stance against China under President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., leading to strained bilateral relations and confrontations in the South China Sea.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines — At a dialogue attended by defense and military officials, Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. criticized Beijing for “disrespecting” international law and the crowd at the Seoul Defense Dialogue after he was slipped a note apparently outlining China’s position and rejection of the landmark 2016 Arbitral Award.

In a video clip posted by the Department of National Defense on Tuesday, September 8, Teodoro, a sitting Cabinet official sanctioned by China, is interrupted mid-answer as someone hands him a note on a piece of paper.

“I have a note here. I think this is from China,” said Teodoro, among the loudest voices in the Philippines against Beijing’s actions in maritime, domestic, and even diplomatic spaces. Teodoro spoke during the first plenary session of the forum, titled “Collaborative Architecture for International Stability.”

Teodoro went on to comment on China’s stand on the landmark ruling, which affirmed the Philippines’ 200-nautical mile exclusive economic zone in the South China Sea that it calls the West Philippine Sea. The same award found China’s historical claim of the vast waterway without basis, and said Beijing’s island building activities damaged the fragile marine ecosystem.

China has refused to recognize the award and calls it “illegal, null, and void” even if it ought to be binding under United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), of which Beijing is a signatory to.

blocks.caption: Teodoro hits China at Seoul forum: ‘Maging disente naman kayo’

blocks.text: After criticizing Beijing’s stand line by line, Teodoro said: “How can you deal with a country in an international forum — beyond the question asked to me — disrespecting the organizers of this forum? How do you expect to deal with it civily?”

“Is this the right paper to post to me when I’m asked a question on the floor? And how will you treat this kind of behavior? If this is a Chinese position sent to me, it not only disrespects international law — throwing UNCLOS to the floor and trampling upon it — but it also disepresects the basic decency that should be accorded to our most gracious host, the Republic of Korea and the audience here. Perhaps basic decency and behavior is what China needs to do,” said Teodoro.
The audience at the dialogue erupted into a strong, albeit initially hesistant, round of applause.
He added: “In Filipino, maging disente lang kayo ng kaunti, mahiya naman kayo ng kaunti (Try to show some shame and decency).”
Teodoro said the note was proof of “actual coercion, bullying, and aggression.”
“We need to coalesce,” he said.
The plenary session that Teodoro was a part of was centered on how “norms and multilateral institutions… [are] once again being tested by today’s international security environment.”

The conference note for the session reads: “Discussions will focus on restoring strategic trust, preventing crises and managing conflicts, strengthening the effectiveness of multilateral institutions, enhancing the roles of international organizations and regional security frameworks, and designing governance mechanisms that encompass security, economic, and technological domains.”

“I will keep this paper as a memento of how desperate China, is and how ineffective its position is in the face of a real audience. Thank you very much to the person who gave me this piece of paper. You have just done your country a great favor and I hope you don’t suffer in a gulag for it,” said Teodoro, eliciting another round of applause.

This is not the first — and is unlikely to be the last — time Teodoro has taken China to task at an international forum. At the Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore, the region’s premier defense forum, Teodoro has twice openly lambasted Beijing over its actions in the South China Sea and beyond.
At the 2026 edition of the forum, Teodoro warned against trusting Beijing as Southeast Asian countries and China seek to conclude negotiations on a code of conduct for the South China Sea.
Shortly after those remarks in Singapore, Beijing imposed sanctions on Teodoro, his wife, and son. He is the first sitting Cabinet member of the Marcos administration to be sanctioned by China.

Bilateral ties between Manila and Beijing have been strained in recent years, as the Philippines under President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has taken a stronger stance on the West Philippine Sea and in implementing the 2016 Arbitral Award.
Manila’s assertion of both its entitlements and claims has meant tense confrontations between Philippine and Chinese maritime forces in flashpoints in the South China Sea. — Rappler.com

articles.title: ‘It breaks my heart’: far-right’s big election victory sparks dismay in German state capital
articles.summary:
Fears expressed for immigrants and for country’s future after AfD vote hits historic high in Saxony-Anhalt

Maryam and her best friend were ambling through Magdeburg toward the railway…

blocks.text: Maryam and her best friend were ambling through Magdeburg toward the railway station, talking over the dramatic events of the previous evening and the surge by the far-right Alternative für Deutschland to a historically high vote in the Saxony-Anhalt elections.
“Don’t laugh at me,” she said, “but I wish we could go back to the days of Angela Merkel, when things were OK in Germany”.
The teenagers, from nearby Wolmirstedt, said they were shocked by the AfD’s landslide win. But they felt powerless to do much about it and felt afraid about where it might take their home state.
“We talk about it all the time,” said Maryam, whose name has been changed. “It’s on my mind constantly. My dad came to Germany from Syria in 2015. My mum and I joined him two years later.”

The first clause of the anti-immigrant AfD’s 100-day programme says that – “from the first moment” of being in power – the party will deport people it deems “irregular migrants”. Maryam believes her family could well face deportation.

blocks.caption: Franz Josef and Christiane Jäker say populists are ruining everything Germany has created since the second world war.  Photograph: Kate Connolly/The Guardian

blocks.text: “We have to renew our residency permits every three years as it is. We’ve always lived in a state of uncertainty. Now after these election results we face going back to Syria which we don’t think is safe, and I can’t even read or write Arabic.”

The AfD won almost 44% of the vote in Sunday’s election, more than even it had hoped for. Doreen, 54, did not immediately admit to having supported the party, but said later in an interview she had put her faith in what she termed “the blues” “out of a sense of desperation”.
When challenged about the human impact the party’s policies could have, for example on immigrant families, she shrugged: “It is what it is.”
“If they [refugees] hadn’t turned up here in such large numbers in the first place, they wouldn’t have to go through such heart-breaking situations now,” she said.

Doreen, a cleaner, said she hoped the pro-Russia AfD would be able to take power and act on promises to end refugee status for Ukrainians (as well as aid to Kyiv). “The winners will hopefully straighten up a few things right away,” she said. “They [Ukrainians] come here in their fancy cars, pretending they’re escaping devastation, but most of them have far more resources and designer clothes than I do.”

Doreen is speaking close to a stolperstein, or stumbling stone – a brass plaque embedded in the concrete – commemorating Ernst Fliess, a Jewish lawyer. Born in 1877, he lived on the spot where a glass-fronted fitness club now stands until he was “humiliated, disenfranchised … (and) took flight in death” (a euphemism for suicide).

blocks.caption: The memorial stone of Ernst Fliess, a Jewish lawyer hounded to his death by the Nazis. Photograph: Kate Connolly/The Guardian

blocks.text: But she angrily rejected any parallel between the AfD’s rise in popularity and the Weimar era rise of the Nazis. “Don’t tar me with that brush,” she said. “We are in a different age, with different problems.”

Returning from their daily stroll to the Elbe river, 88-year-olds Ernst and Judith, a retired boiler maker and a design engineer who have been married for 64 years, said they did not want to talk about the election result. But it soon became clear that they were shattered by the news. Voting data has shown a stark drop-off in support for the far-right party among the over-70s.
“It’s not like we didn’t see it coming,” said Judith. “But we don’t quite know what to do with the information. The reality of it hasn’t quite kicked in.”
The couple said they had voted for the far-left Die Linke. Judith said she was “devastated that a party that has so little regard for refugees” had won, and by such a large margin.

Her own life story – she was forced to flee her home in Silesia in 1945 and spent years in temporary accommodation before settling in Magdeburg – has greatly sensitised her to the plight of refugees, she said.

“I see the look in their eyes, it doesn’t matter where they come from, who they are, and I am so empathetic to their situation,” she said. “It breaks my heart to think that almost half of the population has voted for a party that is so anti-immigrant, particularly after all Germany has gone through as a nation in the last century.”

Sitting on a heart-shaped rainbow-coloured bench in front of Magdeburg’s gothic cathedral, Christiane and Franz Josef Jäker, 67 and 71, on holiday from North Rhine-Westphalia, were also digesting the news.

“The populists are ruining everything,” said Franz Josef. “Everything that Germany has built up again after world war two. They promise a lot that they can’t deliver, and they also suppress a lot – such as what is going on in Ukraine – so that they can argue for the resumption of Russian gas imports to Germany.”

Eric, a paramedic cheerily drumming up funds for a hospice, said he was kicking himself for not having voted. The 21-year-old son of a German mother and a Guinean father who spent 10 years applying for a German passport, said: “I try not to think about what the installation of the AfD in government might mean for me as a dark-skinned man.”
Most of all he is worried about “the constitutional changes they might make, and the domino effect that might have across Germany”.
Luisa, a bank teller who says she voted for Die Linke, fears for the image of her state.

“It’s really bad for the reputation of Saxony-Anhalt. A lot of people have said that foreigners here will now choose to leave, but I know enough low-paid foreign workers who won’t be able to afford to do so, and will just have to put up with being badly treated.

“I saw some interviews with Holocaust survivors and they drew parallels with the mood around what’s happening now and the rise of the Nazis. We have to pay attention to this similar sense they say they have – they’re not making it up.”

articles.title: DOLE's Tolentino, party-list rep clash over suspended NCR wage hike
articles.summary: The House budget hearing of the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) became heated Tuesday after Secretary Francis Tolentino clashed with Kamanggagawa Party-list Representative Eli San Fernando…

blocks.text: The House budget hearing of the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) became heated Tuesday after Secretary Francis Tolentino clashed with Kamanggagawa Party-list Representative Eli San Fernando over the suspended wage hike in the National Capital Region (NCR), with the latter even moving to defer the agency's budget.

A Pasig court issued a preliminary injunction against the NCR wage hike that was supposed to be implemented in July. Fernando, together with several labor groups, have previously argued that the court should have no jurisdiction over wage hikes.

Citing the Office of the Solicitor General, Fernando told the House appropriations committee that since the petitioners failed to pay the P10-billion bond posed by the court, there is no writ, so nothing is stopping DOLE from implementing the wage hike.
"Ang pagli-lift ng injunction is not a matter of self-help," Tolentino said. (Lifting an injunction is not a matter of self-help.)

Tolentino cited two several Supreme Court (SC) rulings. Quoting Lukang vs. Pagbilao Development Corporation, Tolentino said the court cautioned against "treating a bond effect, including the non-filing thereof, not as an automatic license to disregard injunctive relief, failure to fix a bond or post a bond, did not itself, justify quashing the injunction."
He also said that in the case of the Development Bank of the Philippines vs. Carpio, the SC said that "there is no such thing as a doctrine of unilateral disregard."
"Hindi po ang DOLE, hindi po ang litigants ang magdedesisyon kung mali 'yung proseso. Ang magdedesisyon nito, ang husgado," Tolentino said.
(It is not DOLE, it is not the litigants who will decide if the process is wrong, it is the court.)
Tolentino further argued that the court itself would need to come up with a final resolution, since the lack of a bond does not automatically mean that the case is resolved.
He used the purchase of an airfare ticket as an example: The airline issuing a person a wrong ticket does not mean that the person could automatically go to the airport and board the right plane.
However, San Fernando said that there was no bond, so there was no writ.
"So in simple words, hindi po ipapatupad ng Department of Labor and Employment ang dagdag sahod?" San Fernando asked.
(So in simple words, the Department of Labor and Employment will not implement the wage hike?)
Tolentino insisted that the agency will, but it has to follow the order. He said San Fernando and other labor groups recognize the Pasig court's authority since they filed a case in the SC.

However, the party-list representative refuted this, saying that they went to the SC because they believed that the Pasig court did not have the right to issue orders about the wage hike, as it is stated in the Article 126 of the Labor Code.

"Mayroon kayong kapangyarihan Mister Secretary, iginawad 'yan ng Kongreso sa inyo! RA 6727! Ibinigay sa mga Regional Wage Boards ang exclusive power in determining wages," San Fernando said, referring to Republic Act 6727, or the Wage Rationalization Act.
(You have the power Mister Secretary, that was given to you by Congress! RA 6727! The exclusive power to determine wages was given to the Regional Wage Boards.)
San Fernando said that even if P60 a day does not sound big, it already has an impact on workers.

"Kung hindi niyo kaya ipagtanggol ang manggagawa, wala kayong karapatan humingi ng budget na nanggaling din naman sa pawis, dugo at sakripisyo ng mga manggagawang minimum wage earner," San Fernando said.
(If you cannot defend the rights of the workers, you do not have the right to ask for a budget that came from the sweat, blood, and sacrifice of minimum wage earners.)
San Fernando then made a motion to defer the budget of the DOLE, with Akbayan Partylist Rep. Perci Cendaña seconding the motion.
However, Cagayan de Oro Rep. Rufus Rodriguez raised an objection.
Rodriguez said that while San Fernando was defending workers, discussion with the DOLE is still ongoing. The former even suggested filing an administrative order against the judge.
This led to Appropriations Vice Chair Rep. Romel Rico Angara calling the matter to a vote, with seven yes votes agreeing with San Fernando and 31 objections.
With this, the House appropriations panel will continue deliberations on DOLE's budget. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: 50,766 nabbed, P11.5B illegal drugs seized from Jan. – Aug. 2026
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines—Police arrested 50,766 individuals and seized an estimated P11.51 billion worth of illegal drugs nationwide during the first eight months of the year. The Philippine National…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines—Police arrested 50,766 individuals and seized an estimated P11.51 billion worth of illegal drugs nationwide during the first eight months of the year.
The Philippine National Police (PNP), in a statement on Tuesday, said its units carried out 43,383 anti-drug operations from January to August 2026.
In August alone, the PNP arrested 6,044 individuals and recovered an estimated P599.89 million worth of illegal drugs.
Police data showed that the PNP confiscated approximately 1.36 million grams of suspected “shabu” or crystal meth.
The anti-drug operations last month also resulted in the confiscation of more than 3.61 million grams of dried marijuana leaves and over 8.9 million marijuana plants.
PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said the results demonstrate the importance of sustained police presence and coordinated action.
“We will not let up in addressing the illegal drug problem, but our approach will remain clear: effective enforcement, proper procedure, and accountability,” said Nartatez.
“It is our duty to protect the public, and we will do this with discipline and respect to the law,” added Nartatez.
Last month, Las Piñas Rep. Mark Anthony Santos mandated all drug-concerned agencies to regularly report to the House of Representatives.
The agencies include the PNP, the Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency, Department of Health, Department of the Interior and Local Government, Department of Justice and the Bureau of Customs.

Santos said this will allow Congress to have greater oversight on the government’s anti-drug campaign under his watch as the new chairperson of the committee on dangerous drugs. (with a report from Sheridan Delfino) /gsg

articles.title: WATCH: Robin asks colleagues to uphold Constitution amid vote questions
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – “Ginawa ito ng Konstitusyon para galangin, bigyan ng boses, at patibayin ang karapatan ng bawat Pilipino… Uphold the Constitution.” (The Constitution was created to respect,…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – “Ginawa ito ng Konstitusyon para galangin, bigyan ng boses, at patibayin ang karapatan ng bawat Pilipino… Uphold the Constitution.”(The Constitution was created to respect, give voice to, and strengthen the rights of every Filipino… Uphold the Constitution.)

This was how Senator-judge Robin Padilla reminded his fellow senator-judges to uphold the Constitution as questions arose over the impeachment court’s voting threshold amid the absence of several members.

Currently, Senator Loren Legarda is on sick leave, while Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa is in hiding. Two other senator-judges—Rodante Marcoleta and Jinggoy Estrada—are detained in connection with plunder cases.
The Constitution requires 16 votes, or two-thirds of all 24 senators, to convict an impeached official./dp

articles.summary: Trump says Bombardier must build aircraft in the US as Canada imposes tariffs of up to 50% on US imports.

image.caption: Bombardier said it supports tens of thousands of US jobs through its operations [FILE: May 1, 2024]Image: Carlos Osorio/REUTERS

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump late on Monday threatened to block Canadian aircraft maker Bombardier from selling planes in the United States unless it manufactures them domestically, escalating a trade dispute with Ottawa as Canada's retaliatory tariffs on billions of dollars in US products take effect on Tuesday.
"NO MORE SELLING ⁠BOMBARDIER ⁠IN THE UNITED STATES! Their products aren't good enough!" Trump said in a post on Truth Social.
"If they want our Market, they must build here, and stop treating America like a 'piggybank',” he said.
He did not specify how a ban would be enforced.

blocks.caption: Trump's post came amid an escalating trade dispute between Washington and Ottawa [FILE: August 23, 2026]Image: Daniel Torok/B66/Avalon/Photoshot/picture alliance

blocks.text: What did Bombardier say?
Bombardier responded to the US president's claims saying it supports tens of thousands of US jobs through its operations and a supply chain of about 2,800 American companies across 47 states.
It also spends more than $2.5 billion (€2.15 billion) annually with US suppliers and said its aircraft use American-made engines, avionics and other components.
Canada's retaliatory tariffs on US goods come into effect
Trump's threat came just before Canada's retaliatory tariffs of up to 50% on $20 billion worth of US imports took effect on Tuesday.
The tariffs cover steel and aluminum products, as well as dairy goods such as cheese.
Ottawa's move came weeks after Trump imposed 50% tariffs on a similar value of Canadian products after Prime Minister Mark Carney refused to match US tariffs on China.

articles.title: Tuesday briefing: What happens next after Germany’s far-right breakthrough?
articles.summary:
In today’s newsletter: The AfD’s local election triumph has shocked Europe, and raised questions about how to counter the rising far right

Good morning. Across Germany – and Europe more…

blocks.text: Good morning. Across Germany – and Europe more widely – there has been a palpable sense of shock and disbelief after the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) swept to a historic state election victory in the early hours of Monday.

It was, according to France’s European affairs minister, Benjamin Haddad, “a very grave moment for Europe”. The resonance was stark in the UK too: as the results came in, hundreds of black-clad activists intent on blocking migrant arrivals were battling with police for a second night along England’s south coast.

While seasoned observers stress the context that Saxony-Anhalt, a small state in the former communist east of the country, has traditionally voted further to the right, a red line has been crossed. A far-right party has been propelled to the brink of power at regional level in Germany for the first time since the Nazis – despite 13 years of increasingly desperate efforts by mainstream parties to shut them out of government.

For today’s newsletter, I spoke to the Guardian’s Berlin correspondent Kate Connolly from the state capital Magdeburg, and our Europe correspondent, Jon Henley, about why Germany’s famous firewall against the far right has failed, and what happens next. First, this morning’s headlines.
Five big stories

items: UK news | Batons and synthetic pepper spray were used to repel hundreds of masked, black-clad vigilantes in Portsmouth on Sunday, it has emerged, as the policing minister said officers had been injured as they repelled organised “aggression”.

Israel | Ed Miliband will announce what he has described as a broad reset of the UK’s relations with Israel on Tuesday, promising the government will take a more active approach in supporting the Palestinian cause.

US | The Trump administration has raised “serious concerns” over Downing Street’s plan to force digital platforms to hand more prominence to established broadcasters, warning the move risks “facilitating censorship”.

Climate crisis | Nepal is demanding $20m in climate compensation for the recent devastating floods, as a senior minister called on the world’s most polluting countries to “wake up” and accept shared responsibility.

UK politics | There is little appetite for cuts to disability benefits even among Conservative and Reform voters, and proposals to reduce spending could prove politically risky, according to an authoritative national survey.

blocks.text: In depth: ‘A palpable sense of disbelief’

blocks.caption: Ulrich Siegmund, leader of the AfD party in Saxony-Anhalt, has been labelled Germany’s “most dangerous man” by Der Spiegel. Photograph: dts News Agency Germany/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The first person Kate spoke to when she arrived in Magdeburg on Monday afternoon was a paramedic named Eric, who was fundraising for a local hospice. He explained how his father had spent years working to obtain a German passport after migrating from Guinea. “Already that day he felt the mood on the street had become more hostile,” Kate told me.

I know from experience how difficult it can be to persuade strangers to elaborate on their private voting decisions – especially when you have copy to file in a hurry – but yesterday was different, she said: “Everybody had very profound thoughts to share.”

She described conversations with a “heartbroken” older couple, who had grown up under communism; a 16-year-old who arrived from Syria under Angela Merkel’s open borders policy in 2015 and was frightened she would be first on the list to send back; another woman who’d voted for the AfD and said she didn’t appreciate being “tarred with the same brush” as supporters of Hitler in the 1930s. Kate interviewed her as they stood by a Stolperstein, a memorial plaque to a victim of Nazi persecution.
As we spoke, thousands were gathering at Berlin’s Brandenburg Gate to express their opposition to the AfD, and where there was a palpable sense of disbelief and dread as news of the results filtered.
Why is the AfD on the rise?

The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, was elected leader of the centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in 2022 on a pledge to halve the AfD’s vote. Instead it has doubled, and support for his centrist coalition that has tumbled.
A “deeply shocked” Merz vowed to stay in office yesterday after the nativist party triumphed with 44% of the vote, just short of an absolute majority

The turnout in Saxony-Anhalt was breathtaking. At 77.8%, compared with 60.3% in 2021, it suggests the AfD – classified as extremist by Germany’s security services – has succeeded in energising many who didn’t vote at all five years ago.

Detailed polling analysis suggests that, while one in three AfD supporters align with the party’s extremist ideology, its growing popularity is driven by a diversity of voters who feel alienated from mainstream politics.

Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, is a charismatic former perfume salesman who has weaponised voter discontent around the faltering economy and migration – even though irregular immigration has reduced since Merz came into office. Research from 2023 found a direct link between rent increases – particularly amonglower income voters – and likelihood of supporting the AfD.
Last month, Der Spiegel put Siegmund on its front cover, with the tagline “Germany’s most dangerous man”. He responded by filming himself signing copies for his 800,000 TikTok followers.

Siegmund has capitalised on a mood of ostalgie – nostalgia for communist East Germany – and bubbling resentment among poorer east Germans who view themselves as second-class citizens compared to people from the west. Strikingly, it appears one of the highest shares of the AfD’s vote came from the 35- to 44 age group, who were children or infants when the Berlin Wall came down.
What does the result mean for Germany?

There’s now debate about whether the previous consensus over how mainstream parties should deal with the far right – the so-called “Brandmauer”, or firewall – has horribly backfired. Sceptics believe this non-cooperation with AfD at any level from local councils up to federal government has allowed the party to escape the scrutiny that comes with holding office.

Another criticism is that it has neutered the political mainstream. “The argument runs that in order to keep the far right out, it forces mainstream parties into unnatural coalitions,” Jon says. The compromises that they have to strike have resulted in ineffective government and in turn feeds the extremes further.”

Now, there are complex coalition talks ahead for the parties in Saxony-Anhalt. While Siegmund has rejected leading a minority administration, initial indications are that the AfD could govern with the hard-left, pro-Russian Bündnis Sahra Wagenknecht party, which received 5.3% of the vote.

If he succeeds in becoming the state’s first far-right governor, Siegmund will have control over significant policy areas including education, policing and public broadcasting. AfD has already proposed revisions to the school curriculum, in what one party member described as “more Bismarck, less Hitler”, as well as defunding anti-racism initiatives and removing pride flags. Jon also suggests the AfD might make changes to civil service recruitment “to create a more supportive environment”.

But securing the Saxony-Anhalt government would also give the AfD seats in the Bundesrat upper house: while they wouldn’t have enough seats to block legislation they could still act as a disruptive force.

And with the AfD leading the polls nationally, there’s a likely ripple effect across the country. There are more state elections later this month – including in traditionally liberal Berlin, where the AfD is now polling at 18%, with the CDU maintaining a slim lead in the early 20s. If their vote share rises across states, options for coalition building without the AfD become increasingly convoluted, further flattening the mainstream’s ability to govern confidently.
… And for Europe?

Not all of Europe’s far-right leaders have welcomed this development. Jon, who is based in Paris, has been listening to France’s National Rally – which under Marine Le Pen has spent years successfully detoxifying its image – on the airwaves insisting that, in his words, “these guys are way too extreme for us”.

To give you one example, two years ago the National Rally expelled the AfD from its European parliamentary group, which includes Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni, following revelations that the party backed mass deportations and downplayed the crimes of the Nazi SS.
But any domestic shock waves in Europe’s largest economy will inevitably affect the bloc.

“A weakened German government in complete upheaval would obviously be bad news for Europe,” says Jon. “It could affect things like the bloc’s policy towards migration; the environment, because the AfD is famously climate-sceptic; and Ukraine, because it’s also pretty much pro-Kremlin.”
In a press conference yesterday, an ashen-faced Merz drew a fairly explicit link between the AfD and Russia, noting that “2,500 km in the east, the election results were being celebrated.”

This may reflect growing calls within the CDU and their coalition partner, the Social Democrats, for Merz to toughen his stance on Russia. After a drone attack on Leipzig airport in August, the German government took a month before publicly blaming Moscow, though the language could not have been more direct when foreign minister Johann Wadephul stated: “We are not at war, but we are a daily target of hybrid warfare.”

With a series of federal or presidential elections taking place in Spain, France, Italy, Poland, and Germany over the next two years, the AfD’s landslide can be viewed as an indication of coming peril and a challenge on how to meet it.
after newsletter promotion

“The far right’s ideas have been steadily normalised by the media and the political centre,” says Jon. “They have completely framed the immigration debate, and everybody else is just scrambling to react to them”. As Keir Starmer’s government discovered with Reform in the UK, repurposing populist rhetoric doesn’t convince disaffected voters.

“Political scientists across Europe would say this result is down to that, and the failure by mainstream parties to come up with inspiring policies that will actually make a real difference to people’s lives and address some of the reasons why they choose to vote for the far right,” he said.
For more on the far right in Europe, sign up to This Is Europe, our free weekly with selection of the most pressing stories and debates.

articles.title: Pacquiao joins Marcos Cabinet as anti-poverty czar
articles.summary: Pacquiao returns to government four years after leaving Senate.

blocks.text: September 8, 2026 | 1:44pm

Former senator and professional boxer Manny Pacquiao took oath as the new National Anti-Poverty Commission secretary and lead convenor on September 8, 2026. His oath was administered by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
PCO

MANILA, Philippines — Former senator and boxing icon Manny Pacquiao has returned to government service four years after ending his term at the Senate, this time as the Marcos administration's lead official coordinating anti-poverty programs.
Pacquiao took his oath Tuesday, September 8, as secretary and lead convenor of the National Anti-Poverty Commission before President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. at Malacañang.
He replaced Lope Santos III, who had served as NAPC lead convenor since 2023.
Pacquiao's appointment comes weeks after Marcos transferred administrative supervision of the NAPC from the Department of Social Welfare and Development back to the Office of the President.

Created under Republic Act No. 8425, or the Social Reform and Poverty Alleviation Act, the NAPC coordinates poverty reduction programs among national and local government agencies and the private sector.
The president chairs the commission, while the lead convenor heads its secretariat and holds the rank of secretary as part of Cabinet.
Pacquiao previously served six years in the Senate, with his term ending in June 2022.
He ran for president in 2022 and finished third behind Marcos and then-Vice President Leni Robredo.
Pacquiao later sought a return to the Senate in the 2025 midterm elections under the administration-backed Alyansa para sa Bagong Pilipinas but failed to secure a seat.

articles.title: Tokyo tourist hotspot bans short-term rentals amid surge in complaints
articles.summary:
Shinjuku ward targets accommodation in residential areas and near cultural sites as locals complain visitors disposing of rubbish improperly and being too noisy

A neighbourhood in Tokyo…

blocks.text: A neighbourhood in Tokyo popular with foreign tourists will ban visitors from using thousands of short-term rental accommodations after a slew of complaints about behaviour.

In the latest sign that Japan’s patience with mass tourism is wearing thin, Shinjuku ward – home to the notorious Kabukicho nightlife district and the world’s busiest railway station – will prevent visitors from using private lodgings in residential areas and near schools and important cultural sites, Japanese media reported this week.

The measure, to be introduced through a local ordinance, could encourage other local authorities to follow suit. Shinjuku, with a regular population of more than 350,000, is home to 3,775 private lodgings – or minpaku – the largest number anywhere in Japan.

While tourism has boosted sectors of Japan’s economy and raised the country’s profile overseas, the surge in visitor numbers has created tensions with residents in popular destinations such as Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka.

Shinjuku ward believes the measure will affect as many as 2,000 lodgings in residential areas – almost half the total, according to the Mainichi Shimbun. The number of minpaku residences in Shinjuku has almost tripled since 2022.

Reports said officials had been forced to act after receiving more than 1,300 complaints from residents in the 12 months to March. Many cited disruption caused by visitors who did not dispose of their rubbish properly, made too much noise and smoked in areas where it is banned. There have also been reports of trespassing.

Officials said temporarily revoking the licenses of renters whose tenants misbehaved would not address residents’ concerns. “Even if we crack down on badly behaved operators, the number of complaints remains the same,” a ward official told the Japan Times. “So we decided it’s better to change the ordinance.”
Authorities did not single out particular operators for the ban. But it is likely to affect those using popular companies such as Airbnb. The Guardian has contacted Airbnb’s Japan office for comment.

The ward will ask for members of the public to give their feedback on the proposal next month, with a view to submitting revisions to the ordinance in February. It also plans to reduce the number of days per year that minpaku in residential areas can be rented out from 180 to 120.

Authorities in Kyoto – where tourists flock to view temples and shrines, rent kimono and photograph traditional geisha entertainers – limit minpaku operations in residential areas to just 60 days a year, during the off-peak season between January and March.

“Residents are concerned that their communities could be falling apart,” Kyoto’s mayor, Koji Matsui, said earlier this year. “We have strengthened the oversight of operators, but that is not enough. We need to go further,” the Asahi Shimbun quoted him as saying.

A record 42 million people visited Japan last year, spending a combined ¥9.5tn ($62bn) – also an all-time high. The government has set a target of 60 million visitors by 2030 – a goal critics say will exacerbate “tourism pollution”.

Authorities near Mount Fuji have introduced climbing fees and imposed a daily visitor cap in an attempt to reduce overcrowding on Japan’s highest mountain. In February, the town of Fujiyoshida, a popular Fuji viewing spot, decided to cancel this spring’s cherry blossom festival, citing a rise in disruptive behaviour by tourists.
The mayor, Shigeru Horiuchi, said the decision had been taken to “protect the dignity and living environment of our citizens”.

articles.title: Duterte camp given 15 days to answer prosec’s request on bank records
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Senate Impeachment Court has given Vice President Sara Duterte’s lawyers 15 days to respond to the prosecution panel’s request to admit 104 items as evidence. These pieces…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Senate Impeachment Court has given Vice President Sara Duterte’s lawyers 15 days to respond to the prosecution panel’s request to admit 104 items as evidence.
These pieces are related to Article II of the Articles of Impeachment, or the allegations that she amassed unexplained wealth.

During the resumption of the impeachment trial on Tuesday, public prosecutor and Akbayan party-list Rep. Chel Diokno said that the prosecution panel has submitted a Request for Admission regarding Duterte’s bank records.
The team has a goal of seeking a confirmation whether the bank accounts subject of the court’s subpoena really belongs to her.
“The request from the prosecution side is simple,” Diokno told the court.
“We are just asking the respondent to confirm first, if the bank records submitted by the banks in accordance with the subpoena duces tecum issued by the Impeachment Court are genuine,” he said.
“And second, if the bank accounts in the records is owned by Vice President Sara Zimmerman Duterte, individually or jointly with others,” he lawmaker continued.
“These are matters, Your Honors, which respondent is particularly well-positioned to know or can readily verify,” Diokno told the senator-judges.
“As to whether the identified bank accounts belong to her, respondent necessarily possesses personal knowledge of that fact,” he went on say.

“As to the bank records pertaining to those accounts, respondent has immediate means of verifying their accuracy and genuineness through her own records or directly with the banks that produced them,” Diokno added.
However, the prosecution was seeking a seven-day period for the defense panel’s response to the Request for Admission, instead of the usual 15-day period stated in Rule 26 of the Rules of Court.
The group’s reason is that the Senate Impeachment Court can adjust its rules as the proceedings are ‘sui generis’ (unique) in nature.

Presiding Justice and Senator-judge Francis Escudero responded: “If we tie the hands of the respondents with your seven-day period, instead of the 15-day period provided by the rule you cited – Rule 26 Section 2, I believe, yes.”
“Then, they will just come out with a specific denial for each of your 104 requests for submissions,” Escudero pointed out.
“So, giving them ample time to actually go over it might serve your purpose as well,” he told the prosecution.

“The 15-day period, while that is provided in the Rules of Court for ordinary cases, given the nature of these proceedings, given the fact that the counsel for respondent has an entire team of lawyers assigned to this case, I believe that 15 days would be too long a period,” Diokno told the presiding officer.
“However, we would be willing to submit to the discretion of the Court as far as the period of time is concerned,” he said nevertheless.
After this, Escudero ruled that the defense will be given 15 days to respond to the prosecution’s Request for Admission.

“Chair gives the respondent 15 days from today to file their comment on the 104 Request for Admission under Rule 26, knowing, Atty. Poa, the effect of a general denial, knowing as well that an unreasonable denial will be looked at by the court,” the presiding officer ruled.
Contents
The prosecution panel has not revealed the actual content of its Request for Admission, but Diokno mentioned that these are the bank documents subject of the Senate Impeachment Court’s subpoena.

Last Thursday, another public prosecutor, Bicol Saro party-list Rep. Terry Ridon, confirmed that they have received copies of the bank and tax records of Duterte and her husband, lawyer Manases Carpio, along with the couple’s business interests.
Ridon said they will study these documents so they can present it before the court.
On Tuesday, Diokno said they are not asking Duterte to admit to matters that they know, but only to confirm whether the bank accounts belong to her and her husband and their business entities.
“We are not asking the respondent to admit matters that they do not know anything about, or rather that they have no access to,” he noted.
“We are asking them simply to admit records that they can readily and easily verify, either through their own records or through confirmation with the banks and other institutions,” Diokno said.
“To be clear, we are not asking the respondent to admit a matter that is not true. We are also not asking them to surrender their defense,” Diokno specified.
“What we are asking is simple: If it is true, admit it; and if not, outrightly deny it. If they cannot admit or deny immediately, state under oath why,” he emphasized.

During the House committee on justice hearing on the two impeachment complaints against Duterte last April, Ridon said that Duterte’s actual net worth was not reflected in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth.

Ridon revealed that there was an increase in Duterte’s net worth not proportionate to her salary, as her net worth supposedly rose by over 1,000 percent from 2007 to 2024 — from P7.2 million in 2027 to 2024’s P88.51 million.

Aside from the SALN issue, Ridon also pointed out the confirmation from Anti-Money Laundering Council Executive Director Buenaventura — that they saw covered and suspicious transactions made by Duterte and Carpio, and a total of P6.7 billion in total transactions from bank accounts from the couple.
This includes a total of P4.4 billion in inflows and P1.5 billion worth of outflows. /apl

articles.title: Nepal-like flood risk looms over South Cotabato’s Tampakan project
articles.summary: KORONADAL CITY – An official warned that the thriving of illegal ‘banlas’ or hydraulic mining operations in low-lying areas of the controversial Tampakan project, Southeast Asia’s…

blocks.text: KORONADAL CITY – An official warned that the thriving of illegal ‘banlas’ or hydraulic mining operations in low-lying areas of the controversial Tampakan project, Southeast Asia’s largest undeveloped copper and gold minefield, could trigger catastrophic flash floods similar to the disaster in Nepal.

Neil Ryan Escobillo, barangay captain of Pulabato in Tampakan, South Cotabato, cited a geological hazard assessment conducted by the Mines and Geosciences Bureau – Region 12 (MGB-12) in issuing the warning.
He said what happened in Nepal last Aug. 26, which reportedly killed at least 1,000 individuals with about 5,000 still missing, was a manifestation of how flash floods can be catastrophic.
In Nepal’s case, glaciers collapsed, and landslides with debris blocked the river flow, creating a natural dam and eventually flooding downstream, he said.
Escobillo said this observation is quite similar to the site geological hazard assessment conducted last March in Sitio Campo Kilot in Barangay Pula Bato.

“ (The) introduction of artificial erosion through hydraulic mining further weakens slope integrity, significantly increasing susceptibility to landslides…an increased risk of flooding due to potential artificial damming and sudden release of accumulated materials,” he said, citing the hazard assessment.
“In short, the possibility of flash flood(s),” said Escobillo, an ex-officio member of the South Cotabato Sangguniang Panlalawigan, representing the Association of Barangay Captains in the province.
In a social media post, Escobillo said landslides near the illegal “banlas” mining sites within the Tampakan project have destroyed at least five hectares of forest lands.

“Banlas,” also known as sluice mining, is a highly destructive mining method that involves pouring large amounts of water into a mountain’s surface to loosen the soil and rocks to extract gold ore, which is then panned using mercury.
Escobillo added that aside from landslides triggered by banlas operations, rain-induced landslides are also compounding the situation, forming a natural dam blocking the river flow downstream.
The MGB-12 has recommended intensifying the fight against banlas operators and rehabilitating the areas damaged by banlas mining.
Sagittarius Mines, Inc. operates the Tampakan project, but commercial mining production, using the open-pit method, has yet to commence.
Aside from the open-pit ban imposed by the South Cotabato provincial government, the Tampakan project is facing social resistance waged by the local Catholic Church and environmental groups/coa

articles.title: Sara Duterte trial recap, Sept. 8: Article I winds down, conviction math
articles.summary: Three key moments and developments from Day 2, September 8 of #SaraOnTrial.

blocks.text: September 8, 2026 | 1:18pm

MANILA, Philippines — The House prosecution ended its presentation of evidence on the confidential funds article Tuesday, September 8, by dropping its 15 remaining witnesses and signaling it intends to call Vice President Sara Duterte to the stand before the whole trial wraps up.

With no witnesses to hear, the impeachment court today set a 15-day deadline for the defense to answer the prosecution's 104 requests for admission for Article II on unexplained wealth, and scheduled a September ruling to settle how many votes are needed to convict.
Here are the three highlights from today's proceedings.
1. Prosecution to call Duterte, but not yet

Private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan told the court the panel is forgoing the three witnesses subpoenaed for the day and all 15 who remain on its list for Article I, which accuses Duterte of the misuse, misappropriation, and irregular liquidation of P612.5 million in confidential funds.
The prosecution had listed 27 witnesses for Article I in its pre-trial brief, presented 10 in court and stipulated on two more.
It's the prosecution's belief that they have already established their case with the 12 witnesses presented and thousands of documents shown to the court through them.
The prosecution said that, with the 15 witnesses skipped, it is turning its eyes to eventually compelling Duterte to show up in court.

"All of these pawns and castles and horses and bishops point to only one person, and that accountable person is the vice president. And that is why, in lieu of presenting 15 other witnesses, we will be presenting [Duterte] herself,” Kapunan said.
Lead defense counsel Sheila Sison however argued the Constitution bars compelling Duterte to testify.
She said the defense will file a written comment once a formal motion to subpoena her is filed.

Presiding officer Sen. Chiz Escudero noted that then-Chief Justice Renato Corona took the stand in 2012 and said nothing prevents Duterte from choosing to appear; Sison pointed out that Corona testified voluntarily.
Escudero also directed both panels not to rest on Article I, keeping it open while the court decides whether to summon Cols. Raymund Lachica and Dennis Nolasco on its own.
2. Defense gets 15 days to answer 104 requests for admission

Prosecutor Chel Diokno, who is in charge of Article II on unexplained wealth, told the court the panel served the defense with 104 requests for admission Monday morning under Rule 26 of the Rules of Court.
The requests cover Duterte's bank accounts and records, which Diokno argued the vice president either knows firsthand or can verify against her own files or with the banks.
Anything admitted no longer needs to be proved through testimony, and the rule deems matters admitted if the respondent files no sworn answer in time.

Diokno said the mechanism could allow the prosecution to do away with at least 15 witnesses — further shortening proceedings — and distinguished it from stipulations, which are binding only when both sides agree.

Defense counsel Michael Poa asked for 15 days to respond rather than the seven the prosecution proposed. Escudero sided with the defense and granted them 15 days. This is non-extendable, and Escudero warned that an unreasonable blanket denial would be taken note of by the court.
The trial will not pause during that period.
In preparation for Article II, Escudero canceled the trial for tomorrow so both panels can mark exhibits.
Diokno said more than 1,800 bank and insurance records obtained under subpoena still need marking.

Poa had asked for two weeks to study the documents before the trial takes up Article II, offering to give up an equal number of days from the defense presentation. Escudero denied the request, saying the constraint is the court's calendar rather than any suspicion of delay.
He ordered the prosecution to submit its witness list under the five-day notice rule and said trial proceeds Monday.
3. Court to settle the voting threshold on September 23
Sen. Erwin Tulfo moved that the court decide who counts toward the two-thirds vote needed to convict, given that four senators are outside the chamber's coercive power at the moment.
Sen. Loren Legarda has been on medical leave since early August and remains abroad.
Sen. Bato dela Rosa, wanted by an International Criminal Court arrest warrant, has not shown up to the Senate since May.
Sen. Jinggoy Estrada and Sen. Rodante Marcoleta are currently detained after they were arrested on non-bailable plunder charges.

Estrada has been charged with graft and plunder over his alleged role in siphoning funds from anomalous flood control works, while Marcoleta is facing a plunder case over his alleged failure to declare P75 million in campaign donations during his 2025 Senate run.

If the base stays at 24, conviction requires 16 votes regardless of how many senators can vote. Should nine or more be unable to participate, Tulfo said, the remaining 15 could not reach that number even if all voted to convict, producing an acquittal by default.
He said Escudero's day-one ruling on the vote threshold used total membership, while the Senate has applied Avelino v. Cuenco, which counts only members within its reach.

"I'm not seeking to lower the requirement. My question now is very basic. When we refer to all members, who exactly are we counting? I fear that if we interpret the provisions literally, we might not do so to the point of absurdity, frustrating the mandate of the Constitution to exact accountability from public officials," Tulfo said.

Escudero treated Tulfo's motion as an appeal of his ruling and set a process. To help settle any debate, the court will hear from amici curiae (friends of the court) on September 16. It will then take oral arguments from both defense and prosecution on September 23, with 15 minutes each and a vote the same day.
An amicus curiae is a legal expert whom the court can ask to provide insights or specialized opinions on complex issues in law.

articles.title: DSWD seeks restoration of capital outlay funding for care facilities
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) on Tuesday called on the House of Representatives to restore funding for capital outlay for its care facilities, noting…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) on Tuesday called on the House of Representatives to restore funding for capital outlay for its care facilities, noting that budget cuts may compromise their quality and maintenance.

During the House committee on appropriations’ briefing on the proposed budget of the DSWD for next year, Social Welfare Secretary Rex Gatchalian shared that of the P235.7 billion budget allocated to the DSWD and its attached and supervised agencies, only the Office of the Secretary was allotted a budget of P294.1 million for capital outlay.
Gatchalian said that the funding for capital outlay was only granted for its five residential facilities, learning institute in Davao, and warehouse in Iloilo.
Other than these projects, he said that there is no capital outlay allocated for infrastructure.
Akbayan Party-list Rep. Perci Cendaña pointed out the massive budget cut for the agency’s capital outlay and asked Gatchalian how this will affect the agency’s operations.
Gatchalian expressed concern that many of their care facilities are already old, with some of them built 50 years ago.

“While they are maintained to the best of the ability by our people on the ground, yung mga social worker, house parents, admittedly maraming issues na umuusbong pag luma na ang isang bahay,” Gatchalian said.
(While they are maintained to the best of the ability by our people on the ground, the social workers and house parents, admittedly there are many issues arising when the facility is already old.)
He shared that the agency asked the House committee to restore the P800 million budget for its capital outlay, which he noted was removed from the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP).

“Sana po maibalik yung aming dinudulog na part of the listing we submitted to the committee kahit yung capital expenditure for the upgrade, upkeep, and maintenance of our facilities for poor, marginalized and vulnerable communities na nakatira sa atin pansamantala or long-term kasi wala na silang pamilya,” he added.

(We hope that this will be restored as this is part of the listing we submitted to the committee, for the capital expenditure for the upgrade, upkeep, and maintenance of our facilities for poor, marginalized and vulnerable communities seeking temporary or permanent housing.)
Cendaña aired his support for the restoration of budget for the agency’s capital outlay to support its care facilities.
“This is a very necessary amendment and it has to be done to the NEP at kinakailangang iadjust na,” the lawmaker manifested.
(This is a very necessary amendment and it has to be done to the NEP and this has to be adjusted.) /gsg

articles.title: Remulla: No orders from Marcos on Romualdez’s treatment after arrest
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla maintained that he did not receive any instructions from President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. as to how to treat presidential…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla maintained that he did not receive any instructions from President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. as to how to treat presidential cousin and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez amid the latter’s arrest.
“Walang kapatid na lalaki si President, so ito na ang pinakamalapit na pinsan niya. Kung akala niyo madali para sa kanya, hindi,” Remulla said in a press briefing in Camp Crame on Tuesday.
(The President has no male sibling, so Romualdez is his closest cousin. If you think this was easy for him, it wasn’t.)
“Kung tinatanong niyo may instructions para sa treatment sa kanya, wala. Zero,” he added.
(If you’re asking whether there were instructions on how to treat him, there was none. Zero.)
Romualdez was arrested for plunder at the Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City on Monday night.

Hours prior, he was charged by the Office of the Ombudsman before the Sandiganbayan Third Division, alongside former House appropriations committee chairperson Zaldy Co, his personal aide and the president of a foreign exchange corporation.
The charge stemmed from over P7 billion worth of alleged kickbacks in various government projects from 2022 to 2025.
Remulla also detailed that both he and Romualdez were brothers of the Upsilon Sigma Phi fraternity at the University of the Philippines.
The secretary said they briefly spoke during the service of the warrant.

“Wala siyang request… Sabi ko, ‘Brother, I hope you understand why I am doing this. It’s nothing personal.’ And he said, ‘It’s okay, I understand.’ Ayun lang length ng conversation namin,” Remulla noted.
(He had no requests… I told him, “Brother, I hope you understand why I am doing this. It’s nothing personal.” And he said, “It’s okay, I understand.” That was the entire length of our conversation.)

He previously said Romualdez was admitted to Cardinal Santos Medical Center at around 4 p.m. on Monday due to a “cardiovascular event” and an anxiety attack, just hours after the Office of the Ombudsman filed the charges against him.

Reacting to online backlash that Romualdez managed to be confined at the private hospital prior to the issuance of the warrant for his arrest, Remulla said, “Ayan ang mahirap dito. Wala kaming karapatan na i-intercept sila bago lumabas yung warrant of arrest.”
(That’s the hard part. We do not have the right to intercept them before the warrant of arrest is issued by the court.)
“Na-file na. Alam nila na-raffle na, so inuunahan nila. In this case, actually, dito lang kay Speaker Martin nangyari yan,” he added. “I don’t believe in coincidences, so we take it at that.”

(They knew the charges were filed. They knew the case was raffled, so they got ahead of it. In this case, actually, it’s only with Speaker Martin that that’s happened… I don’t believe in coincidences, so we take it at that.)

Remulla further noted that he did not speak with his brother, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla, regarding the case against Romualdez for the past six days and only spoke with him again after the ex-House leader was arrested.
“Actually, inaalaska niya (Ombudsman Remulla) ako. Pinagtatawanan niya ako dahil nakita niya kung gaano kahirap ang buhay ko kahapon eh,” the DILG chief said.
(Actually, my brother was teasing me. He was laughing at me because he saw how hard my life was yesterday.)
“So, sabi niya, as according to him, he is very confident of the case na mangyayari,” he added.
(So, he told me, according to him, he is very confident of the case that will transpire.) /jpv

articles.title: WATCH: Constitution bars prosec from compelling Sara to testify – Sison
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – Defense lead counsel Sheila Sison says during Tuesday’s trial that the prosecution’s possible move to call Vice President Sara Duterte to the witness stand presents an…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Defense lead counsel Sheila Sison says during Tuesday’s trial that the prosecution’s possible move to call Vice President Sara Duterte to the witness stand presents an “innate problem,” pointing to the Constitution’s prohibition against compelling an accused to testify against herself.
Sison stressed that the right against testimonial compulsion is absolute and fundamental, arguing that the vice president is already represented in the impeachment trial through her lawyers.

Prosecution lawyer Lorna Kapunan earlier clarified that the prosecution is not seeking a subpoena for Duterte yet, but is reserving the right to call her as a witness after all the impeachment articles have been presented./dp

articles.title: Kauai on tornado watch as Hurricane Lowell nears Hawaiian islands
articles.summary: HONOLULU, United States — Residents of Kauai were warned to watch for tornadoes late Monday as Hurricane Lowell edged toward the westernmost Hawaiian islands in the US Pacific island chain, the…

blocks.text: HONOLULU, United States — Residents of Kauai were warned to watch for tornadoes late Monday as Hurricane Lowell edged toward the westernmost Hawaiian islands in the US Pacific island chain, the National Weather Service said.
“Conditions are favorable for tornadoes in and close to the watch area” of Kauai, including the city of Lihue, NWS officials said.
The core of Lowell was expected to pass near or just west of Niihau late Monday or early Tuesday, the National Hurricane Center said in a bulletin at 5:00 pm (0300 GMT).
“Dangerous conditions are expected for Niihau, Kauai and Oahu, with flash flooding, damaging waves and high winds expected from Lowell,” NHC said.
The center warned that the combination of a storm surge and tide would flood normally dry areas near the coast in Kauai and Niihau.
A tropical storm warning was also issued for the island of Oahu, where Honolulu is located.
The storm was expected to dump 4-8 inches of rain on Kauai, with 3-8 inches of rain forecast for the Big Island.
The storm was about 230 miles (370 kilometers) southwest of Honolulu and moving north-northeast, the center said.
Lowell, which was packing maximum sustained winds of 110 miles per hour (175 kilometers per hour), was expected to gradually weaken over the next several days.
The storm briefly reached Category 5 strength earlier this week.
Hawaii is still recovering from the impacts of Hurricane Lala, which grazed the southern part of the Big Island last month, bringing destructive winds and flash floods.

Lowell is one of two storms in the Pacific Ocean right now, where a near-record-strength El Nino climate episode warms the waters. Tropical Storm Marie, about 745 miles southwest of San Diego, was moving west away from land.
El Nino is the warming phase of a natural cycle in the tropical Pacific known as the El Nino-Southern Oscillation. It comes along every two to seven years.
The oscillating climate pattern promotes hurricane formation in the tropical Pacific while decreasing their likelihood in the Atlantic.
Climate change increases El Nino’s global weather impacts. /dl
