This was certainly the case when Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) and his party colleague, Sven Schulze, the state premier of Saxony-Anhalt, discussed the results of Sunday's state election. They described the results as a catastrophe for the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) — an earthquake, a disaster. Merz appeared shaken and devastated, to put it mildly.

He thanked Schulze for his work during the campaign. Then Merz added: "Not only did something change in Saxony-Anhalt yesterday but throughout all of Germany. It will have repercussions, including on the international stage."

This is because the victors in the state election, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), oppose supporting Ukraine in the face of Russia's war of aggression, and many AfD politicians maintain close ties with Russian President Vladimir Putin's government, Merz explained.
No regard for the rule of law?
Speaking about the AfD, Merz adopted an almost confrontational tone. Majorities can change, he said, and democrats must always be aware of that and accept it.

But, Merz said, it is shocking that 60% of voters in Saxony-Anhalt chose parties that disregard the rule of law in Germany. Merz was talking about not only the AfD but also the socialist Left Party and the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), which split off from the Left Party over issues that align the BSW with the AfD.

In contrast, the chancellor said his government will always defend the values of the German constitution: "In our country, these values are not up for debate. Power is granted, not seized. And the minority is not the enemy of the majority."
Historians have long described the Nazis' rise to power in the German Reich as a "seizure of power," which is why Merz's statement is sure to be the subject of much discussion.

Seeking to reassure Germany's international partners in the EU and NATO, he said, "We know that Germany bears a special responsibility because of its history. We will always defend our political order and our firm anchoring in Europe."
What the AfD's Saxony-Anhalt win means for Germany
Could CDU politicians in Saxony-Anhalt help the AfD come to power?

Standing next to him, Schulze remained silent. On election night the previous evening, long after his defeat had become clear, Schulze repeatedly emphasized in numerous statements that the public's widespread dissatisfaction with the Merz government in Berlin had dealt him a massive blow.
As for now, the worst-case scenario has narrowly been averted: the AfD does not have an absolute majority in the Magdeburg state parliament — but only by the narrowest of margins.

And this is a problem for Friedrich Merz: Dissatisfaction is growing, even within his own ranks. Can he prevent individual CDU lawmakers in Saxony-Anhalt from voting — against the official party line — to elect Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD election winner, as head of government?
If not, then both of Merz's seats of power would be in serious jeopardy: his position as chairman of the party and his seat in the Chancellery.
Merz defends his controversial reforms

However, as of today, Merz is still defending the difficult reforms his government has undertaken. One such reform is the overhaul of the chronically deficit-ridden pension system, which will bring great hardship to many people in Germany and faced fierce opposition during the election campaign.

On election night, Vice Chancellor and center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) leader Lars Klingbeil suggested reassessing the reforms following the defeat of the coalition government in Berlin. However, Merz has not mentioned such a change in course.
How the AfD changed its pitch and broke through
AfD displays confidence

Hours before the chancellor's appearance at the CDU headquarters, the AfD took to the stage at the Federal Press Conference. The top candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, Ulrich Siegmund, sarcastically thanked the media, which had largely portrayed him during the campaign as a threat to democracy and the rule of law.
"It was also thanks to you that we made it," Siegmund said, adding, "Thank you very much for the great coverage during this election campaign."
For example, the influential news magazine Der Spiegel had recently labeled the AfD politician "Germany's most dangerous man" in a widely circulated cover story.

Siegmund then looked out triumphantly at the packed hall and declared, "Never before has there been such a wide gap between those members of the media who seek to dictate to us here in Saxony-Anhalt how we should live and the reality of life for the people in this state."

But Siegmund avoided the question about whether the election result is a clear mandate for his party to form a government — even one without a majority of its own, if necessary, or possibly with the tacit support of the economically left, populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW).

Siegmund, however, has said he does not want to be a partner in a coalition — he wants absolute power, and he doesn't have it. The situation in Saxony-Anhalt will surely be the subject of much discussion for many days, perhaps even weeks, to come.
This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: Thousands turn out in Serbia for funeral of 'Butcher of Bosnia' Ratko Mladić
articles.summary: Mladić was jailed for genocide during the 1990s Bosnian war and the EU warned Serbia not to glorify the convicted war criminal.

blocks.text: Thousands of people have turned out in Serbia's capital, Belgrade, to attend the funeral of the convicted war criminal Ratko Mladić.
Widely known as the Butcher of Bosnia, Mladić died at the age of 84 while serving a life sentence in the UN prison in The Hague, the Netherlands.

He was found guilty of genocide by a UN war crimes tribunal for his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, when around 8,000 Bosniak Muslim men and boys were killed. It was described as Europe's worst atrocity since World War Two.

A Serbian government minister had initially said that Mladić would be given a state funeral ​but those plans were changed after objections from some European leaders. On Monday, the EU denounced Mladić's "glorification".
Ratko Mladić commanded Bosnian Serb forces in the 1990s against the Bosnian Croat and Bosniak (Bosnian Muslim) armies.

During the 1992-1995 Bosnian war, his troops committed what became known as "ethnic cleansing" in Bosnia-Herzegovina in a bid to expel the non-Serbian population by force. They besieged the capital city of Sarajevo, with the deaths of more than 10,000 people.
Mladić was arrested in 2011, 16 years after he was first indicted, and sentenced to life in prison in 2021 after a nine-year trial.
Despite his conviction for genocide, Mladić remains a national figure perceived by many Serbs as a heroic defender of the nation.
Many Serb nationalists see him as a hero and protector, particularly in the Bosnian Serb entity of Republika Srpska, where his death sparked vigils.

Several Serbian government ministers joined the crowds paying tribute outside the church where Mladić lay in state before the burial, including the Defence Minister Bratislav Gašić, and the Minister of Justice Nenad Vujić, local media reported.

The funeral service was led by the head of the Serbian Orthodox Church, Patriarch Porfirije, who said Mladić's name would remain "deeply etched in the memory and prayers of the majority of our Serbian Orthodox people, who feel and nurture a deep sense of gratitude towards him".

Early in the day, long queues formed outside the small St Luka church, as people waited to go in and pay their respects to the coffin. Many of those in the crowds were army veterans and some men were draped in flags printed with his picture on.
Crowds arrived several hours before the funeral began to light candles outside the church, accompanied by a choir on a loudspeaker in the sunshine.
Inside the church, Mladić's coffin was guarded by several men, mainly war veterans, while his wife, son, and grandchildren stood inside receiving condolences.
In a sign of the reverence held for the former general, his coffin was flown back to Serbia last week on a government plane, and was carried from the plane by six soldiers and draped in flags.
Free bus services were organised from Bosnia and most towns in Serbia for anyone who wanted to pay their respects.
On Sunday night, fans of the Serbian football club Red Star Belgrade unveiled a display of Mladic before their derby win over Partizan Belgrade.
For others, the funeral has rekindled painful memories of the war.

A woman in Sarajevo called Zdravka Gvozdjar - whose nine-year-old son was killed by Mladić-led forces during the siege of the city - told Reuters news agency it was "really horrible" that the funeral was taking place in Belgrade.
Mladić "deserved to be erased from memory for good, not to be... promoted as a hero," she said.
"He should be remembered only as a butcher."

Thousands attended the funeral because he "remains a figure of national pride and defiance," said Daniella Peled, Editor at the Institute of War and Peace Reporting NGO - who covered Mladić's war crimes trial in detail.

The war crimes tribunal "provided an incredibly detailed historical record of Mladić's crimes," she told the BBC, but the Serbian media and education system "has not reflected the true scale of his crimes or the perspectives of victims and survivors."
Pro-government Serbian media "depict him as a loyal soldier who simply carried out his duties," Peled said.
"It's extremely challenging for post-conflict societies to undertake a national reckoning or acknowledge responsibility for the crimes of the past."

articles.title: Russia announces it is closing Germany's consulate in St. Petersburg
articles.summary: The tit-for-tat reaction comes after Germany said it is shuttering Russia's consulate in Bonn and its cultural center in Berlin.

blocks.text: The Russian Foreign Ministry announced on Monday that it is closing Germany's consulate in St. Petersburg.
The German consulate in St. Petersburg must cease its operations by September 18 the latest, according to Russia's Foreign Ministry.

"It was the German authorities who, once again, provoked a new round of escalation in bilateral relations," the Foreign Ministry said, adding Berlin "bears full and complete responsibility" for the consequences.
The move is a direct response to Germany's closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn and Russia's cultural center in Berlin.

Germany recently announced those measures after it said Russia was responsible for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig Airport. Russia has called the idea that it is behind the attack an absurd fabrication.
More to come...

articles.title: Federal investigators search for cause of Amazon cargo jet crash that killed five
articles.summary:
Theories begin to emerge that plane may have landed too fast and too far down the runway to be able to stop in time

Federal investigators got plans under way on Monday for determining what…

blocks.text: Federal investigators got plans under way on Monday for determining what caused an Amazon cargo jet to barrel off a runway at Miami international airport on Sunday afternoon and crash, killing five people and injuring five others.

Video footage showed the jet wobbling a little and coming in fast and far along the runway, with storm clouds clearly visible in the sky behind, as expert theories began to emerge that the Boeing 767 may have landed too fast and too far down the runway to be able to stop in time.

The aircraft overshot the runway around 2pm Sunday after arriving in south Florida from San Juan, Puerto Rico, and plowed across a perimeter road used by warehouse workers and other businesses before coming to rest in a parking lot. With its nose tipped forward, flames then burst out of part of the jet and thick, dark smoke began billowing into the air.
Authorities have not named the five who died or the five people injured, three critically, or released exact details on where the casualties were located.

The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said chairwoman Jennifer Homendy would hold a news conference later on Monday. US transportation secretary Sean Duffy said on social media that the agency would “assess the scene after an Amazon cargo plane overran the runway”.

The crash trapped the pilot and copilot in the cockpit and some occupants in cars, said Miami-Dade rescue fire chief Ray Jadallah said. The agency said crews also had to extricate a person who was trapped under a vehicle.
Jadallah described the incident as a “very complex situation” where the plane crashed into multiple vehicles as it ran off the tarmac, trapping several people inside their vehicles.

Video of the Amazon Prime Air Boeing 767-33A, operated by contractor 21 Air, posted to social media show it touching down far along the runway. Other footage shows the plane with a left hand wheel on the landing gear still a little above the ground as the jet speeds down the tarmac, apparently abnormally fast, and then overruns the end of the runway, where the right undercarriage collapsed and the wing caught fire.

Typically, the landing zone is within the first 3,000 ft (914 meters) of a runway. Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said if it was beyond that area, the plane should normally have aborted the landing and gone around for another attempt.

Mary Schiavo, who is a pilot and former inspector general of the transportation department, said video posted online shows the Amazon plane floating above the runway for an extended period without flaring the nose upward to force the main landing gear onto the ground.
Storm clouds can be seen in the area and strong winds reported. Schiavo said that if the plane had a tail wind, that could have contributed to it floating further down the runway.
“A tail wind would certainly add to your troubles if you’ve already given up a good chunk of the runway by not touching down and landing right away,” Schiavo said.

Miami airport is not equipped with “arresting beds”, systems of lightweight, crushable material that the federal aviation authority (FAA) says have been installed at more than 120 airports nationwide at the end of runways to help safely stop planes that overshoot.
Some 200 emergency personnel responded to the incident, finding the plane with heavy flames and smoke from a complex engine compartment fire, the fire department said.

The flight operators, 21 Air, is a cargo carrier based in North Carolina. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines for more than two decades before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24.

More than 160 flights were canceled and nearly 325 delayed by late Sunday, according to FlightAware, a website that tracks flight disruptions. Officials from Orlando international airport, more than 200 miles north of Miami, said some flights were diverted there. Flights later resumed, although two runways at the busy airport remained out of service on Monday morning.

Kelly Nantel, an Amazon spokesperson said in a statement on Sunday: “We can confirm that an Amazon Air plane operated by 21 Air experienced an incident while attempting to land at Miami International Airport today. And Amazon said in a further statement that it would cooperate with any investigation.

“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami international airport,” the company said. “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.”

items: The Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: 'It's incredible,' Winnipeg man says after car blows over onto someone else's lawn in storm
articles.summary: A Winnipeg man says the damage left by Sunday night's thunderstorm was "overwhelming," after his vehicle rolled into the front yard of a nearby home.

image.caption: Darryl Gervais says winds during Sunday night's thunderstorm pushed his car so hard that it rolled over into a nearby lawn on Lindsay Street in Winnipeg's River Heights area. (Gavin Axelrod/CBC)

blocks.text: Manitoba·Updated
A Winnipeg man says the damage left by Sunday night's thunderstorm was "overwhelming," after his vehicle rolled into the front yard of a nearby home.
Some power outages for roughly 4,000 Hydro customers could stretch into Tuesday
High winds and heavy rains led to downed power lines and trees, particularly in Winnipeg's Westwood and River Heights areas, Hydro spokesperson Peter Chura told CBC News on Monday morning.
Sometime during the storm, Darryl Gervais says the wind pushed his Pontiac Vibe, which rolled over into a nearby lawn on Lindsay Street in the River Heights area.
Gervais said he had just finished repairs on the vehicle and left it for his son to use right before the storm hit.
"It looked wonderful, and now it doesn't," he told CBC News on Monday. "The windows are smashed, the roof is crumpled, and there's a trail of parts along the lawn."
But Gervais is glad no one was hurt, saying if the vehicle had rolled another three metres, it would have hit a house.
"It's incredible, the force of the wind that can pick up a 3,000 pound vehicle," he said.
"Yesterday, I was working on it, figuring it would last another two years."

Preliminary numbers from Environment Canada show winds in the city reached 83 kilometres per hour on Sunday night, while 35 millimetres of rain hit Winnipeg overall and The Forks got nearly 70 millimetres.
Robyn Canicula, who lives nearby on Lindsay Street, says her family may be staying in a hotel for the next few days, after the storm damaged her home just before her children head back to school.
"We can't go in the backyard because there's a power line down," Canicula told CBC News on Monday. "Our trampoline's gone, our pergola's up in a tree down the road."
The storm left destruction all over the neigbourhood, including downed power lines and trees, as well as power lines that were cut in half, she said.
"It feels like we're in a movie. It's pretty scary."
Canicula is thankful the community has come together in light of the damage, she said.

"We've had a lot of neighbors reach out," she said. "Actually, somebody's been helping my husband put a tarp on our roof and our neighbour's roof, so it's been really nice, all the support we've been getting from the community."

items: What's open and closed this Labour Day in Manitoba

blocks.text: About 4,000 customers in Winnipeg were without power on Monday morning, Hydro's Chura said.

Although crews worked through the night to repair damage and restore power to some, people in areas that suffered severe damage should expect "extended outages today and likely into tomorrow," Chura said.
"We'll assess the damage and concentrate on the damage that's going to restore the most customers to power at once, and then work our way down from there," he said.
"There's more severe weather in the forecast, so that could complicate repairs and cause further hazards for people."
Hydro is urging the public to stay away from downed powerlines and to report them to 911, said Chura.
"And remember, a downed tree can also be hiding other hazards, so stay away from those as well."
With files from Gavin Axelrod

articles.title: Nathan Fielder teases Elizabeth Holmes documentary with eyebrow-raising trailer
articles.summary: Fielder's new film about Holmes, You Can See Everything, was made with documentarian and filmmaker Lance Oppenheim and centres on the weeks leading up to Holmes's incarceration in 2023.

image.caption: Nathan Fielder, creator and executive producer of the television series The Rehearsal, arrives at the 86th annual Peabody Awards on Sunday, May 31, 2026, at the Beverly Wilshire in Beverly Hills, Calif. (Chris Pizzello/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
Fielder's new film about Holmes, You Can See Everything, was made with documentarian and filmmaker Lance Oppenheim and centres on the weeks leading up to Holmes's incarceration in 2023.
Documentary centres on weeks leading up to Holmes's incarceration following 2022 Theranos fraud conviction
If you were wondering what possible antics Nathan Fielder has been up to after watching the latest season of The Rehearsal, we have your answer.

The Vancouver-born comedian, writer and director released a teaser late Sunday for his next project, a documentary about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes who was famously convicted of fraud in 2022 after her company claimed to have created a type of blood testing that could screen for hundreds of diseases with small amounts of blood.
Fielder's film, titled You Can See Everything, was made with documentarian and filmmaker Lance Oppenheim and centres on the weeks leading up to Holmes's incarceration in 2023.
Oppenheim's previous works include Spermworld (2024), an FX-produced doc about sperm donors and Some Kind of Heaven (2020) about a Florida retirement community.

items: Theranos's Elizabeth Holmes sentenced to more than 11 years in federal prison

blocks.text: Fielder grew to fame with Nathan For You, a series on Comedy Central in which he gives horrible business advice to entrepreneurs. Previously he won (and baffled) Canadian hearts and minds with his appearances on CBC's This Hour Has 22 Minutes, in field segments titled "Nathan On Your Side" in 2008 and 2009.
You Can See Everything is being distributed by Gen Z favourite A24. The trailer features the company's signature high-saturation colour grading and overall eeriness.

It includes a roughly-one minute close-up conversation between Holmes and Fielder. The two intensely gaze at each other, as Holmes says, "Why would I deceive you? There's no — there's no reason for me to do that."
A long-ish silence follows and Fielder — with an incredulous expression on his face — says, "You're being real right now?"

The trailer was released in conjunction with a surprise screening Sunday at the Telluride Film Festival in Colorado. Reviews haven't yet surfaced from the screening, several critics posted their superlative-filled reactions to social media.

Film director Daniel Howat wrote on X after the screening that You Can See Everything "is maybe the most hysterical, shocking, insane documentary I’ve ever seen. Endlessly thought-provoking ... A work of genius."

Los Angeles-based music producer Erik Nordgren called it "easily the best film of the year for me, arguably on my best of the decade list. It turns from an uneasy-as-hell doc into something structurally, stylistically, and formally even more shocking. Like nothing I’ve ever seen."

The exchange harkens back to another uncomfortable, lesser-known interview Fielder conducted on This Hour Has 22 Minutes with former CBC president Hubert T. Lacroix in 2008. The two sit across from each other and Lacroix is put on the spot when he says he's a fan of Fielder's work but struggles to come up with any examples.
You Can See Everything is set to release in theatres next month.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Verity is a reporter for CBC in Montreal. She previously worked for the Globe and Mail, Toronto Star and the New Brunswick Telegraph-Journal.

articles.title: 26 Filipino seafarers awaiting repatriation after Ukraine attack
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines—The 26 Filipino crewmen of the bulk carrier Gingo are awaiting repatriation to the Philippines after safely disembarking following an attack while it was docked in Ukraine, the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines—The 26 Filipino crewmen of the bulk carrier Gingo are awaiting repatriation to the Philippines after safely disembarking following an attack while it was docked in Ukraine, the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) said in a statement Monday.
The DMW said that as of Sept. 4, the 26 Filipino seafarers safely disembarked from the vessel. The seafarers are currently awaiting transit to Moldova before their repatriation to the Philippines.

The DMW said it is coordinating with the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA), Philippine Embassy in Warsaw, Philippine Consulate General in Kyiv and Migrant Workers Office (MWO) in Prague to monitor the seafarers’ condition and facilitate their “safe and immediate” return, including the processing of their travel documents with Moldovan authorities and the ship owner.
Labor Attaché Llewelyn Perez said the Philippine diplomatic posts were working with Moldovan authorities and the shipowner to complete the documents needed for the crew’s return.

“The Philippine Embassy and the Philippine Consulate in Kyiv are coordinating with the relevant authorities, in partnership with the shipowner, to facilitate the processing of their travel documents,” Perez said.
The DMW said it is also coordinating with the licensed manning agency and the ship owner to address the seafarers’ immediate needs following their disembarkation.

“The DMW assures the families of the affected seafarers that it, together with its MWOs, Philippine embassies, and consulates, is facilitating the necessary arrangements for their safe return to the Philippines.” /gsg

articles.title: Germany's far-right AfD says 'democracy demands' parties work with them after state election win
articles.summary: The far-right party is trying to form a government in the state after falling three seats short of a majority.

blocks.text: The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is "very, very close" to taking power, its deputy parliamentary leader has told the BBC, after a historic victory in elections for the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.
Sunday's preliminary results show it fell three seats short of an outright majority, with 43.8% of the vote. It is now seeking support from other parties or individuals in order to govern.
While most German political parties refuse to work with the AfD, Beatrix von Storch called for its opponents to enter talks and said: "You cannot say I do not accept the vote of the people".
No far-right party has controlled a German state since World War Two, and governing at state level would mean powers over policing and local education.
Von Storch said if parties refused to work with the AfD, "then we might end up in severe chaos and maybe we have a new election".
Her comments were echoed by AfD's leader in Saxony-Anhalt, Ulrich Siegmund, who told a news conference on Monday that the party had won a "clear mandate to govern".
Saxony-Anhalt has a small population of 2.1 million and the AfD in the state is assessed by domestic intelligence as "right-wing extremist", a classification rejected by Siegmund, 35.
Siegmund said discussions with other parties were initiated on Sunday night and could potentially take days or weeks to conclude.
"We reach out to everybody first, we will have consultations and then we'll see whether [there are] individual parliamentary groups or MPs who would be willing to help us," he added.
The AfD is currently heading for 39 seats in the 83-seat state parliament instead of the 42 needed for an outright majority, although the result has not yet been finalised.

Von Storch told the BBC the AfD was talking to individuals within the conservative CDU group - the largest party in both the state's outgoing coalition and Germany's government - because they were "very, very unhappy with their own party".
In Saxony-Anhalt, the CDU won 17.2% of the vote, according to preliminary results.
One idea being floated is whether there could be informal deal whereby a small party - the BSW - could give their tacit support to allow the AfD to form a minority government.
The left-wing populist BSW, which is set to win five seats, is also tough on migration and backs importing Russian gas.
The AfD has signalled an openness to talk with other parties but all - apart from the BSW - refuse to co-operate with the far-right.
The AfD leads the opinion polls nationally, ahead of the ruling conservatives of Chancellor Friedrich Merz and the Social Democrats, but their heartland lies in the eastern states.
They also won the 2024 state election in neighbouring Thuringia, but failed to secure enough seats to win power.

Among the AfD's policies is a highly controversial plan for "remigration", which is widely understood to mean mass deportations of migrants, although the party says it refers to deporting criminals and those in the country illegally.

articles.title: Russia and North Korea open first road bridge across their shared border
articles.summary:
Connection across Tumen River is further sign of closer ties between the two countries since start of war in Ukraine

Russia and North Korea have opened

blocks.text: Russia and North Korea have opened the first road bridge across their shared border, in the latest sign of the rapidly deepening ties between the two countries since the start of the war in Ukraine.

The one-kilometre bridge spans the Tumen River between Khasan in Russia’s far east and Tumangang in North Korea, along a remote and sparsely populated stretch of the countries’ shared border just a few miles from the coast.

Speaking by video link during the bridge’s opening ceremony on Monday, Russia’s prime minister, Mikhail Mishustin, said the new crossing would spur development in a range of areas, including tourism, while creating new jobs

“I am convinced that the expansion of cross-border transport infrastructure will provide a powerful impetus for the further development of trade, economic, scientific, technological and cultural cooperation,” Mishustin said.
The road bridge is named after the Soviet officer Yakov Novichenko, who is credited with saving North Korea’s founding leader, Kim Il-sung, from an assassination attempt by a pro-South Korean group.
After the opening ceremony, convoys of vehicles crossed the bridge from both sides.
Russia and the secretive North Korea regime are already connected by a railway bridge across the Tumen, as well as regular flights between Vladivostok and Pyongyang.
Ukrainian human rights groups have warned that the bridge may be intended to provide a discreet military logistics corridor between the two countries.

Truth Hounds, a Ukrainian human rights organisation, has described it as a likely future corridor for moving North Korean troops, construction brigades and military officials into Russia, while allowing Russian technology and resources to travel in the opposite direction with less risk of detection.

Ties between Moscow and Pyongyang have strengthened dramatically since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. North Korea has sent thousands of troops to Russia’s Kursk region to help Moscow repel a Ukrainian incursion launched there in 2024.
In return, Russia is believed to have provided North Korea with air-defence missiles, electronic warfare equipment, drones and spy-satellite technology, according to South Korean intelligence.

Russian and North Korean officials have also touted North Korea as a new holiday destination since the country reopened to Russian tourists in 2024, with thousands of Russians visiting its newly opened beach resorts and ski slopes since then.
Russia’s increasingly close embrace of totalitarian North Korea has raised eyebrows even in Moscow.

During an interview with the Russian broadcaster RBC last month, a reporter asked Sergei Lavrov, Russia’s longtime foreign minister, how the country had “ended up” with just “two allies – North Korea and Iran”.
Lavrov pushed back against the premise, saying there was “nothing wrong” with such company.
At the same time, some of Russia’s traditional partners have shown growing frustration with Moscow’s continuing war in Ukraine and the fallout it has caused across the region.

During a meeting in July, Kazakhstan’s president, Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, a longtime ally of Moscow, told the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, that he was hearing from leaders of many countries who questioned why Russia was still waging the war.
“The nature of the conflict isn’t entirely clear for many, including us,” Tokayev told Putin.

articles.title: Nepal observes national day of mourning for victims of flash flood disaster
articles.summary: Flags flew at half mast on the 13th day since the disaster, the last day of the Hindu mourning period.

blocks.text: Nepalis observed a national day of mourning for the victims of the flash flood on Monday, lighting candles to mark the last day of the traditional 13-day Hindu mourning period.
While flags were flown at half mast, commemorations were scaled back as rescue teams continue to search for survivors. Candlelight vigils were planned for Monday evening.

At least 1,287 people are known to have died after a flash flood, believed to have been triggered by a glacial collapse, swept through villages in a Himalayan valley along border between Nepal and Tibet.
Almost two weeks later, more than 5,000 people are still missing.

Phanindra Paudel of the National Emergency Operation Centre (NEOC) told the Reuters news agency that there would be "no government programmes organised as the rescue and search operation is still going on in the flood-hit areas."
Nepal's president, Ram Chandra Paudel, toured areas devastated by the floods on Monday, an aide told Reuters.
The home ministry said that government offices, as well as missions abroad, would fly the national flag at half mast to mark the final day of the mourning period.

Australian tunnel rescue expert Arnold Dix, who is advising Nepali teams, said in an update on X that the operation meant facing "multiple potential rescues, unfolding at the same time, in different places, each with its own dangers, uncertainties and lives that may still be saved."
Four people have been rescued in recent days, three at hydropower stations or tunnels.
On Saturday, a 64-year-old Nepali woman was pulled from her buried house on Saturday, more than 10 days after a wall of ice, rock and mud partially buried her house in the Nuwakot district.
She was discovered alive on the fourth floor of the building by Nepal's Armed Police Force and airlifted to a hospital in Kathmandu for treatment.
On Sunday rescue workers in China recovered twelve bodies in the Nepal-Tibet border, using excavators, shovels and ground penetrating radar at the site.
At least 5,083 people are still missing in Nepal. On the Tibetan side, the death toll reported by Chinese media on Friday was 31, with 531 people unaccounted for.

articles.title: Israeli strikes on southern Lebanese town kill 11, state news agency says
articles.summary: Israeli strikes on a southern Lebanese town early on Monday killed at least 11 people including two children and two medics, Lebanon's state news agency said.

image.caption: Rescue workers search for victims under the rubble of a building destroyed in an Israeli airstrike in the southern village of Kfar Rumman, Lebanon, on Monday. (Mohammed Zaatari/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World
Israeli strikes on a southern Lebanese town early on Monday killed at least 11 people including two children and two medics, Lebanon's state news agency said.
2 children were killed in the airstrike on the town of Kfar Rumman, news report says

Israel has intensified its bombardment of south Lebanon in recent days despite a June ceasefire that was meant to halt fighting between the Israeli military and Lebanese armed group Hezbollah. At least seven people were killed in Israeli strikes on Sunday.
Just after midnight, Israeli warplanes hit a residential building in the town of Kfar Rumman in southern Lebanon, killing nine people including two children, Lebanon's National News Agency reported.
A separate Israeli drone strike on a civilian vehicle in the town killed two medics inside the car, it said.

According to The Associated Press, Lebanon's Health Ministry said one of the strikes hit a building, killing eight people — including a child and two women. It added that 11 people were also wounded, including four children and two women.
No evacuation warning

The strikes on the town came without an online evacuation warning from the Israeli military. The Israeli military did not immediately respond to Reuters' questions on the strikes, including whether it was aware of the presence of medics and children at the strike locations and why no evacuation warning was issued.

A spokesperson for the Israeli military issued a separate evacuation warning just after 2:00 a.m. local time for areas around a building in another town in southern Lebanon where it said it would strike Hezbollah facilities.

items: Israeli strikes kill 4 in southern Lebanon

blocks.text: Israeli strikes on Lebanon have killed more than 4,300 people since Hezbollah launched rockets at Israel on March 2 — two days after the start of U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran — triggering an Israeli air and ground offensive.
The ceasefire saw violence decrease dramatically, but Israeli troops occupying swathes of southern Lebanon have continued razing villages in the self-declared security zone.
Israel's military has continued carrying out strikes both within the zone and to its north, mostly without evacuation warnings.

articles.title: Weather tracker: Typhoon Saudel causes mass evacuations in south-east China
articles.summary:
Torrential rain causes widespread damage; while north-west South Africa hit by thunderstorms and central-southern US faces oppressive heat

Typhoon Saudel brought days of torrential rain to…

blocks.text: Typhoon Saudel brought days of torrential rain to the Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Fujian and Guangdong provinces in south-east China last week. The city of Putian, in Fujian province, recorded 416.5mm of rain in a 24-hour period between Thursday and Friday, with surrounding villages recording more than 500mm in the same period. In Fujian, authorities estimate that almost 600,000 people were evacuated from high-risk, flood-prone areas. A further 128,000 people in 53 counties were also affected across Jiangxi, with emergency evacuations affecting 9,000 people.

Flooding, landslips and infrastructure damage were reported widely in the region. More than 2,500 teachers and students were trapped in a school compound in the Zhejiang city of Wenzhou on Wednesday after extreme rainfall caused flash floods in low-lying areas. At least 1,260 people reportedly had to be rescued in Putian after a river embankment collapsed on Thursday, flattening 100 homes. On Saturday, a landslip in a village of Suichuan county, in Jiangxi province, killed three people and nine others remaining missing.
This is the seventh typhoon to affect China this year, and Saudel arrived shortly after Typhoon Narra dumped heavy rain on Guangdong, Hainan and Guangxi late last month.

The South African Weather Service implemented several thunderstorm warnings late last week, covering a large swathe of the northern and western provinces. Disruptive rainfall, damaging winds, excessive lightning and hail were all reported, with rainfall totals expected to have reached at least 75-100mm for parts of the Northern Cape and North West provinces over the weekend. In Johannesburg, eight families were evacuated from an apartment building after strong winds tore off a significant part of its roof.

Oppressive heat in the US affected states across the central-southern plains and the Mississippi valley this weekend, with maximum temperatures easily reaching the high 30s (Celsius; high 90s Fahrenheit). However, with high humidities, the heat indices in this region have been closer to 40-43C (105–110F). The unrelenting temperatures will continue across the midwest and southern US this week, with maximum temperatures continuing to reach the high 30s.

articles.title: How quiz-show winnings kick-started coach's career - with Old Trafford next
articles.summary: Lithuanian coach Valdas Dambrauskas cut his teeth in English football, and now returns in the Champions League with Sabah.

blocks.text: On Thursday, Valdas Dambrauskas will walk out at Old Trafford as manager of Sabah in the Champions League.
The Lithuanian's career will come full circle, some 20 years since he made his first steps into coaching with Manchester United Soccer Schools.
"This is beyond my imagination," Dambrauskas told BBC Sport. "To go through that tunnel on to that pitch.
"I've been many times to Old Trafford with the kids, and now I'm going to come as a coach."
This only scratches the surface of Dambrauskas' remarkable story.
It begins with an appearance on the Lithuanian version of Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?, Dambrauskas using his modest winnings to move to London and forge a career in football.

It is a tale of casual jobs, a determination to succeed and a nomadic coaching career across Europe - which now brings the 49-year-old back to England in the Champions League with the Azerbaijani club.
As Sabah's players and staff celebrated reaching the Champions League two weeks ago, unbeknownst to Dambrauskas he was becoming a social media star.
It all related to that appearance on Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? in 2002.
Not because he was on the show, but how he spent the money he won.
"This is so long ago," said Dambrauskas with a wry smile. "A back-in-the-year story that really was forgotten.
"And now suddenly everybody is speaking about this."
Dambrauskas walked away with 4,000 litas (about £725). That might not sound like much, but it was six months' wages to the average Lithuanian.
For Dambrauskas, the real story should be his career and not a game show.
"Everybody now takes only this part, you know, about the money," Dambrauskas said. "But yes, it is a true story.
"My idea was somehow I will try to go on these [coaching] courses to gain the coaching badge, maybe go back one day to Lithuania and start to work as a football coach."
What began with Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? would map out his whole career.
'I was doing two, three, sometimes four jobs'
Dambrauskas says he had known since the age of 12 he would not make it as a player, but coaching would keep him close to football.
He arrived in London in August 2002 aged 25 on a student visa with limited English.

What followed would be eight years of hard work where he would coach for community projects, at a semi-professional club, within professional youth programmes - and hold down multiple jobs while raising two children.
In 2004 he enrolled on a course in sports science and coaching at London Metropolitan University, the first real step in his career.
Then he started out coaching by volunteering with the Access to Sports Project for deprived children in Finsbury Park.
He went on to work with London Tigers, a charitable community organisation which runs teams from junior level right through to semi-professional.
Starting out as a volunteer, across five years he progressed to manage the first team in non-league football in the Spartan South Midlands League, FA Cup and FA Vase.
Dambrauskas became the first Lithuanian to achieve a Uefa coaching licence through the London Football Association.
"I went on every possible course, every possible conference, London Football Coaches Association meetings," Dambrauskas said.
"Everywhere I could go just to gain some information, some knowledge, some extra diploma, extra course.
"That was very important for me and I took my chances."
He got his first break at a professional club when Manchester United Soccer Schools took a chance on him in 2004.
Dambrauskas spent five years coaching on residential courses in the UK and in Europe.
"That was the best thing that could happen in my life," Dambrauskas said.
"I went through three or four interviews. I will be forever grateful to [Foundation chief executive] John Shiels, the way he gave me this chance, because I didn't have experience.
"I'd never been in a place with so many great personalities as I got in the Manchester United Soccer Schools."
After a short spell with Fulham, Dambrauskas moved to Brentford. He credits academy director Ose Aibangee as one of the biggest influences on his career, pushing his limits.
All the while he was juggling home life and working multiple jobs to make ends meet.
"I was a gardener, a handyman, doing newspaper rounds at the beginning, also polishing floors in a pub," Dambrauskas said.
"So many jobs. Working in retail, and then as a sports development officer, then a sports development manager, and the central YMCA.
"I was doing two, three, sometimes four jobs."
As well as the trip to Manchester United this week, Sabah will complete their Champions League group games at Arsenal in January.
This also feels like fate for Dambrauskas - one of the buildings at London Metropolitan University on Holloway Road overlooked Emirates Stadium.
When asked about his time in England, Dambrauskas' face lights up.
"When I hear this word 'England', it for me sounds like opportunities," Dambrauskas said.
"It was really amazing. England gave me all this and I'll forever be grateful."
Dambrauskas was working three jobs - at Brentford, London Tigers and as a sports development manager - when the opportunity arose to coach full-time.
It meant leaving England to return to Lithuania, champions Ekranas appointing him assistant first-team and reserve-team coach at the end of 2010.
After four years at Ekranas he was named manager of Zalgiris Vilnius, Lithuania's biggest club, where his career really took off.
Dambrauskas won two league titles, three Lithuanian Cups and two Lithuanian Super Cups across three seasons - including a treble in 2016.
Then came a series of moves in which Dambrauskas took charge of eight teams over nine years in seven countries.
First RFS, with whom he won the Latvian Cup, and then Gorica in Croatia.
A third league title came with Bulgarian side Ludogorets Razgrad, along with another Super Cup and Europa League qualification.
Dambrauskas then returned to Croatia with Hajduk Split, a time which he described as "absolutely amazing" as the club won the Croatian Cup - their first trophy for 10 years.
Next up was a spell in Greece with OFI Crete, then Omonia in Cyprus - who qualified for the Conference League - and Diosgyori in Hungary.
Finally, in the summer of 2025, he arrived at Sabah, the 10th club of his career.
Dambrauskas completed the league and cup double in his first season, as the club won the title for the first time.
It took his trophy tally to 13 across five countries.
Next stop, the Champions League.
Dambrauskas had to navigate four knockout ties to get Sabah to the Champions League, and they are the only club to make it all the way through from the first qualifying round.
Welsh club TNS, Finland's KuPS, Danish side Aarhus and Israel's Hapoel Beer-Sheva were all knocked out.
The final qualifying game was as dramatic as Dambrauskas' own story.
Sabah were going out, then a goal by Tellur Mutallimov in the fourth minute of stoppage time sent the tie into extra time. They went on to win 5-2 on the night and 6-4 on aggregate.
"To go to the Champions League is something beyond imagination," Dambrauskas said.

"We have never qualified for the Conference League, we have never qualified for the Europa League. We have never passed more than two rounds in a row in one competition, and now suddenly we are here."
Sabah are based in the town of Masazir - 30 miles north of the Azerbaijan capital Baku - with a population of just 19,000.
Known as the Owls, Sabah were only formed in 2017 and on Tuesday will celebrate their ninth birthday.

Like many small clubs, their Bank Respublika Arena home, with a capacity of less than 9,000, does not meet Uefa regulations. Instead, the club are expected to play their matches at the Olympic Stadium in Baku.
Sabah will host Borussia Dortmund, Barcelona and Napoli, and face a trip to Villarreal - as well as the visits to England.
"It can be a very hard draw, and it can be a Sabah draw," said Dambrauskas, clearly excited by the prospect.
"You dream for this, to play in this competition, to play against those teams.
"So now is the time to show that you can handle it, to find a way to compete and we will try to do this.
"We have a good team, we have an ambitious team, we have hungry players who are really keen to show themselves."
Sabah president Magsud Adigozalov last week was full of praise for Dambrauskas' impact.
"His influence goes beyond tactics," Adigozalov told Report. "He has instilled a mindset and winning mentality in the team.
"Even in the most difficult moments, the team never abandons its game or fighting spirit, which is the result of the coach's work."
Twenty years ago, Dambrauskas looked out over the pitch at Old Trafford during one of his job interviews, dreaming that one day he would stand in one of the dugouts.
Now his coaching career will return to where it started.
"I lived in England when the battle between Manchester United and Arsenal was the biggest rivalry. Alex Ferguson and Arsene Wenger," Dambrauskas said.
"Now I'm going to come back as a coach in the Champions League and hear that anthem. It's really amazing."

articles.title: Japanese woman goes viral for giving birth to 7th child
articles.summary: A woman in Japan went viral and captured the public’s attention after announcing the birth of her seventh child, amid the country’s falling birth rate. Japanese writer and former political candidate…

blocks.text: A woman in Japan went viral and captured the public’s attention after announcing the birth of her seventh child, amid the country’s falling birth rate.

Japanese writer and former political candidate Kotoe Hashimoto announced on social media platform X on Aug 29 that she had given birth to her seventh child, thanking the medical staff who attended to them.
The post, which includes a photo of Hashimoto cradling her newborn, has been viewed 27 million times on X and received 10,800 likes on Facebook.
In a follow-up post later the same day, she also thanked the public for their congratulatory messages.
“I believe that now is the time for Japanese women to have children,” she said. “The rise and fall of our nation depends on the active role of women.”
Her post struck a chord among the Japanese.

“I think you’re absolutely right. I feel that the key to changing the current state of Japan, which is heading towards (demographic) collapse, is precisely the conscience of Japanese women,” Facebook user Etsugaku Kankou replied to her post.
Another user, Hideto Umegaki, said: “It’s a national treasure to give birth to seven children.”

Hashimoto, who ran as a candidate under the Party of Hope during the 2017 general election, has used her social media accounts to discuss the country’s demographic challenges and advocating for Japanese women to have more children.
She was not elected, and the conservative party, which was founded by Tokyo Governor Yuriko Koike, disbanded in October 2021.
The baby’s birth comes as Japan’s fertility rate fell to a fresh record low in 2025, extending a decade-long slide despite years of government efforts to reverse the trend.

The total fertility rate – the average number of children a woman is expected to have over her childbearing years – slipped to 1.14 from 1.15 a year earlier, according to data by the country’s Welfare Ministry.
The reading was the lowest since comparable records began in 1947.

Japan, one of the world’s oldest societies, faces mounting demographic pressures. A shrinking workforce and rising social security costs are placing strain on public finances at a time when the government is also seeking to fund higher defence spending and other growth initiatives. /dl

articles.title: Crowds gather for war criminal Ratko Mladic’s funeral in Belgrade
articles.summary: BELGRADE — Crowds began gathering in Belgrade on Monday morning for the funeral of convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic, as Brussels accused some in the country of “glorification” of…

blocks.text: BELGRADE — Crowds began gathering in Belgrade on Monday morning for the funeral of convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic, as Brussels accused some in the country of “glorification” of a man convicted of genocide during the 1990s war in Bosnia.
Mladic died in late August, aged 84, while serving a life sentence in The Hague for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity committed during the war in Bosnia.
Mourners streamed into St Luka church in Belgrade from 7am (0500 GMT) to pay respects, with many kissing Mladic’s closed coffin, as Serbian Orthodox priests read prayers.
Police had closed off streets in the surrounding part of the city as crowds began arriving.
AFP reporters saw large crowds outside the church, many wearing shirts praising Mladic, as doors opened with aerial images showing hundreds already queuing to enter.
Serbian flags had been hung nearby, and a huge banner unfurled across the street read: “Welcome, General, thanks be to your mother for bearing a hero, so that Serbdom’s glory may return.”
“I am here to see off the general, a national hero,” pensioner Radojka Visic, who had travelled from Bosnia’s Serb entity, Republika Srpska, told AFP.
“They couldn’t defeat us on the battlefield, so they sent him to prison and tortured him there instead,” Visic said, referring to the “international community”.
Backlash
Mladic’s casket arrived in the country last week aboard a government plane, where it had been carried by six soldiers and draped in flags.
As it was driven from the airport in a motorcade, groups of young men held banners praising the former general, and some police were seen saluting as it passed.

Last week’s scenes drew condemnation from the European Union’s enlargement commissioner, Marta Kos, who cancelled a forthcoming visit to Serbia on Friday, saying the “glorification surrounding his death is incompatible with the values on which the EU path is built”.
Denis Becirovic, chairman of Bosnia’s tripartite presidency, called it “an act of identification by Serbia’s leadership with one of the worst killers in European history”.
“This has unforeseeable consequences for the future of the entire region,” he wrote on Facebook on Friday.
Mladic’s wartime atrocities during the break-up of the former Yugoslavia earned him the nickname “Butcher of Bosnia” in international media.
The 1992-1995 war left around 100,000 people dead and displaced 2.2 million.
Mladic was the military figurehead of the Bosnian Serb leadership alongside former Yugoslav president Slobodan Milosevic and Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic.
The United Nations war crimes court convicted him of genocide over the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, where Bosnian Serb forces killed around 8,000 Bosnian Muslim men and boys in a UN-protected safe zone.
The atrocity was Europe’s worst act of bloodshed since World War II.
Fadila Efendic, whose son and husband were killed in Srebrenica, told AFP earlier that it pained her “to know that his ideas are not dead”.

Mladic was also convicted of persecuting and forcibly expelling Bosnian Muslims and Croats, terrorising civilians during the siege of Sarajevo and taking UN peacekeepers hostage during NATO air strikes in 1995.
‘Hero’
Mladic was arrested in 2011, 16 years after he was first indicted, and sentenced to life in prison in 2021 after a nine-year trial.
Despite the verdicts, he is still hailed as a hero by some Serbs, particularly in Republika Srpska, where his death was marked with vigils and gatherings.
Many from the entity have applied to travel to Belgrade for the funeral.
Mladic’s son Darko, who is officially organising the funeral, said he was “proud of the role” his father played.
On Saturday, around 300 people gathered at a commemoration for Mladic at a military facility in Belgrade, organised by an association of retired and active Serbian army generals.
Darko and other family members also attended, as well as Serbian Justice Minister Nenad Vujic and officials from Republika Srpska, including President Sinisa Karan.
Speakers at the ceremony praised Mladic’s wartime role, describing him as a “towering figure both as a man and a soldier”.
Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic said that tens of thousands of people were expected to attend the funeral and that the state would ensure the event passed “safely”.
He would not attend in person due to a prior engagement, he explained. /dl

articles.title: Man given 6 months to live; spends it finding home for autistic son
articles.summary: SINGAPORE — Jeon Gyeong-cheol, the author widely known as the “Peter Pan Dad” for documenting his search for a home where his disabled son could live after his death, died Saturday.…

blocks.text: SINGAPORE — Jeon Gyeong-cheol, the author widely known as the “Peter Pan Dad” for documenting his search for a home where his disabled son could live after his death, died Saturday. He was 64 and had been fighting late-stage liver cancer.

Jeong Yu-jin, head of the Developmental Disabilities Support Expert Forum, announced Jeon’s death on social media Sunday, saying the funeral would be held without a formal wake, in accordance with his wishes.
“He is currently at the hospital, and no separate memorial hall will be set up. We extend our deepest condolences,” she wrote.
Jeon spent more than two decades as the sole caregiver for his son, who is now 27 and has autism, with his developmental level assessed as that of a 2- or 3-year-old.

After receiving a terminal diagnosis of late-stage liver cancer in April last year, Jeon traveled across the country, reaching out to nearly 1,000 care facilities in hopes of finding a place that could look after his son once he was gone. Few, however, were able to take him in.

Jeon later began writing about his search on the content publishing platform Brunch, and his accounts struck a chord with many readers. His story soon reached a wider audience through television programs including MBC’s “True Story Expedition” and tvN’s “You Quiz on the Block.”
Jeon later compiled his writings on Brunch into the essay collection “Annyeong, Peter Pan,” published in June.

Readers moved by his story raised some 80 million won ($59,000) in donations, and with growing nationwide support, Je-won was able to move into a community village for people with profound developmental disabilities.

“I want to tell him to forget about his dad and live happily. But I don’t want him to forget me completely. I hope he remembers me with a faint sense of longing, as an old man who once looked at him with warmth,” Jeon said on “You Quiz on the Block” last month.
Jeon also sought to help families facing struggles similar to his own, working to establish a welfare foundation for adults with severe autism-related disabilities, like his son.

On Aug. 26, shortly before his death, he announced the launch of a preparatory committee for the foundation. With the committee now in place, its members are expected to carry on Jeon’s efforts and continue discussions on launching the foundation, according to news reports. /dl

articles.title: Israeli strikes in southern Lebanese village kill 11, state media say
articles.summary: Lebanon says renewed attacks jeopardise a US-brokered ceasefire meant to end the conflict between Israel and armed group Hezbollah.

blocks.text: Israeli air strikes on a village in southern Lebanon have killed at least 11 people, including two children, Lebanese state media say.

Nine people were killed in one strike that destroyed a three-storey residential building in Kfar Rumman shortly after midnight, while two paramedics were killed in a second strike on a car, according to the National News Agency.
The Israeli military said it was looking into the reports.

On Sunday, Israeli strikes killed seven people in southern Lebanon, as the Israeli military retaliated for what it said were drone attacks by the armed group Hezbollah on its troops in occupied areas of the country.

Lebanese President Joseph Aoun warned that the attacks were a "dangerous escalation" that jeopardised the US-brokered ceasefire agreed in June, which was meant to end the conflict between Israel and Hezbollah.

articles.title: How climate change and food insecurity could fuel conflicts
articles.summary: The world’s food system is under growing stress, and new research is pointing to areas where this could lead to conflict. Severe droughts and extreme weather are damaging harvests in many…

blocks.text: The world’s food system is under growing stress, and new research is pointing to areas where this could lead to conflict.

Severe droughts and extreme weather are damaging harvests in many regions. A developing El Niño event is even threatening to worsen food shortages for millions of people next year. At the same time, wars and geopolitical tensions are disrupting supply chains that keep food and farm supplies moving.
The war in Ukraine has repeatedly shaken grain markets, while the Iran war’s impact on the Strait of Hormuz has driven up fuel and fertilizer prices, increasing costs for farmers everywhere.

Experts have long warned that rising food insecurity could fuel instability. When people can no longer feed their families, they argue over land, water, and other resources — or they move. In fragile countries, these pressures can contribute to social unrest and even armed conflict.

Now, new research has suggested where some of these risks are greatest. The Climate-Driven Agricultural Decline Index (CADI), developed by Laura Mayoral, Hannes Mueller and colleagues, maps how climate change is reshaping agricultural productivity around the world. “The heaviest losses are in the tropical regions,” said Mueller, a researcher at the Institute for Economic Analysis and the Barcelona School of Economics.

Climate change is already reducing food production in many parts of the world. Hundreds of millions of people live in areas where harvests are smaller than 30 years ago. Mueller mentioned Australia, Argentina, Moldova, Nigeria, Romania, the United States, and Sudan as countries where agricultural losses are already being felt.
“Northern Africa is another region we should pay much more attention to. If you look at the map, it just looks terrible. It really looks horrible,” he said.
And climate change is only one part of the story. Wars, trade disruptions, export bans, and rising fertilizer costs can magnify food insecurity.
Within the next 25 years, nearly half of the world’s people could be living in areas where farms are producing less food.
New winners, losers, and conflicts

These pressures can undermine governments, help cause migration, and make it easier for armed groups to recruit fighters. In societies that are already unstable, such factors can push them toward crisis.

Yet CADI’s research points to a surprising reality: Gains in agricultural productivity also appear to increase the risk of violence. Mueller said the key issue is not just scarcity, but change. The climate crisis and other shocks do not simply make some regions poorer. They also create new opportunities, changing the value of land and resources.
In some places, land that had been marginal becomes more productive and more valuable. And that attracts investors and produces competition for ownership and access.

So countries that appear to benefit overall may face new tensions. Sudan, for example, is projected to produce more food as the climate changes. But while some areas could become more productive, others may suffer losses, creating new winners and losers within the country and increasing the risk of conflict.

This looming instability, Mueller said, also applies to areas where the change in productivity hasn’t even happened yet. “If we know that your land is going to become more productive, maybe I want to grab it from you today. That is exactly where negotiations break down and where we will have violence,” he said.

Even in stable, wealthy regions, the climate crisis is creating future problems. It may seem trivial, but the change in grape-growing options in Europe is affecting local farmers. Major producers of sparkling wine have started to buy up land in mountainous regions.

“It is not productive yet, but they already know where future grape harvests will be,” Mueller said. “Big agricultural companies are buying land. This is happening all over the world. Locals are displaced because large producers come in, land prices rise, and you start having fights about something that is still 20 or 30 years in the future.”

One of the CADI team’s most striking findings is that agricultural change is more likely to lead to conflict in non-democracies. When climate shocks, food insecurity, and competition over resources hit democracies, they tend to have institutions that force competing interests to negotiate rather than fight.

“Democracies may look annoying and cumbersome. Nothing moves as fast as people want. But this is a great thing because it makes people talk to each other,” Mueller said. “There is a platform for negotiation. There are institutions that help people negotiate. That process of constantly finding solutions is at the heart of what prevents conflict.”
South Asia as a warning sign

“We do not pay enough attention to the threats to the source of our livelihoods,” said Abdullah Fahimi of the think tank German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP). “These threats can trigger major crises and displace millions and millions of people. The regions we should watch most closely are South Asia and the Sahel, where climate vulnerability and rapid population growth mean the number of people affected could rise dramatically.”

blocks.caption: As India counts its population, researchers warn that climate change could make it harder for parts of the country to produce enough food for a growing number of people Image: Diptendu Dutta/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Fahimi said South Asia stands out because it depends on both vulnerable water supplies and global food markets. Food prices have already risen significantly over the past decades. “South Asia, with a population of around 2 billion, is highly dependent on imports,” he added. Those imports include wheat, maize, and palm oil from countries including Russia, Ukraine, Canada, and Malaysia.
At the same time, local agriculture is increasingly threatened by heat waves, floods, declining land productivity, and saltwater intrusion from rising sea levels.

As well as the immediate human toll, events such as the devastating floods that struck Nepal in August 2026 offer a glimpse of the long-term challenges that could become more common in the future. “The Himalayas and the Hindu Kush mountain ranges supply most of the water for agriculture and drinking water in the region,” Fahimi said. “Because of climate change, the glaciers and snow are melting very fast.”
In the short term, meltwater could increase water availability. But later in the century, he warned, the region could face “a huge humanitarian crisis that could affect around 2 billion people.”

blocks.caption: Farmland was covered in mud after severe flooding along Nepal’s Bhotekoshi River in late August Image: Ambir Tolang/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: As food insecurity deepens, the social and political consequences can multiply. “When resource scarcities or the impacts of climate change force people to look for other livelihood opportunities, sometimes they end up being hired by terrorist groups,” said Fahimi, who cited examples from Nigeria and Afghanistan.

In other cases, public frustration is directed at governments if they fail to mitigate the effects on people’s livelihoods. Their legitimacy is questioned, and this can escalate into violent conflict.

That echoes Mueller’s broader conclusion. Climate change, wars, and trade disruptions do not automatically lead to conflict. But climate adaptation cannot just be about growing different crops or using new technologies. People and societies also need to adapt to changes in who has access to land, water and jobs.

The key question is whether societies have institutions that can manage these changes. Where governments, courts, and local institutions can help communities negotiate new realities, shocks may be absorbed. Where those institutions are weak, the pressure on food systems may become a pressure on peace itself. /dl

articles.title: Germany, Kosovo unite against ticks carrying deadly virus
articles.summary: It can spot its prey from up to 200 meters (about 650 feet) away — but unlike many of its fellow species, it doesn’t lurk in the grass waiting for its victim to come closer. Instead it runs…

blocks.text: It can spot its prey from up to 200 meters (about 650 feet) away — but unlike many of its fellow species, it doesn’t lurk in the grass waiting for its victim to come closer. Instead it runs after it, chasing animals and humans alike.

The Hyalomma tick, often called “the great hunting tick,” was previously found mostly in Africa, Asia, and southern Europe. But climate change means it can now survive further north and it has already been spotted in Germany and various Eastern European countries. Kosovo, in southeastern Europe, has been a hot spot for the tick for some time now.

The Hyalomma tick is also a vector of the highly pathogenic virus for Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, a potentially deadly disease with a high fatality rate. Symptoms of the disease are comparable to those of Ebola fever or the Marburg virus. These are capable of destroying blood and lymphatic vessels, which can lead to internal bleeding and death.

Kurtesh Sherifi first read about Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever in the newspaper in 2005, when he was completing his studies as a veterinarian in Berlin. The article said that 11 people in his homeland, Kosovo, had contracted the disease and five had died. He was already interested in pathogens that can be transmitted between animals and humans, known as zoonoses, and Crimean-Congo fever intrigued him.

Back home, Sherifi started work with the faculty of agriculture and veterinary medicine at the University of Pristina. But the budget for research was tight. Kosovo, a small country with only about 1.6 million citizens, didn’t have a high-security laboratory or the equipment necessary for investigating the Crimean-Congo fever virus.
Seeking German cooperation
Sherifi got in touch with Germany’s largest institution for study in this area, the Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine in Hamburg.

One of the researchers was Petra Emmerich, a virologist and expert on what are known as Risk Group 4 viruses — viruses that cause severe, often fatal, diseases and usually have no widely available treatment. The Crimean-Congo virus is in that risk group.

Emmerich also acts as a reservist in the German military, which is especially interested in viruses that could be used as biological weapons. She was sent to Kosovo in 2009, which is when she met Sherifi.

blocks.caption: While the much smaller common longhorn beetle (left) waits for a suitable victim to pass by, the Hyalomma tick prefers to go hunting Image: Fabian Sommer/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A lively exchange began between the researchers. In Kosovo, a structure was established to monitor the spread of the Hyalomma tick and the virus. In 2013, the researchers’ joint work began to receive funding through the German Biosecurity Program, run by the country’s Foreign Ministry and “intended to help partner countries tackle biological threats.”

“It’s give and take,” said Emmerich of the scientific partnership. “We have the diagnostic expertise and the necessary resources but we don’t have the patients.” Doctors from Germany regularly come to Kosovo with Emmerich where they can exchange information with their counterparts there.
Raising public awareness is another important pillar of the Germany-Kosovo cooperation.

Farmers in Kosovo are particularly susceptible to infection — and not solely due to ticks biting them, but because they often use their bare hands to remove ticks from animals. If infected blood from the animals gets into a small wound on the human hand, the virus can be transmitted to the human.
“This is quite likely how a large proportion of the [infected] population in Kosovo got infected,” Sherifi explained.
Patients require intensive care, isolation
He and Emmerich have visited schools to educate students about the dangers of the virus and how to protect against it. For example, certain tick repellents help, as do long pants and sturdy shoes.

Not all Hyalomma ticks carry the virus, and most people who are bitten by a Hyalomma tick do not become ill. However, the larger problem is that there is neither a vaccine nor any specific course of treatment for those who do end up suffering from Crimean-Congo fever.

blocks.caption: Farmers in Kosovo are at particular risk from the Hyalomma ticks Image: Idro Seferi

blocks.text: “If you do get sick, it’s particularly severe,” Emmerich explained. The disease begins with nonspecific, flu-like symptoms including fever, chills, aches and headaches. In severe cases, a patient will begin bleeding from the skin, nose and gums and may also experience gastrointestinal bleeding. The worst causes can result in organ failure.
Patients require intensive care and isolation because they are highly contagious.

Much of the treatment in intensive care focuses on maintaining a patient’s vital functions, but they are also given the antiviral drug, ribavirin. But, as Emmerich said, “ribavirin is not all that effective in acutely ill patients.” That is something the scientists have seen firsthand with cases in Kosovo.

The best answer is prevention, which is why it’s also very important for the researchers to monitor the spread of the Hyalomma ticks and for them to recommend avoiding certain areas where the ticks are prevalent, if possible.
Successful tick tactics

Over the years, the researchers have not only collected thousands of the ticks but they have also conducted so-called seroprevalence studies. These use blood tests to find antibodies from past infections. This allows the scientists to determine whether humans or animals have come in contact with the virus.

Farm animals are particularly suitable for this type of study, Sherifi said, as the virus doesn’t affect them. And unlike wild animals and humans, they usually remain in a clearly defined area. That means that if antibodies are detected in the blood of these animals, it’s clear the virus is circulating in that area.

In Kosovo, the number of serious infections has dropped drastically in the past decade, amounting to just five cases in total. In the previous decade, there were about 100 cases. Sherifi and Emmerich believe this indicates how successful their work has been.
Of course, that doesn’t mean the ticks and the virus won’t spread further in Europe, and the researchers both expect this to happen.
Hyalomma ticks with the Crimean-Congo virus have just been detected in France although, so far, no humans have been infected there.
“Over the past 13 years, Hyalomma ticks have spread geographically,” said Emmerich. “As a virologist, that’s something to think about, and it needs to be closely monitored.”

This is why it’s important for the German and Kosovar scientists to pass on what they’ve learned to countries that haven’t yet had as much experience monitoring the Hyalomma ticks, such as Macedonia and Albania. /dl
